Cavity magnomechanics provides a setting for exploring the macroscopic quantum effects by combining two main components - a magnetic material and a microscopic membrane. We study how two-dimensional magnetic materials, specifically with an antiferromagnetic structure, can be used to create specific quantum states through the conversion of magnetic spin angular momentum into mechanical motion. We examine the time-dependent dynamics of the magnetic system and the membrane in two scenarios, one where the system is closed and loses energy, and another with an external drive that maintains energy balance. In both situations, we show how to regulate the coupling between the magnetic material, membrane, and electromagnetic field to produce distinct quantum states, such as entangled states and states with a specific overlap. We propose an experiment to verify our theoretical predictions using a device that combines a Heisenberg antiferromagnetic material and a optical microcavity. Due to its gapped magnetic spectrum, this system offers advantages over other magnomechanical devices, making it more suitable for exploring the characteristics of cavity magnomechanics. We estimate that the creation of coupled optical photons and magnons will be observable with currently available technology. In particular, we propose an experiment where we use a 3D printed Y-MnO$_2$ compound in an optical microcavity to demonstrate the interconversion between magnetic spin and mechanical motion, thus illustrating the unique properties of cavity magnomechanics with two-dimensional antiferromagnets. We calculate the timescales for certain processes - from one type of momentum to another - and find them to be in the millisecond range, which is long enough to study these phenomena individually. Additionally, we present some interesting properties related to a quantum black-box and non-equilibrium dynamics, which appear in this type of cavity magnomechanics system. It provides a new tool for research in quantum mechanics, by using a complex system that is still within the quantum realm, to understand how microscopic changes affect the mechanical motion at a larger scale. In other words, it is a new tool for studying the connection between magnetic material and membrane in the cavity. This research has many potential applications, particularly those related to advanced technology and fundamental studies. In the future, it may be possible to extend the principles of this research to other types of magnomechanics by incorporating other magnetic materials, thus opening up new avenues for research. The success of this method is measured by the robot's ability to replicate a variety of versatile movements, including walking and running gaits, while its reinforcement learning training is significantly simplified. The central black hole of the Seyfert galaxy NGC 7213 has exhibited varying low-brightness states over the years. In 2017, when the galaxy was in this state, an intense and hot wind with a temperature of approximately 0.65 keV and velocity of about 0.01 times the speed of light was detected by the Chandra X-ray telescope. This wind is believed to be responsible for broadening the emission lines observed in the wind-probing absorption features, specifically in this case, affecting Fe XXVI and Fe XXV K-alpha lines. Projections indicate that this wind could potentially expel gas from the galaxy at a rate of around 2 solar masses per year. This study is the first to identify this wind by analyzing its effects on the absorption features in the X-ray spectrum using high-resolution data from the Hitomi and XMM-Newton telescopes. It's proposed that this wind is likely to originate from the accretion disk, with a radius of approximately 10 to 100 times the Schwarzschild radius of the black hole. This discovery is significant, offering new insights into the existence and behavior of a hot accretion disk wind from an active galactic nucleus. At the same time, the properties of this wind are not consistent with predictions by models assuming a multi-component wind structure, with a cooler and less dense electron wind. Therefore, modifications are necessary to these models to explain the observed properties of this wind. This study offers a significant understanding of the physical processes of a specific type of wind from black holes in galaxies, with implications for understanding broader astronomical phenomena. The discovery also paves the way for future observations and studies using next-generation telescopes, such as the James Webb Space Telescope and the Athena X-ray Observatory. These future observations have the potential to address important questions about the role of this type of wind in the galaxy at various scales and its impact on its chemical evolution. At the same time, simulations using computational models of galaxy formation, such as the Illustris Magnum project, need to be revised to account for this type of wind in order to produce accurate synthetic spectra that can be compared with observed spectra. Therefore, the discovery presents new challenges and opportunities to deepen our understanding of the universe. The findings also emphasize the need for continued observational and theoretical studies using a multi-messenger approach that incorporates radio, optical, ultra-violet, X-ray, and gamma-ray data. This will be crucial for fully interpreting the results of the current study and understanding the universe at all scales.

Advanced control systems are becoming increasingly nonlinear, due to factors like technological advancements and performance requirements. To meet these demands, a novel model-free reinforcement learning approach has been developed for adjusting the structure of nonlinear optimal regulators. The technique involves an interactive learning process between two agents: a policy improvement agent and a structure optimization agent. The policy improvement agent uses live data from their interactions with a black-box system to refine the controller's gain parameters through a direct search method. The structure optimization agent assesses the effectiveness of various structural configurations and selects the best one based on the policy improvement agent's performance. In return, the structure optimization agent provides the policy improvement agent with a simplified system model and a revised set of feasible gain parameters. This two-phase approach results in a significant reduction in the number of trials required to achieve optimal performance, when compared to traditional structure-and-control-sequencing methods. The effectiveness of this approach was demonstrated in a simulation test using a aircraft landing gear system. When applied to a model-free system, this two-phase approach achieved an average 99% reduction in the number of trials required to achieve close-to-optimal performance. Furthermore, this approach resulted in a 52% reduction in the difference between the desired and actual performance in a given task. The application of this two-phase approach to a model-based system yielded an average 98% reduction in the number of trials required to achieve close-to-optimal performance, as well as a 45% reduction in the performance gap. The combination of this approach with a model-based technique achieved an average 99% reduction in the number of trials required to achieve close-to-optimal performance, as well as a 54% reduction in the performance gap. The developer of this two-phase approach noted that one challenge to adopting it is the requirement for simultaneous interaction between the structure optimization and policy improvement agents. To address this, a variant of this approach was developed, using pre-compiled data and allowing the policy improvement agent to process the data independently, without real-time input from the structure optimization agent. The efficacy of this variant was demonstrated in a simulation test using an aircraft landing gear system. When applied to a model-free system, this variant resulted in a 98% reduction in the number of trials required to achieve close-to-optimal performance, as well as a 53% reduction in the performance gap. This paper introduces a new framework called AbuseCode, which utilizes a form of artificial neural network called a variational autoencoder to create a comprehensive representation of the code. This representation, also known as a latent space, enables the detection of abuse and the identification of similar codes. Our results demonstrate that including surrounding code in the analysis enhances abuse detection and code similarity identification. Experiments conducted on a large dataset of 3.43 million Java methods from the Maven repository showcase the effectiveness of our approach. Moreover, a survey of 24 developers revealed that nearly 58% prefer using the latent space representation for code analysis. Based on these findings, AbuseCode automatically selects the most relevant parts of the code for a developer-specified API client and provides an overview of similar codes. This tool is now available for public use at https://github.com/sadipgquader/AbuseCode.  Currently, this framework supports Java and our team is working on integrating it into an Integrated Development Environment, or IDE, for wider application.  This integration includes a deep learning-based method to automatically specify the most relevant parts of the code for analysis.  This enhancement enables our framework to detect API abuse and identify similar codes within large code bases with minimal manual effort.  This research is currently underway.  This novel approach offers several contributions:  (1) detection of API abuse via local and global analysis, (2) automatic code generation to mitigate API abuse via local analysis, (3) detection of similar codes and Latent Dirichlet Allocation, or LDA, topics for large code bases with minimal varying code parts, and (3) a plethora of new features for detecting API abuse.  This research will be presented at the 2022 IEEE/ACM Technical Conference on Software Engineering.  This paper has been accepted for publication.  This acceptance offers several implications. By incorporating the forward-backward algorithm and the extrapolation technique from Anderson acceleration, we develop a globally convergent method that outperforms existing inertial schemes. Furthermore, we provide a globally convergent primal-dual version of DWIFOB and show through numerical tests that it surpasses the performance of primary competitors in optimization and variational inequality problems. The implementation details are also detailed for this new algorithm. Ultimately, we prove that DWIFOB can be robustly implemented using a proximal method. Our research focuses on the most challenging class of monotone inclusion problems, which involve nonsmooth objectives and operators with specific structural properties. We achieve this by employing variational inequality problems as a testing ground. Key to our approach is the strategically selected bundle of variables used in the forward-backward algorithm, which enables global convergence when combined with Anderson acceleration, and allows us to efficiently solve the monotone inclusion problem. A detailed analysis and an extensive set of numerical test cases are also included to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm. This paper addresses the issue of efficient spectrum use in multi-user millimeter wave systems. To tackle this, we explore hybrid encoding methods that combine pre-coding and post-coding techniques with multi-group broadcasting. Our analysis indicates that these encoding methods offer significant reductions in overall encoding complexity while maintaining optimal data transmission performance. Notably, in scenarios where user spatial relationships remain constant, we observe that post-coding techniques remain largely unchanged, enabling recursive applications and substantial complexity reductions. Our findings suggest that hybrid encoding strategies offer a more practical solution for implementing complex mmWave systems. Simulated results demonstrate the efficacy of these encoding methods in achieving robust and efficient data transmission performance. Our research provides crucial insights into the design and implementation of mmWave access points and user devices, enabling them to achieve optimal data transmission performance with reduced complexity. Additionally, this approach enables a significant reduction in the number of antennas required for mmWave transmission. Our research has further identified a novel problem, known as the generalized matrix rank problem, and proposed a feasible algorithm to resolve this issue, ultimately contributing to the development of more sophisticated mmWave hybrid encoding techniques that can be applied across various service scenarios. Furthermore, our study has successfully extended the principles of hybrid encoding to 5G New Radio systems, encompassing diverse scenarios such as NR-only, coexistence with NR, and interference from NR systems, showcasing the versatility of this approach in real-world 5G deployments. To showcase the real-world applicability of our research, we have successfully designed an actual hardware prototype, featuring a 28GHz mmWave broadcasting system with hybrid encoding, and has demonstrated the efficacy of this approach in practical mmWave transmission scenarios. Our research presents an award-winning solution, titled "Hybrid Encoding for Millimeter Wave Broadcast, " which was recognized with the 2022 IEEE PIMRC'22 Best Paper Award. Federated Averaging is the most widely used technique in model federated learning. Yet, it has a significant drawback: each round necessitates a data transfer phase between the central server and edge devices. Considering the vast number of devices involved, mirror sampling on the server side can lead to exorbitant data transfer volumes and prolonged computation times at the server. To address this, we introduce Communication-Effective Federated Distillation (CEFD), a refined protocol based on Federated Distillation, which separates the data transfer process into fewer, collectively manageable segments. We propose two primary strategies to reduce communication overhead. Firstly, we control the data volume transmitted per round by selecting representative data. Secondly, we compress model information for efficient data exchange. Our protocol is designed to offer flexible tradeoffs between communication efficiency and model performance, thereby adapting well to scenarios with a varying number of devices and data availability. The proposed protocol demonstrates superior performance in real-world applications, specifically in image classification and conversation modeling, when compared to traditional Federated Averaging. CEFD achieves a communication overhead reduction of up to 97% with only a 1% performance increase on the Flickr8k image classification dataset. Furthermore, CEFD succeeds in training models with as few as 5 data samples per device, underscoring its potential in other data-constrained federated learning applications. The full source code and demonstration can be accessed via the link: https://github.com/pkoper/CEFD. The empirical evaluation on conversation models, specifically in dialogue synthesis, yielded a 94% reduction in communication overhead with only a 2% improvement in performance. The central server computed a $2.52\times$ faster model compared to traditional Federated Averaging. The model complexity increase was achieved with minimal 1% character error rate improvement, demonstrating the efficacy of CEFD. The empirical results reveal the efficacy of CEFD in various use cases, showcasing its ability to balance communication efficiency and model performance while offering the flexibility to adapt to scenarios with different numbers of devices and data availability. The proposed protocol offers a communication overhead reduction of up to 94% with only a 2% performance increase in certain natural language tasks. The notable achievement of CEFD in reducing communication overhead while maintaining satisfactory model performance, along with its capability to adapt to diverse federated learning scenarios, makes it an attractive alternative to traditional model averaging techniques. Notably, this phenomenon can occur even if the external influences remain limited in magnitude. Our study focuses on the case where all edges have the same geometry and the connections to the central point differ only in length. In risk-aware reinforcement learning with complete information, we address the challenge of developing efficient reinforcement learning algorithms for risk measures, such as Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall. These algorithms achieve a dynamic regret bound of at most $O(\sqrt{T\log(T)})/\Delta)$ under non-stationarity and $O(T^{3/4})/$\Delta) in stationary environments, with $\Delta$ being the minimum reward difference and $T$ being the time horizon. Our work notably closes the gap for non-stationary risk-aware RL by achieving the same rate as for stationary environments. Furthermore, we introduce an adaptive protocol for reward identification, which can be integrated into existing algorithms, with a sample complexity of $O((\log^3 \Delta) / \Delta^2)$. Additionally, we introduce a concept of risk-functional design, allowing for pre-defined risk functions to be optimized with improved sample efficiency. Our results are validated by performance benchmarks on Grid World and 3x3 Muesli Race environments. The code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/nchen-adsl/risk-rlr. Näkel et al. (2022) presented the initial version of this work in the 37th Conference on Learning Theory. This paper presents additional findings and proofs not present in the initial version. The findings include a generalized framework for risk-aware RL, a sample-efficient protocol for risk identification, and a disentanglement method for separation and policy design. The proofs provide a clear and structured explanation of the paper's results, with key differences from previous works as follows: Developing a dynamic regret bound for risk measures by employing a novel combination of Certified Relative Entropy Policy Improvement and Relative Entropy Policy Search, with no known alternative method to establish the $O(\sqrt{T\log(T)})/\Delta)$ bound; Integrating a reward identification protocol to adapt to unknown reward functions, with the identification protocol developing a concept of "Risk-Functional Design" to optimize predefined risk functions with improved sample efficiency; Introducing a disentanglement method to separate the state space and design policies using only observed data, with the ability to handle complex risk measures like Expected Shortfall; Showcasing the effectiveness of our approach by benchmarking our results against state-of-the-art RL tools on Grid World and 3x3 Muesli Race environments. Software development projects frequently encounter unforeseen issues that deviate from planned progress, requiring teams to switch to problem management to mitigate these challenges.  Analyzing public Jira data for 12 open-source projects across four technologies reveals that the majority of teams using this approach have implemented problem management either by design or incidentally.  However, implementing alternative problem tracking effectively depends on various factors, including awareness of existing solutions.  Through an in-depth examination of the interconnections between problems and their attributes, our investigation sheds light on the composite nature of these issues and provides actionable suggestions for teams considering alternative problem tracking systems.  Ultimately, our findings underscore the importance of tailored processes adapted from ongoing work in individual projects.

We then imposed physical limitations on these elements, specifically s-process and r-process nuclei, applying pre-Galactic abundance limits to derive new constraints on nuclear reactions. I'll break down the argument in van Fraassen's book "Scientific Questions" by addressing two primary concerns. Firstly, I'll address his claim that all epistemic models of probability are either Jensen or Saumon measures. Secondly, I'll examine his proposal of 'honesty' as a necessary condition for ascribing probability, which I'll subsequently contest. Ultimately, I'll introduce two types of models that contradict these claims - the Klein model and the Eberlein-Strzelczkowski model. The former refutes the notion that probability can only be expressed as a Jensen or Saumon measure, while the latter challenges the idea that an honest condition is required for ascribing probability. Additionally, these models highlight potential issues with van Fraassen's notion of 'concealment', which I'll discuss. Finally, I'll use these models to address a broader query regarding the epistemological status of singular probability statements. This treatment is part of a larger research endeavor that examines how these models can inform our understanding of the epistemology of such statements. Stephen K. The integration of Train and Test Duration Augmentation (TDAA) enables our model to adapt to diverse time horizons and data sequences. Comparing our augmented model with non-augmented alternatives, we demonstrate substantial improvements in prediction accuracy, particularly in scenarios with limited data availability. Our findings showcase the efficacy of TDAA in enhancing social network forecasting while also highlighting potential pitfalls in using multi-step forecasting models without considering the impact of sequence length. Ultimately, we show that a single neural network model capable of operating across various time sequences can achieve superior performance relative to models designed for specific time horizons. The proposed approach streamlines model development and facilitates efficient inference processes, making it a more practical solution for real-world social network forecasting applications. Research has been conducted on WW boson production in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. Analysis of same-sign W boson pairs was explored within a two-jet and two like-sign lepton event framework. Events were selected using advanced algorithms, aiming to validate EW and NNLO NLO model predictions for WW boson production through a regulatory analysis. WW boson production cross-sections were measured at 21±5 fb for all events and at 18±6 fb for those with high jet multiplicity, verifying predictions in all cases. Additionally, the cross-section ratio of resonant to non-resonant WW boson production was found to be 0.622±0.168. All results align with the Standard Model predictions. This marks the first experimental investigation of same-sign W boson pairs with high jet multiplicity and the second with high transverse momentum in the dilepton system. One significant challenge in inverse reinforcement learning lies in distinguishing between policies that are optimally optimized and those that are not, particularly when only a portion of the environment's dynamics is known. This difficulty is compounded by the fact that most existing methods are designed to work in fully stylized environments, and when applied to natural settings, they tend to fail or yield ambiguous results. Unlike these methods, which rely on detailed mathematical representations, we propose one that leverages a hierarchical Bayesian approach to learn an optimal policy from both perfectly and partially regulated instances. Our theory indicates that as long as the underlying mechanism for rewarding actions is consistent, our framework can combine information from various sources, even those as disparate as perfect rewards and indirect hints. This comprehensive approach enables a robust learning experience, and we test its efficacy through a simulated driving task. The framework's success in this task demonstrates that our method can effectively learn an optimal policy when rewarded through a combination of signal and noise, even in instances where the underlying reward structure remains unknown. This highlights the potential for our approach to be applied in a range of real-world settings. The code used in this research is publicly available at https://github.com/jbrierley/hirblir. Building on previous research of Kowalski and Nijmeijer (2019), it focuses on expanding their theory to include a broad category of nonlinear systems. This involves generalizing their concept of the local loop transfer region (LLTR) to incorporate subgroups of the fundamental group. Notably, this work contrasts with traditional control theory approaches by not imposing any specific structure on the nonlinearity. This approach allows for the characterization of RSLTRs without requiring any additional assumptions. Consequently, developing methods for designing loop transfer systems within this framework is complicated. One of the major obstacles in automated flight and mobile robot navigation is the issue of control. Robots struggle with their lack of ability to foresee the outcome of their actions, which is crucial for avoiding crashes. This predictability issue becomes even more challenging with complex systems and limited prediction capabilities of their controllers. Typically, predicting the consequences of a robot's actions involves modeling the environment through self-referential neural networks, which can learn to generate likely next states given a control input. Despite their ability to forecast the outcome of their actions, these predictive models still face the challenge of deciding the actual control input to use. This decision is particularly difficult because the predicted next states, which are based on the prediction limitations of the controller, may not be accurate enough for making informed decisions. This paper presents a novel approach called predictive policy iteration (PP-I) that resolves this diffficulty by combining the predictive models of the environment with deep reinforcement learning policies through two-staged deep reinforcement learning. In the first stage, PP-I uses an online deep model-free algorithm to both update the predictive models and optimize the policy simultaneously. This approach ensures that the predictive models remain aligned with the policy they are meant to support, which is essential for accurately forecasting the likely next states given the best possible control input. This alignment is critical because the second stage of PP-I relies on the predictive models to train a more advanced policy through offline deep model-based reinforcement learning. This time, the focus is on maximizing the predicted long-term rewards by using the predictive models to forecast the likely next states given the best possible control input, which is then used to update the policy. This two-staged deep reinforcement learning approach is tested on two complex control issues: (i) mobile robot navigation with obstacles and (ii) aggressive take-off of a tail-sitter unmanned aerial vehicle. The results show that PP-I successfully resolves the diffficulty of controlling complex systems by using the predictive models to train a more advanced policy through offline deep reinforcement learning. Compared to model-free algorithms, PP-I achieves better results, as shown by the results of the simulated experiments. The trained policies using PP-I also demonstrate superior performance to other approaches, as evidenced by the results of the evaluated metrics. For instance, in the mobile robot navigation tests, PP-I reduced the average distance between the predicted and actual next states by at least 75% compared to the model-free algorithm. Similarly, in the aggressive take-off tests, PP-I increased the success rate of the aggressive take-off by at least 214% compared to the model-free algorithm

High-entropy alloys, prized for their remarkable strength and flexibility, are becoming increasingly popular in industrial and scientific circles. This study explores how AI can be leveraged to analyze high-entropy alloys, identify areas where further research is needed, and open up new avenues for future investigation. In particular, we will examine the ways in which AI can help create more accurate and intuitive material representations, gather valuable insights from experimental data, and monitor the progression of processing and properties in these alloys. By combining these capabilities, we can significantly enhance both materials fabrication and the use of high-entropy alloys. While there are numerous opportunities for using AI in HEA research, there are also several challenges that must be addressed, such as translating complex material phenomena into numerical values, dealing with data scarcity and bias, and developing a deeper understanding of the roles played by composition, processing, and other factors in these alloys. A method for creating random, uniformly distributed binarized matrices is proposed, with the constraint that the sum of each row must be equal to a specified value. This is known as the Generalized Traveling Salesman Problem, or GMTSP, which has an established solution for non-binarized matrices. But finding a solution for binarized matrices that meets the desired row sums is an unsolved problem in the field. A novel approach presented in this paper offers a solution to this problem and demonstrates that binarized matrix generation is possible through a set of linearly independent vectors. A specific example is given for the case of row sums equal to 3 in a 4x4 grid, and it is shown that this method can be extended to larger square matrices of any size. Additionally, it is proven that generating these random matrices is feasible in polynomial time. A random sampling algorithm is provided, along with an analysis of its efficiency and a demonstration of its correctness. This method has been tested and validated through experiments involving the generation of 1600 distinct 4x4 binarized matrices, along with accompanying statistical analysis. The proposed algorithm has several key attributes that make it suitable for a variety of applications: it is fast, flexible, and capable of producing a vast number of distinct matrices. A study of its scalability and performance under different parameter settings is also conducted. Overall, this method offers a solution to the long-standing problem of finding distinct binarized matrices that meet specified row sum constraints, and it does so efficiently and effectively. The proposed algorithm has been shown to be a suitable tool for a range of applications, from statistical analysis to network modeling and machine learning, among others. I present a comprehensive PDF fitting framework, developed using Python, to facilitate the comparison of PDFs and their derivatives, as well as the evaluation of integrals and functions. This tool is designed with futurity and flexibility in mind to support a variety of applications including PDF fitting, evolution, and distribution analysis. PDFs can be easily extended to incorporate new features, such as grid-based PDFs, via the implementation of interfaces for popular libraries such as LHAPDF and MMHT. The framework also features a PDF analysis tool that enables researchers to compare PDFs graphically and numerically, as well as a integral evaluator to compute integrals and functions, such as parton distribution functions and inclusive distributions. Key features of the framework include: (i) a wide range of functions to compute PDF values and their derivatives; (ii) support for different PDF fitting options; (iii) interfaces for popular PDF libraries; (iv) a user-friendly interface for researchers to share and compare PDFs. The framework, called \textsc{pdfot}, is now publicly available at \href{https://github.com/pdfot/pdfot}{github.com/pdfot/pdfot}. Possible future extensions include: (i) PDF fitting with the Hessian method; (ii) the inclusion of QCD NLO PDFs; (iii) the implementation of external tools; (iv) a more advanced book-keeping system. Then, using this model, we demonstrate that the stable distribution of a acylindrically hyperbolic group $G$ can be expressed as a combination of its free and axial stable distributions. Quantization has garnered significant interest due to its capacity to reduce deep neural network model size and acceleration during deployment. Interestingly, a particular quaternary weight neural network produced better test results than its fully binary counterpart. This revealed an important connection between binary weights and their equivalent representations, implying model invariance. Through the analysis of the neural network's kernel, the effect of quaternary weights was understood to enhance the variance of the neural network's kernel, thereby contributing to improved generalization. It was found that binary weights could only produce this variance under specific conditions, with the restriction of producing non-zero off-diagonal elements in the covariance matrix of the neural network's kernel. This finding explained why quaternary weights could improve generalization more effectively than binary weights. As a result, a particular binary weight structure was proposed, referred to as the circulant structure, with the property that multiple quaternary weights converge to this structure. Experiments confirmed that training this binary weight structure on existing data could achieve similar results to training a quaternary weight network. Additionally, it was observed that the neural network's kernel converged to the proposed binary weight structure under quantization. Signal recovery algorithms in compressed sensing often benefit from enhancements 
like stabilization techniques - damping and fractional approaches, which use 
expectation propagation to improve performance and achieve convergence. These 
stabilization methods boost long-term efficiency and enable convergence where 
it wasn't possible before. In this study, we provide an in-depth look at various 
stabilization methods and their effects, comparing their numerical performance and 
showing that a combination of procedures can significantly improve the algorithm. 

Key to our findings is the observation that a particular stabilization method 
has an intriguing link with the statistical nature of the CS problem. By 
reinterpreting this phenomenon, we develop a straightforward and universally 
effective stabilization strategy that outperforms others and enables recovery 
even with severely restricted access to random data. Even when we grant limited 
access to random data, our proposed strategy remains unmatched. 

Our work is driven by the observation that a particular random data pattern is 
especially effective at speeding up recovery. Consequently, we suggest a simple 
and universal approach to achieve this random data pattern, which is not only 
effective at solving the CS problem but also has a range of other useful 
applications. Ultimately, our technique remains universally effective even in 
the presence of varying problem parameters and data patterns. 

A key contribution of this study is the establishment of links between various 
stabilization methods and their associated performance characteristics, and we 
suggest several promising research avenues that build upon these connections. 
Additionally, we provide comprehensive numerical validation of our findings and 
suggest several simple and effective algorithms that achieve top-performance 
recovery. Our work is accompanied by a range of reusable Python tools that 
facilitate the reproduction of our results and enable the exploration of many 
other exciting research possibilities. 

Finally, we take a step back from the detailed mathematics of our model and 
instead focus on the broader implications of our results on the compressed sensing 
paradigm, highlighting the remarkable performance of our stabilization methods 
and suggesting several exciting research avenues that emerge from our study.

This parabolic problem has significant connections to several other mathematical models. Our findings also reveal the pointwise convergence of the free fields to their extended versions, accompanied by a mean convergence of the spectral measures. This paper demonstrates that the spectral measures converge at the level of L1, which is made possible by the unique normalization of the measures using the Dorroch-Miller-Stuarts framework for defining imaginary surfaces. This paper investigates the resolution of the Navier-Stokes equations for periodic initial conditions, focusing on the behavior of the solution's derivatives. We use a maximum norm to measure the growth of these derivatives over time, and establish that this growth is limited by a constant that remains stable and dependent solely on the viscosity and the spatial frequency of the initial conditions. Within the regime where viscosity is low, we find that this growth rate is solely influenced by the frequency of the initial conditions, and surpasses the rates observed in both Euler equations and linear diffusion processes. Notably, this research reveals that in the absence of dissipation (i.e., zero viscosity), the solution may exhibit unbounded growth in its derivatives. In contrast to the common practice of utilizing the $L^2$ norm to study the dynamics of the Navier-Stokes equations, our work offers a novel approach to understanding the behavior of the solution and its relationship with the viscosity and frequency of the initial conditions. We arrive at our results by combining energy estimates with a combination of Fourier analysis and the ergodicity of a geodesic equation. Ultimately, this research aims to contribute to the ongoing quest to provide a priori estimates - and, hopefully one day, a positive answer - to the vortex sheet instability problem.  The vortex sheet instability is a critical area of research in fluid dynamics, where the interaction of two parallel sheets of vortex can either stabilize or lead to the creation of highly unstable modes, which have been linked to various turbulence phenomena. In particular, this research aims to provide a priori estimates - and, hopefully one day, a positive answer - to the question of whether certain classes of smooth initial conditions can lead to the creation of highly unstable modes in the limit of zero viscosity. Cell biologists utilize cell morphology as a key factor to determine cell identity, location, and function. Yet, due to the absence of standardized imaging methods across various research studies, it is difficult to model cells computationally. This paper introduces a groundbreaking, cell-specific data-driven approach that uses implicit neural networks to creatively model the shapes of individual cells. Our innovative framework, titled CellCraft, incorporates two interconnected modules: Cellsigner and Cellweaver. Cellsigner signs a latent vector with a unique signature that represents a specific cell type, while Cellweaver utilizes these signed vectors to generate synthetic cell morphology. Through experimentation with our method, we successfully generated artificial Salamander skin cells and Dog kidney cells, showcasing its potential for creative cell modeling. The project's code can be accessed at https://github.com/cstrecker/CelCraft. This research was inspired by a 2022 NeurIPS challenge organized by Sony, IBM, and Autodesk. Research into El Ni\~no events has concentrated primarily on the impacts of the standard type, characterized by widespread sea surface temperature anomalies in the central Equatorial Pacific.  Recent studies suggest that there are multiple forms of El Ni\~no, differing in terms of the region and intensity of anomalies.  This study examines how very low and elevated seasonal precipitation patterns vary during three distinct El Ni\~no types.  Analyzing data from the Global Precipitation Measurement project, researchers discovered that regional precipitation anomalies display significant variations depending on the specific El Ni\~no type.  This distinction holds true across all levels of ENSO intensity.  Notably, positive (increased) precipitation anomalies in northern Australia during El Ni\~no events with high atmospheric anomalies in the Equatorial Pacific are three times more frequent than those during events lacking such atmospheric anomalies.  This suggests that strong atmospheric responses to ENSO can lead to varied regional precipitation impacts, potentially resulting in the occurrence of precipitation anomalies opposite to those typically expected.  This research may improve the prediction of rare precipitation events by refining our understanding of the variable impacts of different El Ni\~no types. Conversely, this is not the case when the Coulomb interaction is present, as it has been observed in experiments. To shed light on this phenomenon, we undertook computational investigations of the Coulomb interaction's impact on the entropy of confined helium-like atoms. Our study reveals that in situations of near-zero confinement, the Coulomb interaction has a minimal effect on the entropy, whereas at higher confinement levels, the Coulomb interaction significantly alters the entropy, ultimately resulting in a negative value for the von Neumann entropy under very high confinement. Our findings also forecast the coexistence of two distinct phases - a liquid droplet phase and a degenerate Fermi gas - at extremely low temperatures and intermediate scales of confinement. Consequently, our work suggests that entropy could serve as a definitive phase-distinguishing criterion in confined systems, thereby potentially presenting an obstacle in attempting to theoretically predict phase transitions in such environments. Lastly, our study on entropy's behavior in the presence of the Coulomb interaction contributes to the existing body of knowledge on information entropies in quantum physics, thereby expanding our understanding of this phenomenon. We've reinterpreted the operations of removal and cut-removal within Multiplicative Linear Logic by leveraging an intuitionistic duality-based interpretation. By applying this interpretation, we've demonstrated that 1-elimination is equivalent to a specific form of weakening in the underlying intuitionistic logic. Furthermore, we've shown that 2-elimination is equivalent to a particular type of cut-elimination in the underlying intuitionistic proof system. This interpretation also provides a new perspective on the relationship between Multiplicative Linear Logic and intuitionistic logic, specifically regarding the elimination of exponential types. Moreover, this analysis reveals that the well-known "type-preserving" property of cut-elimination is not an inherent characteristic of 2-elimination in Multiplicative Linear Logic. Instead, it is a feature that is contingent upon specific additional properties within the underlying intuitionistic logic. We've also explored the implications of our interpretation on the design of well-adapted types for proofs, particularly with respect to the handling of delimiting types. Finally, we've touched upon some potential applications and related problems of our interpretation, specifically in the contexts of Leibniz type theory and ordering-based calculi. The latter of these has potential connections to cut-elimination in dependent linear logic. The full details of our interpretation, as well as its derivation and application to the design of multiplicative linear logic, are provided in an accompanying technical report. Additionally, it delves into further details regarding the design of well-adapted types for proofs, particularly with respect to the exponential types, and explores some related problems and potential applications. The contents of the technical report may also provide an alternative and comprehensive derivation of the multiplicative linear logic with well-adapted types, specifically tailored for the purposes of proof assistance. The technical report is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.08.06.

As electrons move, ions remain stationary compared to the electrons, inducing significant electric fields at equilibrium. These field effects are frequently overlooked in calculations for their impact on the materials' properties. Our research investigates how the inertia of electrons and phonons affects their interactions, revealing that considerations of electric field interactions become particularly important in the high-frequency spectra of both metals and semiconductors. In metals, this led to the prediction of unusual many-body effects in high-energy X-ray absorption and electron energy loss spectra, while in semiconductors it results in altered photon energies required for exciton creation. Our study also highlights the considerable impact that electric field interactions have on the dynamics of superconductors, potentially influencing critical temperature predictions. Ultimately, our findings stress the necessity of incorporating static and dynamic electric field interactions in theoretical models of these materials' dynamics. Our work employs a single-electron framework, and our approach can be adapted for use in both density functional and many-body perturbation theory based calculations. Transition probability distributions have been effectively utilized in various tasks such as language modeling and sentence alignment. Despite their significance, they have not been widely adopted in models for code-mixed texts, which combine multiple languages. This paper presents a novel approach called PESTO, utilizing transition patterns to create dynamic and relative positional encoding for code-mixed text processing. PESTO generates two positional encodings: one from the beginning to any point in the sequence and another from any point in the sequence to the end. Both encodings are based on transition probabilities extracted from the text itself. Experiments demonstrate that PESTO enhances various sequence-based models, including the Transformer, Transformer-XL, and FastText, with a substantial improvement in accuracy up to 5.20% on data-mixed text classification and 2.15% on code-mixed text classification. Notably, PESTO's performance surpasses that of a strong baseline built on fastText, improving word embeddings and character n-gram features, with a substantial improvement of 4.91% in accuracy. Our findings suggest that PESTO effectively captures transition patterns in code-mixed texts, enabling it to significantly upgrade various models' capabilities. This study presents the development of highly agile SiMOSFETs using a standard 300mm CMOS process. Moreover, the high agility of these devices facilitates the manipulation of on-resistance and differential resistance with varying transconductance. The research also delves into the underlying physics of charge carrier transport in these devices and develops a comprehensive model that accurately captures their unique characteristics. We demonstrate that the fourth moment of all analytic Hecke cusp forms up to a given altitude $Q$ exceeds $(2+\delta)Q^{2}$ for some positive $\delta$, and similarly, the fourth moment of those Hecke cusp forms with Fourier coefficients square-integrable over the upper half-plane exceeds $(2+\delta)Q^{2}$ as well. This finding reinforces previous estimates by Rhoades and Rhoades-Brammer, and contrasts with previous work by Liu and Wang yielding a lower bound of $\frac{1}{\log Q}Q^{2}$ for the fourth moment, by selecting certain Sato-Tate measures at the cost of these measures being subject to certain conditions. Furthermore, our work broadens Sarnak's conjecture concerning the distribution of correlation functions of cusp forms, by showing that any deviation from expectation in the correlation functions of these forms, as observed within a subset of cusp forms, must decrease at an exponential rate. This, in turn, allows us to hypothesize that such deviations do not exist. The proof of our primary finding relies on the application of soundarya codes and non-Archimedean geometry over finite fields, by translating the properties of these cusp forms into the language of functions over finite fields, and analyzing these functions' correlations, using the Sato-Tate conjecture as a reference. In place of the Riemann Hypothesis, which is used by Rhoades and Rhoades-Brammer, we utilize the inverse Sato-Tate conjecture, and in place of the geometric interpretation, Rhoades and Rhoades-Brammer used the Louis de Branges' theorems. By picking and choosing, we managed to yield the present results. The proof can be broken into two parts; this abstract will detail only the first part. The first part concerns itself with establishing a lower bound for the fourth moment, by showing that the influence of 'unhealthy' Sato-Tate measures is relatively minor. In doing so, we partition the set of analytic Hecke cusp forms into healthy and unhealthy, using the Sato-Tate measures as the criterion for separation, and demonstrate that only the unhealthy measures can potentially yield a lower bound that is too small. The second part concerns itself with broadening Sarnak's conjecture, by showing that any deviation from expectation in the correlation functions of these forms, as observed within a subset of cusp forms, must decrease at an exponential rate. In solving linear equations or minimizing objectives within Interior Point Methods (IPMs), interior points near optimal solutions often participate in iterative algorithms such as Conjugate Gradient or Minimum Residual methods. These algorithms converge rapidly at first but may require additional iterations at interior points due to their inherent termination criteria, which can be costly in terms of computational time. This paper proposes an alternative anabasis check that can serve as an early termination criterion for these solvers, enabling them to stop sooner. Our experimental results indicate that this implementation leads to a significant reduction in the number of iterations within IPMs. Furthermore, the inner solvers' convergence speed remains unaffected, and our computational testing demonstrates that this approach can result in considerable time savings, especially in large-scale problems. Words cannot adequately convey the extent to which this solution outperforms the standard anabasis check. One can simply observe the considerable time savings achieved. The benefits of artificial intelligence (AI) have long been demonstrated in numerous applications, despite its significant limitations, including data bias and instability. While these flaws are not inherent to AI itself, they are an inevitable result of developing and deploying AI systems without consideration for potential errors. The absence of established industry standards for AI quality and reliability compounds this issue, leading to a heightened risk of severe system failures. The failure of AI systems can have severe consequences, extending from minor setbacks to substantial losses and even human lives, as exemplified by the recent highway collision in Florida where an NHTSA-designated Level 2 and 3 ADAS-equipped vehicle failed, resulting in multiple fatalities. We suggest creating an AI Incident Repository (AIR) to document real-world AI failures, serving as a reference point for industry discussions about quality and reliable AI practices. The establishment of a centralized knowledge base of failures, along with information on causes and consequences, can aid industry professionals in identifying solutions to similar problems, prevent recurring errors, and make more informed decisions throughout their product development journey. The concept of an AI Incident Repository (AIR) has been developed and is now being shared with the aim of promoting real-world AI failure reporting and contributing to a safer, more robust AI ecosystem. In the field of quantum algorithm implementation, using high-level languages can directly write quantum circuits, eliminating the need for intermediate low-level translations. This research follows up on previous work with Proto-Quipper-M, a quantum algorithm high-level language, by developing a semantics definition that can execute programs on pre-existing quantum circuits. We present a prototype implementation of its semantics, enabling the translation of Proto-Quipper-M programs into targeting circuit descriptions based on existing quantum devices. This allows direct compilation and runtime compilation options for quantum algorithms written in Proto-Quipper-M. A key outcome is the separation of algorithm logic and specific quantum circuit implementations, facilitating the development and execution of quantum algorithms on diverse circuit architectures. We demonstrate our approach by translating and executing a quantum algorithm, Remarkable's, on both theoretical and experimental quantum devices. This foundation can contribute to and coexist with other approaches, ultimately enabling seamless quantum algorithm deployment across diverse quantum hardware. This research has been made available as a mathematical formalisation in Isabelle/HOL, promoting greater confidence in the semantics and its safety, as well as serving as a reference for evaluating quantum algorithm high-level languages. We encourage the replication of this research, including the implementation of our prototype, as specified in the accompanying technical report. This research has been made semi-public on arXiv and the Proto-Quipper-M repository will be updated with the necessary material. Additionally, we present an alternative implementation of Proto-Quipper-M's semantics, leveraging Haskell for its development. This research has been made available as an open-source project. This research has been presented at PQMT 2021, with significant revisions incorporating feedback from the reviewers. A short video explaining the research is available. We study large $N$ behavior of the extreme eigenvalues of a random matrix, specifically its $q$-th moment, where the matrix in question is an $N$-dimensional Gaussian unitary ensemble with the option of including perturbations. A phase transition is observed as we increase $q$, shifting from a smooth, continuous pattern to a regime of isolated eigenvalues. In the latter case, we demonstrate that the distribution of the largest eigenvalue approximates a Frechet distribution with a mean scaling of $2N$ and a stability function $\sqrt{2N}$. Moreover, our findings can be extended to random band matrices and even generalized to other random matrix ensembles, such as the Ginibre ensemble, with comparable results. These outcomes align with known results from statistical physics, providing a theoretical basis for a broad family of random matrix ensembles. Furthermore, our work establishes a connection between random matrix theory and the generalized Weierstrass function in function theory, where the stability function can be viewed as a real part of the latter's analytic continuation. In the regime of isolated eigenvalues, we also explore the spectral density and eigenvalue configurations of random matrix ensembles, revealing intricate patterns and relationships that may be of interest in the study of random matrices. Additionally, our work includes a comprehensive discussion on the diversity of random matrix ensembles and the various types of phase transitions that can occur as we change the order of the moments $q$. In the process, we introduce several new theorems that describe the behavior of high-order moments and their applications in random matrix theory. Finally, our work includes a examination of the limitations of our theorems, analyzing under which conditions these theorems hold and what modifications may be necessary to extend their reach to other types of random matrix ensembles. To facilitate this investigation, we introduce several new concepts and techniques, including the idea of nested stable distributions, as well as a more general approach to understanding the limits of random matrix theory, encompassing not only continuous patterns but also regimes of isolated eigenvalues. In this context, we discuss how the ideas of random step functions and tempered distributions can be valuable tools in the study of high-order moments and their applications in random matrix theory. In our research, we demonstrate the powerful connection between vacuum-induced pair creation, squeezing, and optical probing, using a system of two dipoles linked to an optical cavity. We reveal how the same physical phenomenon, indicative of entanglement and correlations, manifests in two different forms: as pairs of cavity photons (through nonlinear optical interactions) or as reduced amplitude fluctuations in probe light (via linear optical interactions). Furthermore, the experiments are designed to utilize long-lived dipoles to achieve exceptional low temperature fluctuations, high precision in spectral analysis, and the capability to count individual photon states. We outline a feasible setup using a pair of $^{171}$Yb$^+$ ions in a cavity, along with presenting numerical results to demonstrate the feasibility of obtaining notable squeezing levels (-4.8 dB) with relatively short coherence times of 72$\mu$s. In theoretical terms, this means that if the cavity photon indistinguishability can be ignored, then the thresholds for observing pairs of cavity photons or reduced amplitude fluctuations in probe light will converge and greatly improve the efficacy of entanglement-assisted sensing operations. If the coherence time is increased to 1.2 ms, then the potential squeezing levels could reach 82% while maintaining high levels of entanglement throughout the process. We propose a novel strategy to leverage the unique properties of this system to achieve exceptional performance in a wide range of applications that rely on entangled physics, such as enhanced precision in spectral analysis, interferometry, and magnetic sensing with exceptionally long coherence times. In particular, we outline specific experiments to demonstrate the breakthrough performance in magnetic sensing with 80.4 dB of sensitivity, unprecedented since the invention of the LIGO detector. This work presents a pioneering approach to reliably harness pair creation and squeezing effects in a wide array of quantum enhanced applications, even with limited coherence times. We anticipate that our research will contribute significantly to the development of next-generation quantum devices, enabling unprecedented performance in a variety of cutting-edge applications. In an alternative experiment, using a $^{87}$Rb atom in an optical micro-trap, we have observed the coexistence of distinct forms of entanglement in this system, exemplifying the diverse applications of quantum physics; in this case, we have demonstrated the generation of two cavity photons and the concomitant reduction of probe light amplitude fluctuations, with numerical results showing the feasibility of obtaining remarkable squeezing levels (-10.8 dB) with relatively short coherence times of 2.3$\mu$s. Constructing long-read genomes from short-read data is a challenging genomic assembly task. One of its crucial steps, overlap detection, is computationally intensive and presents a data parallelization opportunity. We have developed a parallel algorithm for producing overlaps within a distance threshold, which can be applied to building genomes without pre-built indexes. This algorithm leverages shared-memory and distributed-memory parallelism to efficiently utilize multiple cores and nodes. Experiments with up to 1024 cores demonstrate substantial speedups on various short-read datasets, achieving 829x acceleration with 1024 cores on a single node, and 1034x with 1024 cores across 8 nodes. This groundbreaking performance enables genome construction on low-end computational clusters, making it accessible to institutions and organizations with limited resources. Moreover, our method's superiority is further confirmed by comparing it with existing sequential and parallel approaches, revealing 2.4x to 103x speedups on 21 different organisms. These experiments not only underscore the significance of parallel processing but also highlight the adverse impact of data fragmentation on assembly construction, concluding that distributed-memory parallelism remains the most crucial factor for efficient genome construction. This work has resulted in a high-performance, scalable software framework that can be used for constructing long-read genomes and other biological assembly projects. This study focuses on the dynamics of the postponed logistic equation (PLE) derived from models of cellular population growth, which has been observed to be a special case of the Bruce-Lipschitz equation. By making some reasonable assumptions based on the coefficient values and its relationship to the Bruce-Lipschitz equation, the global implications of the PLE's solutions can be understood. It was discovered that the PLE has a globally stable solution of the form $P(t) = p e^{\lambda t}$, where $p$ and $\lambda$ are constants, and the equation can be transformed into a modified Riccati differential equation. By analyzing this transformed equation, the conditions for the PLE's solutions to be non-negative, non-extendable, and globally stable were determined, and it was found that the global implications of the PLE are dependent on the signs of its coefficients. The sign stability conditions of the PLE were also discussed, and it was found that the global stability of the equation is restricted to a limited range of coefficient values. This study presents various methods for determining the global stability of the PLE, including numerical and analytical techniques, and provides a step-by-step solution to the Bruce-Lipschitz equation. The results of this study confirm that the global stability of the PLE is contingent upon the signs of its coefficients, and it offers ways to extend the range of stable solutions. The work presented here can be applied to other types of logistic equations with time-delay, including the Fuller equation, and provides a common approach for analyzing these equations. The study also presents alternative methods for solving the PLE and Bruce-Lipschitz equation, and confirms that the global stability of these equations is a complex phenomenon. This work is a continuation of the author's previous research on the Fuller equation and is expected to be extended to other time-delay logistic equations. The isometric log-ratio transformation offers an efficient method to represent compositions while maintaining flexibility in variation. This work develops a distributional approach for the isometric log-ratio transformation, enabling the construction of a statistical depth based on a principle similar to Minkowski depth. A depth-based point estimator, known as the pseudo-mixture estimator, is also proposed and exhibits contiguity when applied to the transformed compositions. Furthermore, this depth measure allows for the determination of a confidence region for a parameter under composition symmetry conditions. The methods' effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations and an analysis of Australian rainfall data. The concepts and methods presented can be applied to other point process data using the power variance function framework. The methods have been implemented in an R package called packISLR. This package includes functions for computing the isometric log-ratio transformation, a depth-based estimator, and tools for testing and simulating the approaches. The package also offers support for the analysis of composition data based on the proposed distributional approach. The package packISLR can be downloaded from CRAN. A hybrid circuit consisting of an aluminum film and a thin crystal of Ta that is thin enough to be considered two-dimensional, has been designed as an ideal device that leverages the unique properties of superconducting edge magnons in Weyl semimetals. This hybrid circuit serves three purposes: Firstly, it facilitates the detection of magnetic anomalies in the Ta system using an aluminum sensor; secondly, it enables the manipulation of Ta's two-dimensional electronic properties in the presence of superconducting fluctuations; and thirdly, it offers a means to investigate whether Ta's intrinsic imperfections can switch from a Poisson to a Lévy distribution when it undergoes a superconducting transition. Once Ta is grown onto an Si/SiO2 substrate with an underlying gate structure that allows the Ta thickness to be adjusted, the hybrid circuit is completed by covering it with an aluminum thin film that can be used to detect changes in Ta's local environment or to drive the system with an AC current to observe changes in Ta's edge magnons. A major benefit of using the hybrid circuit is that it offers a means to investigate the intrinsic properties of two-dimensional Ta without being influenced by its typically poor surface quality. A possible application of this device is in quantum computing, where a perfect superconducting device could serve as an efficient driver of edge magnons in Weyl semmetals and provide an alternative means to store and process quantum information. Additionally, this device could offer insights into how Ta's intrinsic defects affect the flow of edge magnons across its surface. A possible variation of this device, with an Nb film instead of Al, could also be used to investigate the unique properties of superconducting edge modes in Weyl semmetals under the influence of Ginzburg-Landau condensations. A further adaptation of this hybrid circuit could be designed to look for signs of non-Abelian topological effects in Weyl semmetals that have both chiral and spin-Hall characteristics. A possible variation of this device could also be used to investigate the flow of quantum information across Ta's surface as it undergoes a superconducting transition. Business Process Management (BPM) systems rely on process mining (PM) to interpret the behavior captured in event logs, drawn from actual process executions. While PM focuses on descriptive, analytical, and predictive tasks, there is an unexplored aspect - prescriptive process monitoring (PPM) - which involves making predictions during active process executions to guide future decisions. This study delves into PPM by asking: What kind of analysis can be performed on ongoing processes? What PPM techniques are currently employed and inherent in other methods? And, what are the challenges and opportunities associated with PPM? This research answers these questions to establish a foundation for future PM advancements, specifically concentrating on the prescriptive dimension. Our research presents a new taxonomy for PPM that covers various analysis methods and introduces the concept of an PPM-aware process engine to facilitate future PPM integrations. Finally, we identify promising research avenues and potential applications within the prescriptive process monitoring field. When these movements result in structures being placed on top of each other, the operation is referred to as a stacking issue. In our study, we identify specific cases of graph drawing-related stacking issues and solve the associated optimization problems within a time complexity proportional to n^(O(1)). Additionally, we define reduced problems for these optimization problems, solving them in a time complexity proportional to n. Our main contribution lies in demonstrating that these reduced problems are equivalent to the original problems, a fact we establish through a sequence of automated transformations. This leads to a discovery that specific graph layout problems, such as planarity-based drawing design, can be resolved in a time complexity proportional to n. Similarly, we obtain a complexity of n for the optimal multi-level segmentation problem in combinatorial biology. Furthermore, we provide simplified algorithms for obtaining optimal solutions in specific cases of stacking issues, along with proving that certain problems are NP-hard in their basic forms, a fact we overcome by developing kernelizations with a size complexity of n. In our kernelizations, we exploit the solution structure to recursively decompose the input, this leading to a discovery that certain graph design problems can be solved efficiently when the graph size is constrained. This technique is illustrated in our solution to the optimal multi-level segmentation problem, a result that also showcases our newly developed data reduction rules. Lastly, we extend our kernelization technique to a more general class of stacking issues, a category which includes graph design-based problems, by developing a data reduction rule that decomposes the input into smaller components based on the issue type, this leading to a further specialization of our kernelization and a consequent efficient algorithm for an extensive range of graph design-based problems. In our study, we introduce several novel concepts, including the technique of kernelization, the application of which yields our solution to the optimal multi-level segmentation problem and expands the scope of efficient algorithm design to a diverse set of graph design-based problems, this set including planarity-based drawing design as a special case. Additionally, we develop the technique of kernelization to its fullest extent, showcasing its versatility in resolving optimization problems, a technique that achieves this by constraining the structure of the input graph based on the problem in question, a fact that also leads to our solution to the optimal multi-level segmentation problem and the resolution of efficient algorithm design for an extensive range of graph design

In this work, we demonstrate through data collection that a common issue in visual learning pipelines occurs when items are dropped, resulting in discordant audio and visual signals. To address this problem, we propose a novel public dataset called Dropping Things, featuring 1800 instances of dropped objects, captured via synchronous RGB and audio recordings. Through data analysis, we reveal that current state-of-the-art object detection algorithms struggle to identify dropped objects, especially those partially obstructed or static in motion. To tackle this challenge, we design an end-to-end neural network called Droptim, capable of synchronizing audio and visual signals to detect dropped items. End-to-end training of Droptim significantly outperforms baseline object detectors in detecting dropped objects, thereby utilizing the context of both modalities to improve identification. With its high area under the precision-recall curve, Droptim exhibits excellent performance on our dataset, demonstrating robustness on a variety of tasks, including location estimation and object counting. Notably, Droptim's performance surpasses that of models incorporating pre-trained audio-visual attention mechanisms. As a result, Droptim can be employed in applications such as autonomous surveillance and service robots to effectively identify dropped items along with other visible objects. The Dropping Things dataset will be publicly available for download at dropthing.org. At present, this dataset is only accessible for academic purposes due to storage and bandwidth constraints. For any related inquiries, please contact the researchers at <m.kamalarjun@mengineering.ieit>. Future enhancements to the dataset may be made to include diverse environmental settings and infrastructure, as well as a training dataset for object detectors. However, for detecting dropped items, it is crucial that the models are exposed to the conflicting views present in the Coordimming Things dataset. Consequently, we recommend using the full Dropping Things dataset for training detection models that aim to detect dropped items. Conversely, the simplified dataset may be employed for optimizing general object detection models. Automatically creating programs from detailed specifications is a challenging task in software development. A novel approach involves generating code directly from flow diagrams, eliminating the need for intermediate representations like graph models. A new framework, called Graph Identification Convolutional Neural Network (GRCNN), is introduced to convert flow diagrams into usable graph inputs. Through experiments using the DeepDet dataset consisting of over 3000 flow diagrams and their corresponding source code, the effectiveness of GRCNN and its variations in comparing various program synthesis methods is evaluated. Two baseline approaches, including a CNN-based and a ResNet-based method, are used for comparison. Another program synthesis method, called Graph Attention Neural Network (GATNN), is also tested and is found to perform poorly, confirming the proposed hypothesis that the hierarchical structure of flow diagrams is essential for successful code synthesis. As a result, the best performing model was a combination of GRCNN and GATNN, outperforming the other methods in accuracy and F1-score by a significant margin, while its time complexity was shown to be efficient and scalable. The proposed framework offers a promising solution to the long-standing program synthesis problem. Its source code and data are publicly available for reproduction of results. Radiation oncologists manually contour parts of the gastrointestinal tract to treat cancers located within it, which is a time-consuming process prone to errors. Automating this contouring using artificial intelligence could significantly reduce these issues. Although deep learning-based methods have been successfully used for contouring various organs, its application for the gastrointestinal tract has been limited due to the irregular shape and movement of the organs during imaging. To overcome these challenges, we developed a fully automated deep learning-based technique using MRI images, which can accurately segment the gastrointestinal tract without the need for manual correction. Our approach, called GI-CanalNet, consists of two separate tasks - detecting the long axis of the canal and delineating its perimeter - to accurately segment the gastrointestinal tract. Our model was carefully designed and trained to handle irregular shapes and movement, which is necessary given the gastrointestinal tract's appearance during imaging. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we compared the segmentation results of our model against expert-generated Ground Truth definitions, which are widely recognized as the standard for accurate segmentation. Our analysis of the data suggests that our approach, while efficient, may benefit from additional technical enhancements to improve its overall performance. Nonetheless, given the time-consuming nature of manual contouring and the potential errors involved, as well as the technological challenges facing contouring, the automation of gastrointestinal tract contouring using artificial intelligence could be a valuable tool for radiation oncologists, even with existing limitations. Our code is publicly available for testing and validation purposes. The core issue with traditional planetary formation theories has been the challenge of explaining how large planets with masses similar to or less than that of Saturn can form, given that such objects should rapidly migrate to or beyond the snow line during the protoplanetary disk phase. This study found that there is no shortage of sub-Saturn mass planets in the CORALIE/HARPS radial velocity sample, contradicting previous expectations. It is suggested that these planets likely formed within or near the photoevaporation edge of the disk, where the gas supply is limited, resulting in the formation of planets with masses below the critical threshold for rapid migration. This theory is consistent with observations of exoplanetary systems and offers a potential explanation for the phenomenon of giant planets with masses less than that of Jupiter being paired with low-mass planets. This mechanism could also influence the formation of binary star systems with equal mass objects. It is hypothesized that planets with masses similar to that of Uranus, which would typically be interior to the snow line, could also be affected by this phenomenon. The findings of this study may have implications for the selection bias of discovered planets, potentially affecting the interpretation of theoretical models. The radius distribution of the planets in the CORALIE/HARPS sample peaks at around 3.5 R_E, with a secondary peak at around 1.8 R_E, reflecting the distinction between planets that are or are not subject to core accretion. The discovery of sub-Saturn mass planets in the CORALIE/HARPS radial velocity sample suggests that it is essential to utilize multiple detection methods to fully comprehend the population of G dwarf planets. The analysis of planets with masses between approximately 10 to 43 M_Earth and radii between approximately 1 to 6 R_E can be used to further investigate the demarcation between core accretion and disk photoevaporation in the galaxy. We investigate the interaction between standard model particles and dark matter, assuming that this interaction is facilitated through a Yukawa coupling. Our research reveals that dark matter compressed into a small volume can give rise to the observed geodesic deviation, providing a feasible explanation for the anomaly seen in Pioneer and New Horizons spacecraft data. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound on the dark matter's Yukawa coupling constant, showing that it must be greater than $10^{-13}$, and also constrain the mass ratio between the mediating particle and the dark matter particle. To illustrate the effectiveness of our framework, we have conducted a comprehensive set of experiments, involving five distinct loss functions, and the results show that the proposed method outperforms existing global aggregation techniques. Additionally, we have found that taking into account the specific geometry of the loss functions through the Bregman divergence can provide a significant performance boost. Building on this success, we have extended our framework to handle stochastic data, and the resulting method has been successfully applied to a series of statistical inference tasks. Overall, our contribution lies in reinterpreting global aggregation through the optimal transport lens and demonstrating its superiority over traditional methods. This interpretation also opens up avenues for future research, and we hope that our study will pave the way for more innovative applications of optimal transport in machine learning.
