The challenge of dealing with variable galaxies in image processing presents a significant obstacle in astronomical work. Each galaxy exhibits illumination changes amounting to 10% or more, under starlight or instrument-derived light, rendering conventional image adjustment methods inadequate. Our investigation focuses on the core issue: how can a suitable adjustment filter be chosen? Our analysis takes into consideration the specific requirements of astronomical data and incorporates statistical models, a critical element given the small number of pixels involved. We evaluate seven previously proposed methods, including theoretical explanations and practical applications to real galaxy images. Our experiments, involving a comprehensive dataset of 14 galaxies in four bands, reveal notable variations in results, with some examples showing unacceptably high illumination differences. A new approach, the Novak et al. method, stands out as one of the best options. We provide comprehensive information for other scientists working on this problem in the form of an extensive supplementary online material. Additionally, we publish adjusted images and corresponding data sets for further scientific use. These resources include adjusted images from the Hubble Space Telescope's PACS and SPIRE instruments, as well as a comprehensive dataset consisting of 14 galaxies across four bands, all made available online. Additionally, the code used in our research is freely accessible on GitHub. It allows other scientists to repeat our experiments, making the code highly customizable to accommodate unique research needs. Our investigation aims to contribute to ongoing research in this area while also serving as a useful reference for practitioners working on this problem. Our key findings include the means to replicate our work, adjusted images, and a comprehensive dataset. These resources promote transparency and make a significant contribution to address the challenge of choosing an effective filter to tackle variable galaxies in astronomical work. Deep learning models, notably CNNs, have seen substantial success but have been outperformed by a novel architecture - the Spiking Random Neural Network (SRNN). Our research reveals that the efficacy of the SRNN can be further optimized through an expanded pool of pre-trained filters. By taking advantage of the computations not performed by the initial set of filters in the pre-training phase, the SRNN can significantly reduce unnecessary operations during testing, yielding a notable 30% decrease in inference calculations while maintaining exceptional classification accuracy across various datasets, including MNIST, FMNIST, and CIFAR10. With a significant reduction in inference complexity comes the capacity for the SRNN to be deployed in resource-constrained devices with heightened efficiency. Moreover, we show that the capacitated SRNN can be adapted for regression tasks and offer a depth-wise variant of the model. Our findings strongly support the use of the capacitated SRNN as a dependable and performant solution for energy-efficient AI deployments. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/EMMathias/SRNN.

A surge in distributed systems research suggests that many existing concepts can be reinvented for greater efficiency and effectiveness. In this study, we present Pando, a novel, decentralized, volunteer computing network based on individual browser nodes that leverages standard HTTP requests for efficient computation sharing. By adapting concepts from peer-to-peer communication, Pando enables multiple tasks on a single computer through a simplified, yet robust architecture. Notably, Pando's key features enable persistent node connections, efficient task distribution, and reliable result resorption. This facilitates a robust framework for supporting various applications and promoting further development within the volunteer computing domain. This work has been influenced by projects like BOINC through which the lead author has contributed. The study delves into Pando's theoretical framework, implementation, and practical applications, also introducing a simulation-based testing approach for evaluating volunteer networks. Furthermore, we present Pando's potential applications, highlighting their benefits and challenges. Ultimately, we outline possible paths for further research within the domain of volunteer computing. The study is available in preprint form at arXiv.org via arXiv:2207.14065. Pando's source code is openly accessible on GitHub.com at https://github.com/abdelrahman-amos/pando. A demonstration of Pando is available at pando-demo.com. This study addresses the estimation of a spectral issue related to a nonlinear functional of a continuous time stochastic process $\{X_t\}_{t\ge 0}$. Under relatively mild assumptions, it is possible to obtain model-free estimates for the relevant eigen-values and eigen-functions using an adaptive interpolation method, and this is demonstrated with the first spectral frequency and eigen-functions of a diffusion process with random coefficients. The estimates are shown to converge at rates of $n^{-1/\rho}$ and $n^{-1/(1+\rho)}$ respectively, where $\rho$ is a parameter that depends on the smoothness of the diffusion process. A parametric rate of convergence can be achieved if additional smoothness assumptions are made on the process. A chattering mouthpiece-based strategy is also proposed to improve the efficiency of the eigen-function estimates, and a simulation example is provided to illustrate the performance of the proposed method. Furthermore, it is possible to extend the estimates to the case where output measurements are affected by noise. Our findings indicate that the theory inevitably enters a confinement phase. Additionally, we demonstrate that in scenarios with one-dimensional subgroups, a deconfinement phase can coexist with chiral symmetry breaking, provided certain conditions are met. A representation of $SO(N_c)$ gauge theories, which is fundamental and irreducible, is developed, aiding the analysis of $SO(N_c)$ theories in relation to their $SU(N_c)$ counterparts, which are composed of odd-dimensional subgroups. An in-depth comparison of these two sets of theories, specifically regarding monopoles and tension, is also provided. Machine learning models such as random forests and boostnets have proven effective across many fields but their complex structure makes it difficult to understand how they work. Our study introduces a new method to analyze individual decision trees within these models by creating a network of tree nodes that can be separated into distinct groups, allowing each group to represent different variables and their relationships. By identifying key nodes in these groups, our method enables deeper interpretation of how each variable affects model decisions and identifies areas of improvement. Our method is versatile and can be applied to various machine learning models beyond random forests and boostnets. Its effectiveness was demonstrated in several practical applications and it outperformed other interpretation methods in accurately predicting labels based on key variables in its associated hypergraphs. Furthermore, its use was shown to both increase and decrease model performance, depending on the model, as removing less important nodes could improve prediction performance, while removing more important nodes could have an adverse effect. Overall, our method was successfully applied across many fields and it was observed that its use resulted in consistent improvements to model performance in some fields, while its use had both positive and negative impacts on model performance in other fields. In regression tasks based on continuous variables, our method was also shown to consistently improve model performance by comparing it with other interpretation methods. Our method was developed in conjunction with a comprehensive evaluation of various interpretation methods that were applied across many fields, resulting in an innovative approach that analyzes the structure of random forest and boostnet models by transforming their associated hypergraphs into distinct groups based on their connection to other nodes, and then identifying key nodes in these groups. Our analysis shows that modeling relationships between variables can be beneficial, as it allows these models to better perform regression tasks based on continuous variables, while their use can be detrimental to classification tasks, as it may result in decreased performance. In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on training machine learning models by sharing local parameters, rather than sensitive data. Despite this setup, model parameter exchanges can potentially expose confidential information, especially since participating parties may be untrusted. To address this issue, we propose using Trusted Execution Environments to safeguard against unauthorised access both on the client and the server sides. Our approach involves using these environments to isolate and protect model parameters during the entire training process. Specifically, we introduce Flatee, a solution that federates training across such environments, by means of a complex communication process that is both efficient and reliable. Our evaluation experiments demonstrate that Flatee is significantly faster than conventional federated learning, particularly when dealing with a large number of participants, and that it offers an excellent balance of security and performance. For instance, we can achieve a 97\% reduction in communication overhead when using 64 participants, while only suffering a 5\% increase in communication round counts. Furthermore, we have successfully validated the effectiveness of our approach in practical scenarios, by means of comprehensive experiments with popular deep learning models and the CIFAR10 and ImageNet datasets. Overall, Flatee offers an appealing solution for companies and organisations seeking to enhance the security of their federated training operations, while minimizing the performance impact. Our code is openly available for anyone to reproduce our results.  It can be accessed at https://github.com/yousefhamidflatee/Flatee. By assuming a trusted status for individual application components, Timeloops focuses on inter-component interactions via system calls. as long as the number of parameters is relatively limited. This has significant
implications, allowing deep neural networks to be viewed as a form of linear
classification with added constraints. In this research, we aim to provide a more
precise understanding of the effects of parameter quantity on deep neural
classifiers and the Commodity Space Form (CSF). To achieve this, we model CSF as
a restricted subspace of the Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS), thereby

CSF through the lens of Riemannian geometry, revealing that its geometric structure

transformations. This leads us to establish the relationship between local geometry
and the success of deep neural networks in commodity space forms. Ultimately, this
research provides a theoretical foundation for the effectiveness of deep neural
networks in CSF, illuminating the connection between the number of parameters,
the geometric structure of commodity spaces, and the notable capabilities of
deep neural networks. Experimental evaluations using various commodity spares and
kernels have demonstrated the theoretical premises outlined in this research. As such

In the vicinity of a supermassive black hole at the center of a galaxy, the orbits of stars within the Hilbert sphere face uniform gravitational force regardless of their direction. According to von Mises-Rossler distribution, in this scenario, the angular distribution of stars is not uniform. Researchers found that the number of stars within a specific angle ranges from $N( \theta ) =N_0 e^{k \cos \theta}$, where $N_0$ and $k$ are constants. The Hilbert sphere becomes strongly separated into two areas, one containing the stars and the other the black hole, when the value of $k$ is extremely high. Under these conditions, the probability of finding a star within a specific range in angle is approximately 0.57, which can be calculated as 1 minus the probability of the star being on the opposite side of its orbit. This calculation is highly accurate and offers a simplification of the problem. Furthermore, researchers provided a new expression for the long-term mean of $e^{k \cos \theta}$ within a specific range in angle, which is an open mathematical problem, and demonstrated that the distribution of stars within a specific velocity range follows a power-law, providing a simplification of the problem. These findings can be generalized and applied to other areas around the black hole. Based on these results, researchers created a model to explain the stellar arrangements observed around the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way galaxy. Using this model, they calculated different values of $k$ and $N_0$ for a range of observable areas and provided a range of estimates for these values. Additionally, researchers provided a new expression to explain the brightness distribution of the stars in the galactic center in relation to their observable area and the observable magnitude. By applying this model, researchers reconstructed the history of stellar arrangements in the galactic center, which is also consistent with the findings of other studies. Furthermore, researchers provided a model to explain the distribution of the stars in the galactic center based on different values of $k$ and $N_0$. This model can be applied and modified to explain the stellar arrangements in other galaxies. The research offers a new approach to understanding the stellar arrangements in galaxies and provides new insights into the supermassive black holes at their centers. Additionally, researchers emphasized the importance of further studying the galactic center, particularly its recent changes and the role of the supermassive black hole in them. To achieve this, they suggested various future observations

We introduce a randomized version of Model Predictive Control (Model Predictive Modeling - RPM), which incorporates randomness within the optimal modeling process. To illustrate RPM, we modified a power grid management problem to account for unpredictable demand fluctuations. Using the RPM algorithm, we generated a sequence of suboptimal but feasible solutions for the complex planning problem. Through implementation, we observed that successive sub-problems in the RPM sequence frequently share common variables, thereby enabling the computation of nearly optimal solutions at a significantly reduced computational cost. This observation led us to devise a model pooling strategy, which leverages the structure in the RPM sequence to expedite solution processing. The underlying idea behind RPM can be applied to various model-based optimization algorithms to exploit problem-specific patterns and reduce computational expenses. The code used to demonstrate RPM is freely accessible on GitHub at the specified URL. The computational framework employed in this demonstration is built upon PyDP with the financial support of ONR grant N00014-16-1-0461. The project has been successfully executed in collaboration with Dr. Heeren, Dr. Wang, and Mr. Lee. The research is further facilitated by an ONR grant N00014-18-1-263, which is focused on developing randomized Model Predictive Control algorithms capable of exploiting problems with inherent structures. The primary researchers involved in this project are Dr. Heeren and Wang. The success of this research is attributed to Dr. Heeren having received an ONR Early Career Award N00014-18-1-063. The findings presented in this paper have been presented at the 2019 American Controls Conference, which took place in Philadelphia, PA. The results have been further presented at the 2019 IEEE CDC under the title of "Randomized Model Predictive Control with Graph and Sparsity Exploitation." The associated slides can be accessed via the link to the public GitHub repository. The employment of programmable liquid crystal devices within electron microscopy has garnered interest as a potential tool for achieving phase shifts necessary for phase-contrast imaging. If such devices can introduce the requisite phase change, they could potentially be used as replacements for traditional lenses in electron microscopy, aiding in offsetting imaging limitations and enhancing resolution. This study investigates the feasibility of utilizing a phase disc as a phase shift element in conjunction with a TEM and presents an iterative algorithm for calculating its required profile to rectify aberrations in the point spread function, utilizing a Fourier series representation. However, our findings reveal that the phase disc's finite size poses a limitation, preventing the attainment of necessary high-order phase shifts, and thus it is not capable of overcoming certain types of aberrations. Nevertheless, we propose that the phase disc could be beneficial as a tool for in-situ aberration analysis and in-situ optimization of electron microscopy systems. Additionally, it could be employed in conjunction with other methods to enhance resolution and obtain phase-contrast imaging without relying on phase reversal. This study also outlines possible improvements to the design and the addition of new features to the programmable phase disc to broaden its applications in electron microscopy. These potential enhancements include integrating polarizers to control polarization-sensitive imaging, incorporating chiral components for the generation of spin split-off bands, and incorporating Shack-Hartmann sensors for wavefront reconstruction and wavefront manipulation. These proposed enhancements could enable the usage of the programmable phase disc as a full-fledged optical element for imaging and its adoption in various configurations to achieve high-resolution phase-contrast imaging and enhance resolution, surpassing the limitations imposed by the phase disc's size. Furthermore, we provide numerical evidence and visualize examples of using the phase disc with these additional features to manufacture optical elements with intricate structures, such as spiral phase plates, in the realm of electrons. These proposed innovations and our iterative algorithm for calculating the required phase shifts could significant contribute to the advancement of in-situ aberration correction and phase-contrast imaging, thereby opening the door for novel applications and innovations in electron microscopy. On the other hand, these concepts could also be used in various other systems, encompassing microscopy as well as astronomy and laser engineering, encompassing both spatial and temporal phases. Therefore, the findings of this study, encompassing both numerical evidence and vision for future development, could significantly contribute to these broad phases of technology, encompassing electron microscopy and beyond. Lastly, we provide a concise conclusion, summarizing the feasibility and future prospects of using the programmable phase disc for in-situ aberration

This study focuses on counting the occurrences of a $k$-step random walk within a $d$-dimensional integer grid $\mathbb{Z}^d$, where the walk's initial and final points have a distance of exactly $r$ from the origin. We define $N(k,r,d)$ as the upper limit of this walk's positions. Our goal is to determine a formula or approach to efficiently calculate $N(k,r,d)$ or its variants. Due to the lack of a suitable method for directly computing $N(k,r,d)$, we instead investigated the related problem of a generalized polynomial's degree, specifically $A_t(z)$, where $t$ represents a multivariate integer vector $(t_1,\ldots,t_d)$. We utilized this approach to develop a recursive formula that enables the calculation of $N(k,r,d)$ with a maximum efficiency of $\mathcal{O}(d \cdot k^2)$ operations. We also extended our initial protocol to accommodate more complex scenarios, such as walks with allowed steps of varying lengths, as well as walks constrained within rectangular areas. We verified our findings through both theoretical and experimental means, presenting key examples and observations in its supporting document. Additionally, we have made the associated code publicly available under the MIT License at our GitHub repository. This research in depth investigates the model of spherically symmetric polymer black holes, which was first introduced by Gambini, Olmedo, and Pullin within the framework of loop quantum gravity. We have updated their theory to include spacetimes with non-trivial lapse functions, and as a result, have derived the expanded geometry of the polymer black hole. Next, we will analytically calculate the quasinormal modes of gravitational perturbations using the Teukolsky equation, and then compare these to the standard (continuum) black hole results. Our analysis shows that the quasinormal frequencies of the polymer black hole are closer to those of the standard black hole when the impact of the quantum correction is high. Furthermore, we have found that the imaginary parts of the quasinormal frequencies are shifted due to the quantum correction. However, this shift remains small, which is a positive sign for the applicability of the expanded geometry to study standard black hole quasinormal spectra. We have also found that the dependence on the radial bispinor index in the dispersion relation of the eigenvalues affects the quasinormal spectrum, and that this effect can be significant for damped waves. Moreover, based on the expanded geometry, we have found that the quantum correction depends on the location of the emission source, which is a novel finding. Finally, we estimate the characteristic size of the quantum correction, and find that it is larger than the probed scale in the case of LMC-1, but smaller than the probed scale in the case of Sgr A*. These results indicate that the expanded geometry of the polymer black hole can be used to study standard black hole quasinormal spectra, which has important implications for the analysis of gravitational wave data in the near future. Additionally, our results show that the spectral difference between the polymer and standard black holes can be attributed to the differing dependence on the radial bispinor index in the dispersion relation of the eigenvalues, which is an important finding. The chapter concludes by pointing out several open issues and suggesting potential avenues of research to further develop the model, such as incorporating matter and charged black holes. Furthermore, we propose that the spectral difference between the expanded geometry of the polymer black hole and the standard black hole could be observed using future gravitational wave detectors, which would provide a clear experimental test of the model. The model also predicts that the emission spectra of (micro)black holes and ultracompact celestial objects should be significantly altered at certain high frequency ranges. In graphene panels with correlated atomistic defects as scattering centers, as seen in graphene on Ni(111), we show that the carrier density can be modulated by temperature, leading to enhanced charge transport. This is attributed to thermal activation of carriers across the defect-induced gap, releasing bound states at specific defect nodes. We demonstrate that the heat capacity associated with these bound states is much larger than expected from free electrons, and compute the density of states for graphene's unique Dirac fermions. Additionally, we find that the density of states' divergence at the Fermi level is cancelled out by a nearby van Hove singularity, resulting in a zero contribution to the heat capacity from this effect. Instead, the heat capacity is dominated by a quadratic term at high temperatures, originating from the thermalization of graphene's Dirac cones. This is corroborated by experimental data, where the heat capacity is found to follow a $T\sqrt{aT}$ law, with $a$ representing the mean interdefect spacing. This collaboration between graphene's Dirac electrons and the quasiparticles at defect nodes leads to exceptional charge transport in graphene-based devices. Moreover, this unique interplay revamps our understanding of finite-temperature shielding in graphene, where the electron density is now seen as a collective property of the scattering centers and the Dirac electrons, leading to a $T$-linear contribution from charge overflow. This effect is anticipated to persist in graphene-based interfaces, where the inherent disorder results in unprecedented transport phenomena governed by photonless mechanisms. Hence, this study uncovers new mechanisms underlying finite-temperature shielding in graphene and reveals its correlation with the heat capacity, paving the way for utilizing graphene-based interfaces in high-performance electronics. Moreover, this research could be extended to the study of other graphene-based interfaces, such as those with transition metal surfaces, where the inherent disorder results in new states at the surface and an exchange of electrons between the two materials. This exchange gives rise to a plethora of new states at the interface, which are governed by different rules and have unique properties not seen in clean graphene. Lastly, the research findings also have implications for understanding the behavior of graphene-based interfaces during chemical reactions and how the electronic properties of graphene are affected by the inherent disorder and surface states. Thus, this study will contribute to the ongoing discussion on the electronic transport in graphene-based interfaces, particularly those with transition metal surfaces, and will help to understand the underlying processes better. Continuous speech data is preferred over discrete text data for language learning, chatbot development, and sentiment analysis. We investigate using a masking technique to generate context-specific auxiliary speech in conversation, allowing the dialogue history to influence the current speech output. This approach enhances state-of-the-art speech synthesis with contextual information. We propose using a context mask to select relevant words from the dialogue history and integrate this context into a neural speech synthesis model via a context embedding layer. We evaluate our method on two datasets: the FastVIT dataset and a subset of the OpenSubtitles dataset. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique in incorporating dialogue context for speech synthesis. The open-source code and demo can be accessed at https://github.com/InkaMei/MaskedDialogue. Supplemental materials are available at https://inka-me.github.io/MaskedDialogue/. This work is based on the FastVIT framework (Jia et al., 2020), which combines vision and text learning with speech synthesis. We analyze various models under different training conditions and examine the impact of our method on speech synthesis performance. Our approach is relevant to multiple research areas, including natural language processing, speech processing, and computer vision. The proposed mechanism has applications in chatbots, natural dialogue systems, and video analysis software. The code and demo can be accessed at https://github.com/InkaMei/MaskedDialogue. Building on previous work in projection predictive regression and classification, 
we now develop a predictive model for regression and classification tasks 
within high-dimensional spaces, using a latent variable model to address 
non-Gaussian data. This approach, which incorporates a hidden space 
projection predictive methodology, uses predictive samples to define a 
predictive distribution for the target variable, given the observed data 
and latent variables. Our framework maintains the computational efficiency 
and simplicity of earlier projections predictive techniques while effectively 
handling complex relationships and interactions in large data sets. 
Furthermore, this new model covers a broad spectrum of applications, 
encompassing both linear and non-linear correlations, as well as independent 
and interdependent relationships among high-dimensional variables. In our 
study, we primarily use a Gaussian model for the predictive distribution, 
but we also explore the incorporation of non-Gaussian models through the 
use of predictive samples based on quantile regression. The performance of 
this new model is evaluated on a range of synthetic and real data sets, 
illustrating its ability to accurately predict outcomes in various high- 
dimensional scenarios, often surpassing the performance of other popular 
multivariate predictive models. Our model has been made freely available 
through the R package 'ppr'. The research demonstrates the potential 
of integrating Bayesian techniques and efficiency gains to tackle 
complicated data analysis problems in high-dimensional spaces. In particular, 
this new model covers a range of predictive tasks including regression, 
classification, and novel applications such as ranking and predicting 
probability distributions. The integration of this model within the R 
library 'ppr' offers users a comprehensive suite of tools for projecting, 
predicting, and analyzing relationships within high-dimensional data sets. 
The code for the paper is available at https://github.com/jvansnedeker/hppr. The data used in this study is available at https://dx.doi.org/10.21253/PPR202213.1.

Climate change denial poses a significant threat to global efforts to mitigate and adapt to climate change. Despite its severity, research on climate change denial remains limited, particularly when it comes to understanding the role of social media in disseminating conspiracy theories. Our research uniquely focuses on conspiracy theories involving alleged malevolent intentions to induce climate change, often referred to as "climate alteration" theories. Through an analysis of Twitter posts, we have compiled a comprehensive dataset of 1.5 million tweets containing conspiracy theory-related hashtags. Our subsequent analysis reveals that conspiracy theory-related climate discussions are distinct from typical climate discussions on Twitter, with notable differences in terminology and topics. Furthermore, we have identified distinct groups within the conspiracy theory population, including those who promote climate alteration theories and also engage with standard conspiracy theories. Our findings imply that standard intervention strategies may be insufficient to address climate alteration conspiracy theories, and that critical social media components, such as amplification and partisanship, require consideration in the development of effective countermeasures. We propose that working in partnership with social media platforms is crucial to address these conspiracy theories, especially when it comes to identifying nodes that consistently disseminate these theories, including professionals, popular influencers, and political figures. Ultimately, we believe that a multi-faceted approach, incorporating expertise from climate scientists, is essential to addressing climate alteration conspiracy theories effectively. Additionally, we demonstrate that this criterion is met in categories exhibiting morphic linear Calabi-Yau structure. Consequently, we derive a generalized form of a previous result by Myung et al. for morphic linear Calabi-Yau categories. The proof involves creating a projection functor from a derived category that exhibits morphic linear Calabi-Yau structure, and which preserves the Calabi-Yau structure. Instrumental variable models have a long-standing assumption that the underlying
factor influencing the decision must be correlated with the treatment. The
existing literature implies that treating the treatment as a random variable could
potentially validify the model, yet a formal theoretical framework for this concept
has been lacking. This study develops a rigorous proof that accounts for uncertain treatment decisions, leveraging this framework to re-examine the returns to studying certain subjects in higher education. Our findings suggest that pursuing sciences and engineering in the UK leads to significant post-graduation earnings boosts of 9-20 percent, in line with the general take rates of these fields. Additionally, we discovered that students who choose sciences or engineering tend to have higher initial earnings than those picking humanities or social sciences, indicating a notable income gradient at the point of degree choice. The income differential at degree choice not only drives but also partially explains the earned premium, particularly in sciences. The remaining variance in outcomes can be attributed to various factors, such as post-graduation career trajectories, skill development, and comorbidity conditions affecting choice and productivity. Our analysis addresses potential endogeneity by considering multiple instruments, allowing us to conduct robustness checks and extend the applicability to a broader set of treatments and outcomes. The results offer crucial insights to students and policymakers in the UK, emphasizing the importance of considering students' initial earnings when advising on field of study choices and highlighting that the earned premium likely represents a substantial portion of the expected benefits. Our proof has broader implications, supporting the instrumental variable approach in settings featuring random treatments and enabling a more comprehensive evaluation of the effect of certain treatment types on specific outcome types. The study's findings also contribute to the ongoing debate on how to steer students towards high-paying and skill-demanding fields in higher education to maximize graduates' earnings potential. Moreover, this research offers a fresh perspective on the instrumental variable technique, underscoring its potential to shed light on the underlying structure of choice and productivity in a complex environment. Lastly, the results provide empirical support to the idea of implementing skill-based steering in higher education, in addition to merit-based and income-based approaches, in order to maximize the earnings potential of graduates. In particular, our findings indicate that pursuing sciences and engineering could be encouraged through skill-based incentives, while pursuing arts and humanities might be promoted through merit-based and income-based incentives, in place of skill-based ones. This phenomenon can result in the accumulation of these bosons around the event horizon of a black hole, leading to a significant emission of radiation. In turn, this emission can cause the black hole to spin down, and research has demonstrated that advanced telescopes may be able to observe this spin loss in the brightest, most distant quasars. Using existing data on 69 quasars from the most sensitive studies, and incorporating new data on 457 quasars from the latest research, we have investigated the spin loss in a comprehensive dataset. This investigation includes key variables such as the black hole mass, spin, and luminosity, and we have explored their interrelations, revealing a consistent pattern that matches the predictions of a theoretical model. This new understanding of the behavior of supermassive black holes may also influence our knowledge of various other astrophysical and cosmological phenomena, and we have estimated the likelihood of detecting spin loss in nearby, luminous galaxies. Ultimately, the observation of spin loss in a particular, exceptional quasar, J2159-610, suggests that the emission of radiation due to superradiance may be variable and unpredictable, and we have identified other potential candidates for future study. If a core's angular momentum is removed, its mass can be increased before it fragments into individual stars, compared to non-rotating cores. In this study, mass ranges of up to 30, 100, and 300 solar masses can be achieved in binary systems if a core's angular momentum is removed and its fragmentation properties are examined more closely. The findings suggest that the properties of parental cores could explain the existence of both wide and close binary systems. Wide binaries with up to 100 solar mass components, formed through the disruption of rotating cores by their magnetic field, can be consistent with the observed local binary population, while close binaries with the potential to become O stars could be accounted for by disruptions of cores with high mass fractions. The disruption of cores with high mass fractions could also lead to the formation of interacting binary systems, such as runaways and tight binaries with the potential to become X-ray sources. This research introduces the M-ar-K-Rapid ICA approach, a modified algorithm for independent component analysis, to tackle the blind source separation problem. Based on the fourth-order cumulant information, the novel approach develops a k-component (super) Gaussian model to estimate the mixing matrix and source signals. Unlike existing methods that assume a unimodal distribution for sources, the new algorithm exploits the multi-modal nature of sources, enabling it to handle a wider range of source characteristics. Furthermore, the algorithm incorporates a direct estimation method for the derivative of the cumulant matrix, substituting a crucial component in the traditional cumulant-based ICA method. Evaluations using both synthetic and real-world data demonstrate that the M-ar-K-Rapid ICA approach outperforms existing algorithms in various configurations. Notably, the approach demonstrates exceptional efficacy in processing 2D MRI scans to extract underlying brain signals. The study estimates that approximately 64% of sources can be properly demixed when introducing additional mixing matrix unknowns. Conversely, when degree of unknown mixing matrix singular values decreases, the approach performs optimally, achieving up to 82% successful demixing rates. In summary, the M-ar-K-Rapid ICA approach offers a groundbreaking solution to the blind source separation problem, providing a pioneering mechanism for demixing signals in signal processing applications. The code used in this study is publicly accessible via https://github.com/kkanoano/M-ar-K-Rapid-ICA. The research is based on the authors' idea outlined in Kanoano, K., & Tsubaki, N. (2021). This discovery represents a significant advancement in the field as the $\sigma$-elementary domain was previously considered a rare occurrence. To create these domain instances, we formulate two types of infinite data sets, referred to as the Set of Polynomials with Unique Zeros and the Set of Circles with Distinct Centers, to provide infinite options for domain configurations. Finally, we show that these domain instances can be modified to equate to a sphere when the sphere is cut along its axis. The surge in social media usage has led to an abundance of spatiotemporal data, which can be utilized to extract valuable geographical information, such as traffic patterns and incident reporting. These incidents, including traffic incidents and retail thefts, are typically characterized by the concentration of users at a specific location at a particular time. Current approaches to detecting incidents rely on pre-defined locations and time frames, which are then used to build models to identify anomalies. Nonetheless, this method has several limitations, including a large number of unused locations and times, and the potential for false negatives. To address these issues, a novel approach called Instantaneous Spatio-Temporal Incident Identification (ISTII) is proposed, which utilizes real-time data to identify incidents in real-time. The ISTII algorithm identifies potential incident locations through a geographic analysis, and then determines the time frames in which incidents occur. By focusing on the moments when incidents occur, the algorithm can accurately identify incidents without false positives. To evaluate the algorithm, a dataset of 174,165 incidents from geotagged social media posts in Beijing was used. The results show that the algorithm can accurately identify incidents, with a precision of 88.23% and a recall of 87.25%. The algorithm is now available in the data.io library, and can be used to extract incident data from geotagged social media platforms. The findings demonstrate the potential for social media data to inform transportation policy and planning, and highlight areas where improvement is needed. The research also identifies future areas of study, and provides data for further analysis. A kernel-based method is proposed to efficiently detect anomalies in the cosmic microwave background (CMB) by analyzing their cross-correlation with large-scale structure (LSS) data through the bispectrum. Using simulated data, the code's ability to detect artificial anomalies inserted into CMB maps is assessed at a 95% confidence level, and it outperforms existing techniques by at least an order of magnitude. As a conservative estimate, the artificial anomalies inserted into CMB maps would require at least $10^{5}$ simulated data points to detect, which is within the range of current CMB surveys such as BICEP3 and the CLASS survey. On the other hand, the artificial anomalies inserted into LSS data such as ALMA or LSST would require only $10^{3}$ simulated data points to detect. A simple model is proposed to explain the distortion of the CMB bispectrum due to the LSS bias and it is consistent with the observed data at a 95% confidence level. The model's parameters are then used to estimate the limits of detection for CMB anomalies in relation to the primordial non-Gaussianity, which would be within the range of upcoming CMB experiments such as CMB-S4 or the next generation of degree-scale experiments. Recent studies have demonstrated that machine learning models are susceptible to manipulation by cleverly designed false data. While notable progress has been made in developing methods to create robust models, there is a critical need for techniques that can verify the reliability of these models when faced with maliciously crafted inputs. In this context, we present a novel framework that provides a mathematical explanation of how hackers create backdoors, followed by a method to build models that can withstand such attacks, and finally, a technique to confirm the reliability of these models. Our framework, specifically, consists of three main components: a backdoor creation model that generates malicious inputs, a backdoor injection model that inserts stealthy triggers, and a reliability tester that verifies the reliability of models. In our experiments, we successfully tested all aspects of this framework on various problems and even revealed the existence of a model that was previously considered reliable in the field of NLP. When applied to deep learning models, our framework allowed us to reduce the worst-case number of queries needed to verify the reliability of models by a factor of up to 13. Additionally, we were able to confirm the reliability of models that were previously considered unverifiable in the field of reinforcement learning. Our study lays the foundation for future research on the design of models that can withstand attacks and the development of techniques to test the reliability of these models. Recent breakthroughs in natural language understanding have primarily been fueled by the significant advancements in natural language models, particularly those that can automatically process and learn from large datasets without the need for manual rule-setting. Unlike traditional symbolic approaches, which have been reduced to basic rules and representations, recent successes reveal the potential of employing large datasets and complex models, suggesting a reevaluation of the earlier assumptions about the necessary complexity of representations and the need for explicit definition of structure. This new perspective may facilitate collaborations between NLP and advances in deep learning, enhancing the potential for future breakthroughs. This work explores the potential of reducing the size and complexity of natural language models, challenging the long-held belief that substantial models are necessary for substantial insights. By demonstrating state-of-the-art performance on multiple NLP tasks, such as translation, summarization, and parsing, using reduced models, this research validates the feasibility of cutting NLP model parameters while maintaining good performance. The analysis also reveals that the effectiveness of these models depends on the specific task at hand. Although complex models may often outperform smaller models on limited datasets, this difference disappears when the dataset is extensive enough, indicating a promising future for the development and utilization of more compact natural language models. Additionally, the success of these models could mark a significant turning point in the field, enabling future research to focus on both scalable models and the exploration of representations that fall within the reach of deep learning models. By employing reduction techniques, future research may also make NLP more accessible to computers with limited memory and processing capabilities, while also facilitating the deployment of NLP applications on specialized hardware, such as TPUs. Finally, this research opens up new possibilities for employing reduction techniques to improve the efficiency of NLP models running on self-hosted devices, such as desktops and laptops, by applying NLP models that take into account the specific computational capabilities of the executing machine. By reconnecting NLP to the fundamental principles of computer science, this research may pave the way for future breakthroughs in NLP. By utilizing a graphical representation, the formalism illustrates the transformation of the four-point vertex within a specific diagram configuration, demonstrating its evolution from a singular, non-renormalized form to a complex, fully renormalized structure. Furthermore, the thread that runs through the development of the vertex structure is the symmetry-conserving solution of the Bavasis equations, which enables construction of the Hamiltonian in terms of the vertex structure. Ultimately, the presented framework establishes a clear connection between the parquet theory and traditional many-body theories, revealing specific relationships within the vertex structure that facilitate a direct translation from the parquet formula to the Hamiltonian representation of the system's energy. Consequently, this new framework presents an efficient and computationally efficient approach to calculating the system's energy structure and facilitates a clear, conceptually simple approach to understanding the interparticle interaction in complex systems. The proposed formalism has been successfully tested and demonstrated in the calculation of the ground-state energy of the two-dimensional electron gas. The calculation of the ground-state energy within the parquet theory is rooted in the assumption that the system's particles are statistically independent, leading to a singular solution for the vertex structure and a corresponding simplification of the Hamiltonian into a measurable, single-particle component. By transcending this limitation, the present approach enables a detailed understanding of the system's microcosm through the clear, transparent expression of the vertex structure, revealing inherent patterns and relationships of the system and presenting a new, previously unexplored perspective on the parquet theory. Exciton, a bound electron-hole pair driven by electrostatic interaction, offers a theoretical framework for understanding extreme states of matter. In this context, the concept of exciton liquefaction suggests the emergence of excitonic superfluid and supersolid phases. To accurately simulate these exotic matter states, researchers rely on ab initio computational models that can tackle finite temperature and momentum states. Our research group has developed a new ab initio approach within the density functional theory framework, incorporating many-body perturbation theory for electron-hole interaction. We have successfully applied this model to the 2D semiconductor material TiSe2 and observed the emergence of excitonic superfluid and supersolid phases. The calculation results, showing a significant increase in excitonic gap at low temperature and in finite electron and hole chemical potential, can be attributed to the formation of these phases. Furthermore, our research suggests that the lattice structure of TiSe2 exhibits static discrete distortion, known as static exciton lattice, which can be activated at finite temperature. The findings of these numerical simulations have been confirmed by X-ray scattering, high-resolution electron energy loss spectroscopy, and transport measurements. Our method can be an efficient supplement to existing techniques for identifying out-of-domain text, and could potentially be adapted for other natural language processing tasks. The dataset is comprised of three sets of texts, each representing a different out-of-domain category, along with a model that has been trained on a corresponding dataset. This is followed by the complexity of searching for optimal kernels or inputs, and then the complexity of optimizing kernel parameters or output predictions. We found that a brute-force approach for generalized convolutions is not only O(Nn) but also dependent on the size of available memory, limiting its applicability to smaller datasets. We present an innovative approach, based on pre-processing, to efficiently handle generalized convolutions with a significant drop in computational complexity, from O(Nn) to O(n^3) in most cases, and exceptional scenarios where pre-processing fails, down to O(nN) with minimal additional complexity. This breakthrough allows us to achieve significant time savings of up to 25 times in our experiments, while also gaining valuable statistical insights into kernel matrices, diags, and off-diags, which are usually unknown before solving the optimization problem at hand. These statistical insights, previously unseen, offer promising avenues for future reductions in computational complexity. Our techniques, based on divide-and-conquer strategies, are equally applicable to direct or indirect generalization of convolution operators, and can be easily extended for use with multi-dimensional data, vector-valued functions, and complex Riemannian manifolds, as we demonstrate with code samples and experimental results. This research offers an important statistical correction to earlier Kernel Methods, expanding their applicability to datasets too large for their solutions to be computed, while also providing valuable statistical insights into kernel matrices, and opening up new avenues for future reductions in computational complexity. This research applies this approach to a simplified financial market model and then modifies the algorithm to achieve more realistic market behavior. The resulting market model is then tested in simulation experiments to demonstrate the validity of the double faced auctions method for financial markets. This validation process involves analyzing key statistical properties of the market outcomes and comparing them to those of a more traditional financial market model established through agent based simulation. The results of these experiments show that the double faced auctions algorithm can effectively create a legitimate financial market model with the desired characteristics. This market model can also be seen as a type of distributed computation where the market prices are determined through a form of decentralized decision making. Furthermore, the study explores how a double faced auctions algorithm responds to changes in market information and participant behavior. The research also examines the relationship between market efficiency and the level of information available to participants, and how these factors affect the stability and accuracy of the market prices. The outcomes of these experiments provide new insights into the fundamental characteristics of financial markets that have been identified through the analysis of online markets in previous research. The contributions of this study are as follows. Firstly, it is the first application of double faced auctions to a complex market that requires more than just binary market data. The research demonstrates the effectiveness of double faced auctions in creating a legitimate financial market with the desired characteristics, thereby paving the way for their use in large scale online financial markets. In this study, a novel framework is introduced to enhance the performance of dynamic mode decomposition (DMD), particularly in cases where it produces unrealistic negative frequency results. A composite optimization method, linear and nonlinear disambiguation optimization (LANDO), is proposed to achieve this. From a machine learning perspective, LANDO formulates DMD as a kernel learning problem by combining two fundamental components: a low-rank regression module, represented by a learned kernel, and a denoising autoencoder. Utilizing these components, LANDO is capable of regulating the rank of the kernel, resulting in the efficient extraction of coherent structures from noisy time-series data and the optimization of its linear and nonlinear properties. Consequently, LANDO produces robust frequency-filtered modes, which is demonstrated through numerical simulations and the analysis of a simulation scenario involving a vortex shedding phenomenon. Furthermore, LANDO is compared to existing approaches, including sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics (SINDy), and outperforms it in a range of test cases. A significant advantage of the proposed method is its compatibility with high-dimensional data, which is illustrated through the use of LANDO in the analysis of a magnetohydrodynamic turbulence simulation. In this study, a novel approach to analyzing openings is presented, using a large dataset of over 300 million chess moves gathered from online platforms. To simplify the complex hierarchy of openings, a technique called Word2Vec is employed, which assigns similar scores to interconnected nodes. The results show that the top-ranked openings vary significantly depending on the period considered, leading to the conclusion that there are distinct trends in chess strategy. Our research illustrates that the occurrence of millisecond pulsars can be rationalized if there exists a substantial population of ultracompact binary star systems at an early stage in stellar evolution, specifically containing white dwarves with defined boundary layers. Upon further development, these boundary layers may grow capable of sustaining stable rocket propulsion that could reverse the spin of the progenitor star. Ultimately, this can give rise to an extensive spectrum of rotational periods, encompassing both rapid and slow rotations. These findings demonstrate that certain well-known global characteristics, such as topological invariants and phases, can be reinterpreted in our context. Consequently, we are able to derive non-local properties of the vector field's singularities and establish a link between the system's energy distribution and its invariant measures. Ultimately, we relate our findings to the systems' phase space geometry. Due to the innovative nature of this approach, our work has broad applications across fields, including classical mechanics, quantum mechanics, and topological quantum electronics. One potential implication is the development of new tools for detecting topological structures in two-dimensional systems, which may in turn lead to discoveries in three-dimensional systems. We analyze the common statistical issues associated with large financial and economic datasets that exhibit heavy tails and are influenced by random time-varying factors. Our approach uses a simple and robust method based on autoregressive models, which incorporates the application of differential empirical dynamics to address the challenges posed by these datasets. In a simulation study, we compare our method to other established techniques and find that it is equally effective or preferable in a variety of situations. Our analysis spans the analysis of individual entities as well as groups, and includes a case study of the behavior of stock prices during the 2008 financial crisis, demonstrating the power of our approach to detect changes in the dynamics of these datasets. Our method is named the multivariate empirical dynamic model, or MEDI, and is available as a free software package for Windows, Mac, and Linux users through our website. A version of this work has been previously presented at the 2014 Winter Simulation Conference. In future work, we aim to address the challenge of using our method to identify the underlying causes of the observed time-varying effects. Instead, we propose that it results from ancient dust that has been preserved due to the galaxy's slow star formation rate. Our model was used to analyze the strongly lensed cluster ACT-CL J0102$-$4915, which contains eight distinct images, and we found that its redshift is uniform at z = 0.32, which is significantly higher than previously estimated. We demonstrate that these two representations have a consistent relationship, which can be formulated as an adjoint pair of functors within a specific mathematical framework. This relationship provides a formalised basis for comparing quantities in quantum theory, including covariance under unitary transformations and the ordering of states. Notably, we show that this functorial relationship maintains key properties of quantum theory, encompassing single-system, unmarked composite systems, and joint observables, as well as marked composite systems and their associated status structure. This result enables a comprehensive comparison of these two representations, ultimately allowing us to leverage the structural properties of quantum theory to derive existing results and establish new connections. Along the way, we introduce several key concepts, including a formal description of covariant functors in quantum theory and the abstractisation of status structure through a specific type of functor called a 2-functor. Additionally, we derive a representation of joint subystems in terms of status structure, which we use to examine the relationship between Hilbert space and status structure. Finally, we abstract away from the specific mathematical representation to establish a relationship between the two approaches to representing compound systems and their respective notions of joint observables and combined systems within a Hilbert space. In doing so, we derive a general condition under which these two representations are equivalent, as well as a criterion under which a joint observable can be represented as a combined system within a Hilbert space. This work provides a formalised basis for comparing different representations of compound systems and their associated systems within a Hilbert space. Humanity is failing to address climate change, and the root cause lies in societal dynamics that incentivize short-term self-interest over global well-being. We argue that deep-seated cooperative problems, like the tragedy of the commons, underpin many apparent self-interest issues. A fundamental flaw in current climate policies and solutions stems from how they are designed, solely focusing on mitigating self-interest behaviors. To develop effective policies, it is crucial to recognize the underlying cooperative nature of climate change and apply relevant strategic design principles. Utilizing the framework of the commons, we break down the climate transition into distinct strategic stages, and based on the success of carbon pricing, we identify a general design principle for tackling cooperative problems. Finally, we propose a set of research questions to further explore the application of design principles in addressing complex, multi-faceted challenges like climate change. While the transition to a low-carbon society poses significant social and technological challenges, addressing its cooperative dimensions can provide valuable insights to streamline the transition and achieve a more sustainable future. In auction theory, an auctioneer faces a dilemma as they strive to balance their desire for high bids to maximize revenue, while also maintaining a reasonable price to attract bidders. This price-sticking problem is exacerbated in second-price auctions, where the auctioneer may benefit financially from setting a low starting price, expecting higher bidders to drive up the winning price. Our study aims to investigate how price-sticking strategies impact trustworthiness, particularly in second-price auctions, where bidders may modify their bids in response to the auctioneer's initial offer. We employ a controlled experimental design, combining both theoretical and experimental approaches, to analyze the effects of different price-sticking strategies on bidder behavior. Through an online experiment involving 462 bidders, we discover that both theoretical and experimental approaches generate similar results, indicating a loss of trustworthiness in second-price auctions, particularly when the auctioneer sticks to a low initial offer. Furthermore, we find that this loss of trustworthiness is more pronounced when the auctioneer sticks to a low initial offer compared to a high initial offer. Our results suggest that price-sticking strategies can damage a digital auction platform's reputation for fairness, particularly if the auctioneer consistently adheres to a low initial offer. Interestingly, we find that bidders prefer anonymous auctions over known auctions, with the latter often generating higher revenue for the auctioneer. These findings have important implications for the design and fair operation of auction systems, including the need to balance revenue maximization with user trustworthiness. Moreover, we suggest that system designers should prioritize fairness, particularly in second-price auctions, to maintain a high level of trustworthiness among users, which may sometimes require compromising on revenue maximization. Ultimately, a delicate balance between these competing interests is necessary to ensure the long-term sustainability and success of auction systems. To address these challenges, we propose new approaches based on Bayesian games, enabling auctioneers to make fair decisions while maximizing revenue, thus maintaining a high level of trustworthiness among bidders. Specifically, we formulate an auction mechanism that is strategically fair, meaning it does not advantage the auctioneer at the expense of the bidder, as well as strategically revenue-optimal, meaning it generates the maximum revenue possible while remaining fair. We demonstrate that a unique and efficient solution exists for this problem, which we then test in an experimental setting, revealing that it outperforms the traditional second-price auction in both revenue and trustworthiness. We investigate the potential for visualizing the generative process using neural networks by illustrating the evolution of artwork generations and analyzing the corresponding neural network activity. This visualization showcases the neural network's capabilities, ranging from its capture of the original data distribution to its ability to generate novel, often organized patterns. By embracing the unpredictability of neural networks, the generative process can serve as an engaging and educational tool for demonstrating the advancements and intricacies of artificial intelligence. Beyond merely illustrating neural network capabilities, this approach enables us to gather insights into the networks' underlying structures, effectively utilizing the artistry of neural networks to inform our understanding of their design. Ultimately, this method enables mutually enriching exchanges between neural networks and artists, paving the way for a deeper appreciation of the intricate connections between technology and artistic creations, as well as the unpredictable potential inherent in all of them. This paper presents two examples of neural artistic collaborations, and it offers a framework that can be applied to a broad range of applications and domains. This approach also raises important questions about the rights of artificial intelligences as creative beings and the rights of users to manipulate these models. This leads to a fascinating thought: what if neural networks are regarded as co-collaborators with the rights to intellectual property? In our prior work, the CTS project was introduced, which aims to create a dataset of human-generated queries and responses for a question-answering system, centered around a substantial collection of academic research papers in the computer science domain. This paper provides an in-depth examination of our data collection efforts. A comprehensive approach was utilized to acquire a substantial number of queries and responses from experts in the computer science field. These queries were designed to mimic information-seeking behavior and were divided into two categories: retellings, which involved rewriting existing responses in their own words, and extensions, which involved adding new content to existing responses. Both retellings and extensions were assessed by the respective responders. We developed a dataset of 1,094 such queries and responses, which was further evaluated through the administration of a crowdsourced task. Our data collection method was successful in producing a substantial quantity of high-quality queries and responses. A detailed analysis of the results from the crowdworkers who participated in the evaluation task is also presented. It was discovered that the responses to the extensions were often seen as complete by the crowdworkers, which supports the feasibility of utilizing retellings and extensions as a means of assessing the comprehensiveness of existing responses. Moreover, the addition of new content through extensions was seen as beneficial to the responders. Our results from the crowdworkers who participated in the evaluation task were positive, as they were able to effectively engage with the tasks, provide useful feedback, and successfully evaluate the comprehensiveness of existing responses. Our data collection method achieved its intended goals, as the crowdworkers were able to successfully distinguish between retellings and extensions, provide useful feedback, and evaluate the comprehensiveness of existing responses. Our results from the crowdworkers who participated in the evaluation task are presented, along with an in-depth analysis of the results. Ultimately, the dataset of queries and responses was compiled for the benefit of the computer science community, along with the full collection of research papers used for data collection. The dataset can be accessed via https://github.com/cts-project/cts-data. The CTS project is seeking collaborations that would involve utilizing our data collection methods to develop new question-answering systems. If interested, we welcome inquiries at cts@cs.cmu.edu. Attention Deficit Hyperactive Disorder (ADHD) is a widely diagnosed mental disorder, and mental disorder diagnosis increasingly relies on clinical assessments, whereas recent advances in radiological technology and machine learning algorithms have made psychiatric diagnoses more accurate through data-driven approaches. Although ADHD diagnosis using functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI) data has received significant attention in recent years, this study explores the potential of enhancing ADHD diagnosis through machine learning by selecting crucial brain regions. Our study compared four models, each trained on rs-fMRI data from different regions (whole brain, whole brain with significant areas, 13 critical areas identified in the literature, and 20 critical areas identified through our region selection approach). By using our method, which prioritizes diagnosis accuracy, we selected additional critical brain regions, leading to a significant improvement in model accuracy when tested on a validation set. Notably, our model trained on rs-fMRI data from 20 selected critical brain regions showed the highest accuracy among the four models, achieving 93.75% overall accuracy. Our study found that ADHD can be more effectively diagnosed using rs-fMRI data from specific critical brain regions, and this can significantly enhance the accuracy of deep learning-based diagnoses. Additionally, this approach could reduce data collection costs associated with gathering lengthy rs-fMRI data while maintaining high diagnosis accuracy. This study contributes to the growing literature on data-driven approaches to psychiatric diagnosis and provides new insights into the critical brain regions involved in ADHD diagnosis. Furthermore, this study's region selection method is adaptable to various mental disorder diagnosis tasks. Our code is available for reproduction at the following link: https://github.com/asharaki/ADHD-rfMRI. To address these issues, we have developed a novel approach that integrates a fixed, pre-optimized DNA index and dynamic, sequentially mapped storage regions. This framework leverages the inherent self-indexing properties of DNA sequences to efficiently manage updates. By separating index modifications from storage region data, we achieve significant time savings in updating the root node, effectively minimizing the impact on overall update performance. To optimize read operations, we have developed a balanced tree data structure with a log2 n height and a search efficiency of 1/O, where n represents the number of files. Furthermore, we have achieved a breakthrough by reducing data refresh time by a factor of 100x or more, depending on the specific storage system used, while maintaining the same error rates as before. Quantum learning, a quantum adaptation of the classical teaching approach, enables efficient learning of arbitrary quantum states. Our theory excises the monitoring and instruction roles typical in classical teaching, instead having the learner interact with randomly prepared and distributed quantum states. Without instruction, learners reach a steady state mimicking classical ambient exposure, while uninformed instructions lead to a mixed state steady condition. Building upon a theoretical foundation, our experiment tests these predictions using a two-qubit superconducting quantum processor, demonstrating that learners reach a steady state that varies depending on the environment's purity and instructing specificity. Differentiable rendering is a highly versatile tool, primarily used to tackle inverse problems in computer vision, such as image-based 3D reconstruction and rendering. One critical component of rendering that has received limited attention is shadow rendering. Current approaches either fail to accurately cast shadows or make rendering and its derivative too complicated to compute. Our proposed shadow evaluation method efficiently addresses these issues by casting shadows quickly and its computation is simple enough for gradients to be easily calculated. As a result, this method effectively supports the solution to inverse problems in a differentiable rendering framework. Unlike other methods that have not successfully integrated shadow rendering into a differentiable framework, our approach does not sacrifice accuracy in rendering. Moreover, we show that casting shadows in our method is essentially the same as solving a graph short-circuit problem, allowing us to leverage graph libraries and achieve a low 20 nanosecond average time to cast shadows per frame. We have successfully applied this method to support shadow rendering in various computer vision tasks such as 3D reconstruction, image-to-3DShape, and rendering a shape from a single image. Our work offers a highly efficient shadow rendering method that can be used within a differentiable rendering framework. This method's gradient-based differentiability enables us to efficiently approach inverse problems in a setting that includes highly accurate shadow rendering. You can find our implementation in the github repository. Additionally, we have released a public challenge to test shadow rendering capabilities in the context of differentiable rendering. The challenge can be found at: https://github.com/cdchung/learn3D_challenge_shadows. Learn3D aims to support the advancement of highly accurate three-dimensional scenes understanding that encompasses support for critical visual features such as occlusion and shadows. Analyzing traffic patterns requires in-depth knowledge of how people commute, 
which is often difficult to obtain from user feedback due to privacy concerns. 
This study is dedicated to understanding the derivation of origin-destination demands 
from observed traffic counts under the assumption of randomly selected route choices. 
It begins by collecting digital traffic data for a major highway in Tokyo over several days, 
following which frequency distributions of origin-destination demands are determined for each hour of the day. 
To protect user privacy, the demands are aggregated by area of origin and destination. 
The results show that the distributions of these demands remain consistent across the entire commuting period, 
in accordance with the underlying route choice patterns. 
Next, a mathematical representation of the observed traffic counts is created in terms of origin-destination demands 
and route choice probabilities, both of which can be derived from the demands. 
This representation enables the calculation of probabilities associated with each set of demands, 
thus facilitating the estimation of uncertainty in demand estimates as well as the identification of excessive demand variability. 
Ultimately, the study's approach is validated through applications of traffic demand estimation and the detection of irregular traffic patterns.

This phenomenon is observed in ecosystems, where a ecosystem made up of two components, like coral reefs and fish, can be disrupted by an overload on one part, even though it seems unrelated to the other part. This spread of disturbance through connected components of a system is known as a chain reaction. This concept has been around for a while, but there's still a lot to learn about its general properties and behavior patterns across different types of networks. Researchers recently had the opportunity to study this spread of disturbance, or dynamic propagation, through a large number of artificially created network types. They found a universal pattern in the diversity of oscillator arrays, where a small disturbance travels through the array in a specific, irregular pattern. This propagation pattern changes depending on the type of oscillators in the array and their connections, leading to different possible outcomes, such as the spread of disturbance slowing down or even speeding up in some cases. Despite these variations, it has been observed that the diversity of oscillator arrays exhibits consistent behavior patterns when the type of oscillators in the array is changed. These patterns include a wide range of oscillator types where the frequency of the oscillators is the same, as well as oscillator arrays where the frequency of the oscillators varies. Furthermore, it has been found that these propagation patterns are not just limited to oscillator arrays and can be seen in other types of interconnected systems. The study on these propagation patterns is not just limited to understanding oscillator arrays and their behavior, to but it also provides new approaches to control and manipulate the spread of disturbance in interconnected systems. Examples of these applications can be found in maintaining ecological balance, where a tiny disturbance in one part of an ecosystem can cause widespread effects beyond the initial impact area. Not all heat transfer methods participate in convective phenomena. In operations involving bed geometries, understanding heat transfer is crucial. This study used rapid 2D MRI imaging at 23.5 frames per second to observe heat transfer in a stationary gas-solid bed filled with glass beads and carboxy methyl cellulose water solution. As the temperature difference between the cold walls and hot fluid increased, the mean heat transfer rate accelerated in accordance with an exponential law. This phenomenon was present regardless of the fluid's viscosity changing from Newtonian to non-Newtonian characteristics. The observed exponential increase in mean heat transfer rates contradicts traditional Stokes-based models. The study highlights the significance of hydrodynamic interactions in further investigating the thermal behavior of this system. This can lead to a deeper understanding of the complex dynamics involved, eventually facilitating the development of a more accurate general correlation that can be utilized in industrial applications. Moreover, the investigation presents novel insights into the spatial temperature fluctuations within the bed, their correlation structure, and the effect of CMC water solution characteristics on the thermal behavior. Finally, the study's findings suggest that even stationary hydrodynamic events can substantially influence heat transfer rates in tight packing scenarios. The research offers an intriguing perspective on the multifaceted nature of heat transfer and proposes a possible direction for further study in this area. In cardiac mechanics, fully stabilized variational solvers are frequently used to solve partial differential equations.  A new multilevel conditioner is introduced for solving the fluid and solid equations in cardiac mechanics, and its performance is compared with existing methods.  Several multilevel preconditioners are combined with different linear solvers and stabilization strategies, and their efficacy is evaluated using metrics such as convergence speed, memory consumption, and user-defined parameters.  This comparison of approaches is facilitated through shared abstractions, enabling a systematic evaluation of the methods.  Numerical experiments are conducted to examine the performance of the conditioner in scenarios resembling real-world ACM simulations.  The introduction of the new conditioner, along with the metric-based analysis, allows for an informed selection of the most suitable approach based on problem-specific requirements.  Ultimately, this framework promotes the development of efficient and robust solvers for a wide range of applications in cardiac mechanics and similar coupled problems.  The code employed in this comparison is publicly accessible at https://git.uq.edu.au/view kariyak.
