We first establish the global existence of Lagrangian solution families for the associated transport equations, ensuring they remain regular for a short time. We demonstrate that these solution families exhibit some robust characteristics. We observe that in the presence of sufficient dissipation, solutions converge to a particular equilibrium distribution via an invariant invariant set. However, without such dissipation, some solution families diverge, leading to long-term growth in certain physical quantities such as energy and entropy. Notably, we document an unusual feature where the entropy grows while its growth rate decreases over time, resulting in a concave graph that may have important implications in studying the temporal evolution of non-equilibrium systems. The study also highlights a critical distinction in the long-term behavior of solutions based on the sign of a particular crucial parameter. Overall, this research contributes to our understanding of the long-term dynamics of solutions to the dumbbell model, shedding light on the characteristics of rigorous solutions and their interaction with the underlying model's physical processes. Implementing Internet Access via Broadcast (IAB) on mobile devices is crucial, 
especially in settings where infrastructure support is lacking or limited. 
Highly cost-effective mobile IAB devices can provide connectivity to individuals, 
although the technology faces significant hurdles in providing quality services. 
This study examines mobile IAB implementation, identifies ongoing challenges, 
proposes viable solutions, and highlights key implementation obstacles. 
Additionally, we have compiled a detailed list of relevant literature on mobile IAB. 
To aid in understanding mobile IAB, we have created an appendix illustrating 
the process of sending data from a satellite to a mobile device and interpreting 
received signals. This work aims to contribute to the ongoing discussion within 
the mobile IAB community and serve as a valuable resource for new researchers and 
implementers facing the complexities of mobile IAB implementation. 

Keywords: Broadcast Internet, Mobile IAB, Satellite Internet, IoT, Distributed 
Storage Systems, Machine Learning, Low-Latency Mobile IAB, Underlay Technology. 

This work is inspired by the IEEE Broadcast Wireless Mobility Conference 2020, 
where we contributed to the discussion on mobile IAB implementation.

For many years, finding the optimal configuration of hyperparameters for black-box optimization methods has been a challenging issue. In the context of these methods, hyperparameters are key variables that influence both the algorithm's efficiency and success, yet their optimal values are often difficult to determine. Various strategies have been proposed to rectify this problem, and one prominent approach involves global sensitivity analysis for defining and adjusting hyperparameters through extensive searching within their possible range. This paper presents a thorough investigation of six effective global sensitivity analysis techniques to help evaluate both the ranking and capability of hyperparameters in genetic programming, a hyperparameter optimization method. The analysis was conducted on seven robust test functions under two different scenarios, and the results show that some of these methods successfully prioritize the regulation of the most crucial hyperparameters, while others need further investigation due to their poor performance in distinguishing between essential and less important variables. The study also highlights the significance of considering the optimal value of hyperparameters rather than their overall range, and encourages future research on this aspect within the realm of global sensitivity analysis for optimizing hyperparameters. The source code is available for download at the website https://github.com/Esperanto-GP/Forge-GP-HPO.git. Additionally, the study's results can be accessed via the EPG forum under the label 'Global sensitivity results.' The research aims to contribute to ongoing efforts in developing global sensitivity analysis for optimizing hyperparameters, and may potentially be applied to other advanced optimization methods as well. In light of this, the paper also explores the possibility of adapting this approach to establish overfitting thresholds, which could greatly enhance its value in practical scenarios. The study also examines the extent to which existing global sensitivity analysis techniques rely on random searches, and identifies natural selection as a potential tool to enhance their efficiency and effectiveness. The research also involves a detailed analysis of its computational costs, and demonstrates the feasibility of a comprehensive trial involving 1,000 evaluations, which could contribute to future research in this area. The study also aims to facilitate its replication by listing all the necessary parameters and showing the results in an easily accessible format. The research focuses on global sensitivity analysis as a hyperefficient black-box optimization method, and explores its performance in a comprehensive set of test functions while monitoring selected hyperparameters. The study also examines its success in a scenario with an extensive search and compares its performance with other leading optimization methods while evaluating its efficiency across six prominent global sensitivity analysis techniques. The research also aims to facilitate its replication by listing all the necessary parameters and showing the results in an easily accessible format

Some unresolved issues surrounding these topics contribute to the ongoing debates and uncertainties in quantum mechanics. Furthermore, our analysis in one dimension will often be compared to its counterpart in three dimensions, with the aim of illustrating inherent differences arising from the respective equations. Ultimately, our examination will shed light on unresolved challenges encountered in quantum mechanics. Specifically, our discussion will derive the general plane wave solutions for the Schr\"{o}dinger equation for a free particle and a particle in a potential, -x^2, in three dimensions. We will then redefine the standard quantum mechanical probability density and current such that they are conserved for time-independent potentials. Using this modified definition, we will reevaluate the concept of a bound state and determinacy in initial value problems. Additionally, we will discuss how the results obtained from our analysis in three dimensions differ from their one-dimensional counterparts. Throughout the paper, we will draw upon both well-known and lesser-known results from quantum mechanics to illustrate the unresolved debates and uncertainties in quantum mechanics. Additionally, we will draw parallels with the wave equation in complex analysis to shed light on the unique aspects of quantum mechanics. Long-term reinforcement learning presents a significant challenge in developing robotic systems that can adapt across various tasks while maintaining stable performance. In contrast to short-term learning, which is typically achieved using extensive robotic datasets, lifelong learning aims to combine knowledge from different sources. Unfortunately, evaluating these methods can be complicated due to instability and inconsistent performance across diverse datasets and settings. A typical approach for validating these methods involves simulating a robotic environment and selecting a few learning algorithms for evaluation. However, this approach often presents data scientists with a multitude of uncertain statements rather than clear conclusions. There is a noticeable absence of comprehensive benchmark tests for assessing the overall performance of lifelong reinforcement learning methods. In order to overcome this limitation, we have developed an open-source evaluation framework called \textit{L2Explorer}, which enables straightforward integration of novel robotic tasks, platforms, and learning methods. Utilizing this framework, we have conducted an in-depth evaluation of six prevalent baseline methods and introduced three new techniques that can learn and adapt to various tasks using both offline and online learning approaches. Our study employs a diverse range of robotic settings, including navigation and object-manipulation tasks, demonstrating the need for a more systematic and comprehensive evaluation process. Ultimately, we present two key observations that can inform the development of future lifelong reinforcement learning methods: offline learning can be leveraged for performance improvement, and multi-task learning is beneficial when tasks are related. A detailed description of the benchmark suite and results can be found on our website at https://l2explorer.github.io/. The code is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/l2explorer. A video showcasing the framework can be found on YouTube at https://youtube.com/l2explorer. All software and dataset are freely available for download. \textit{L2Explorer} offers a versatile benchmark suite that can be adapted for various applications and can serve as a resource for developing, evaluating, and training robotic lifelong reinforcement learning methods. In the future, we will maintain and expand the benchmark suite by incorporating new tasks, platforms, and learning algorithms to ensure the consistency and reliability of our results. Additionally, we will establish a collaborative research community focused on the evaluation and development of lifelong reinforcement learning methods. We welcome contributions from the robotic community and will engage in knowledge sharing with researchers, developers, and users of reinforcement learning methods. A comprehensive guide for contributing to L2Explorer can be found at https://l2explorer.github.io/contribution. We look forward to collaborating with the robotic community. All software and dataset are freely accessible. \textit

The $K$ band Liger project at the W. M. Keck Observatory utilizes a custom instrument to capture 443.6 $\times$ 617.2 arcseconds of the sky at a 0.103 arcsecond pitch, which is equivalent to 41.2 $\times$ 48.8 arcminutes of the sky at a 0.010 arcminute pitch, with 10.3 $\times$ 13.6 arcminutes of the nearby sky at a 0.001 arcminute pitch, by employing a 0.630 arcminute field of view at a 0.020 arcminute pitch. Liger's data is processed with a custom data reduction system called DRsKeel, which performs tasks typical of other data reduction software. Although tailored to meet Liger's distinct requirements, DRsKeel shares many similarities with other reduction software. DRsKeel's development involved a significant connection to the scsst tool, used for extracting data from various formats, as well as other software utilities like amy and csh. The connection between DRsKeel and these tools necessitated a substantial amount of coding and data processing connectivity. The ultimate goal of Liger is to combine the observations from the Keck C. E. K. 30m telescope and the Maunakea Telescope at a high level, which is known as 4D Spectroscopy, and is aimed at future applications. We will discuss the specifics of Liger's data processing and the connections between various software tools. Additionally, we will elaborate on the challenges we faced and our plans to address the forthcoming challenges as the Maunakea Telescope comes online. By applying a linearly polarized excitatory optical field, we demonstrate the capability to consistently align two or more excitonic condensates without relying on carrier transport. The systematic investigation of our findings indicates that the degree of alignment can be optimally manipulated by adjusting the optical driving power and linear polarization angle, as well as the system's anisotropic splitting energy. Notably, our research also reveals the presence of robust two-component excitonic condensate that forms as a result of the spontaneous generation of circularly polarized components. The applicability of this alignment method to emerging fields such as biophotonics and micro-nanoscale optics holds great promise for future development. Overall, our research provides a foundation for the exploration of linear alignment in excitonic systems and their potential implementation in all-optical linear lithography and other applications. The development of this technique may also lead to the discovery of other unforeseen applications in the field of biophotonics and micro-nanoscale optics. The underlying mechanism of our method could potentially be translated to other systems such as superfluids, Bose-Einstein condensates, and spinor exciton condensates among others. Furthermore, the all-optical alignment of excitonic systems in our research may also be interpreted as a form of optical induction of macroscopic spin polarization, thereby opening avenues for implementing various optical writing techniques in excitonic systems. The technique described in this research may also be generalized and applied to the alignment of multiple excitonic condensates with distinct excitation profiles and polarizability patterns, thereby expanding its practical applications in the alignment of complex multi-component excitonic systems that may be of considerable interest in the field of biophotonics and micro-nanoscale optics. Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, of size k and comprised of integers, share a sumset with a size near 2k, then A and B exhibit considerable similarity to arithmetic progressions. In this paper, we enhance this by eliminating the 'near' condition, allowing for a more precise representation of A and B in terms of arithmetic progressions. To achieve this, we utilize Euler's exponential polynomial equation solution to tackle a corresponding issue involving subgroups of abelian groups. Additionally, this proves a long-standing conjecture of Pl\"{u}cker. The method we've developed could yield further significant outcomes. Lastly, a related question concerning the sumsets of two k-element sets, also of integers, remains open in this paper, yet it holds implications far beyond the scope of this paper. The problem is particularly relevant to a long-standing Carnoley-Littlefield conjecture. 

Note that the solution to both the previously mentioned problems will likely require a heavy reliance on analytical tools not used here. In particular, solving the sumsets of two k-element sets, also of integers, could likely involve heavy integration with Deligne's work on Gaussain sums. 

To conclude, we apply an enhanced version of Freiman's 3k-4 theorem to tackle Euler's exponential polynomial equation solution, yielding significant outcomes in this paper. Furthermore, this paper generalizes and reworks many existing proofs to provide this new enhancement. Lastly, we apply this new theorem to tackle both the subgroup and the sumsets of two k-element sets, also of integers, problems. 

Finally, we note that the key challenge in freiman's 3k-4 theorem lies in its characterization of the 'near' condition, yielding size constraints on A and B that can be relaxed as shown in this paper. To do this, we use transmission eigenfunctions in both media and assume they are analytically extended into the other. By examining their asymptotic behavior near the interface, we solve for the boundary using the Kelvin transformation, effectively reducing the problem to a special case of the generalized Dirichlet-to-Neumann map. This approach enables us to solve the inverse problem either by transforming the Kelvin map into a linear operator or by resolving the boundary explicitly through its Taylor series expansion. These methods are demonstrated with numerical examples showcasing the effectiveness of boundary identification in the case of a sphere. Since transmission eigenfunctions are used, the identified boundary is common to both media. The methods employed here can also be adapted for solving non-coinciding interface problems by incorporating weights based on the established methods. A key advantage of our approach is its reliance on relatively few parameters for boundary representation, thereby facilitating efficient numerical projections. In the realm of finite groups, a subgroup is inherently fixed by an element of the group G, denoted as G-subgroup. We introduce a new parameter, α(G), which represents the maximum number of subgroups of a finite group G, all of which are subgroups of a fixed subgroup H of index d in G. We prove that α(G) is finite and establish an upper bound, showing that it cannot exceed (2e_G)^(m+1), where e_G signifies the largest prime exponent that divides the order of G, and m represents the largest prime factor of the order of G. We further demonstrate that this upper bound is effective and can be easily calculated in numerous instances, thereby providing a definitive upper limit on the quantity of subgroups of a finite group. We gather substantial evidence to support the conjecture that α(G) is indeed less than or equal to (e_G^2, m+1), which would yield an optimal solution. We also present comprehensive data on the quantities of subgroups with specific indices and orders in various finite groups to illustrate the utility of the proposed parameter, α(G). We incorporate the use of contemporary computational tools, encompassing the functionality of GAP-4, to acquire this data. Finally, we record an intriguing open question related to the general framework of finite subgroups. We derive two distinct approaches to address this query, both of which offer valuable insights but require additional investigation to resolve the issue. We also make a distinct representation of finite subgroups, encompassing their orders and indices, which might be useful in the broader context of finite group theory. We present two distinct systems of linear equations that represent finite subgroups, thereby offering a novel perspective on the underlying mathematics. We also obtain a remarkable connection between the combinatorial domain of finite subgroups and the analytical realm of linear equations, which might facilitate the application of powerful tools from analytic number theory to the study of finite subgroups. In 2002, Adams-Bashforth-Moulton Sympson proposed an H2 formula for evolving Hamiltonian differential equations with variable time steps. Although the H2 formula has been widely used due to its stability and high order, our current study reveals that it achieves only second-order accuracy. We demonstrate this by performing a thorough varational analysis, and then derive an improved formula of order 2.5. In order to refine this new formula, we carried out a comprehensive 14-stage Adams-Bashforth Forecasting Finite Difference analysis. Furthermore, our results also indicate that the standard 4-stage Adams-Moulton formula possesses order 1.5, and we have therefore developed a 6-stage Adams-Moulton variant with order 2. We also investigate the behavior of our new formulas in the presence of singular forces, and showcase their effectiveness through various numerical examples. Our study has therefore provided a basis for the improvement of the Adams-Moulton H2 formula. (C) 2018 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved. The problem of visual relationship detection (VRD) encompasses a range of difficulties in computer vision and natural language understanding that converge in the form of a challenge: accurately identifying and describing the relationships between objects within an image. A key aspect of this task is mitigating the issue of false positives, which not only hinders deep learning model performance but also hinders human interpretation. To address this, we introduce the False Positive Mitigation (FPM) dataset, consisting of 20,000 human-annotated false positive samples, alongside the development of a new dataset, FPM-Arts, derived from the SemAnt dataset. A comprehensive framework for mitigating false positives, referred to as the FP-Mixture Framework, is also proposed. By integrating the principles of this framework into existing models, the accuracy of deep learning models can be enhanced, as demonstrated by our experiments on the VRD task. Furthermore, we introduce the FPM-Arts dataset and conduct an in-depth analysis of its anomalies, leveraging its unique characteristics as a counterbalance to the challenges posed by real data. By examining these anomalous data points, also known as mode II errors, the underlying reasons for model dysfunction can be understood, as opposed to mere accuracy augmentation, allowing for a deeper grasp of model flaws and their implications. A comprehensive approach to new task creation, grounded in theoretical knowledge and informed by counterbalanced data, is presented, which can be applied to a range of problems in the area. Efficient implementation of NMMs (Numerous Constant Multiplications) is crucial for various applications where infinite precision calculations are performed in a finite number of bits to avoid overflow issues at high speeds. In this study, we explore new approaches for achieving low hardware costs in NMMs through multiplierless design techniques. By comparing different hardware configurations for implementing NMMs, such as those based on Selective Linear Combination (SLC) and Linear Combination of Selective Weighted Linear Search (LC-SWLS) methods, we identify key hardware factors that affect multiplierless design and propose several hardware optimization strategies. Additionally, we examine hardware corruption which can occur in multiplierless designs and propose a novel error analysis method that identifies the most sensitive coefficients in SLC and LC-SWLS designs. Our experiments demonstrate that, compared to previous methods such as GenO, existing hardware configurations can perform optimally with minimal hardware requirements. Furthermore, we have enhanced the hardware efficiency of multiplierless designs based on SWLS without compromising the functional accuracy. As a result, we have obtained a significant reduction in hardware costs of up to 87.5% for certain applications over previous implementations. Our proposed design has also shown a significant performance improvement, with up to 2.16 times faster speed, and requires significantly fewer inputs, with up to 10.3 times fewer bits, for certain applications. This substantial gain in efficiency was accomplished with the support of advanced hardware design tools. Our study presents the first investigation on the hardware efficiency of multiplierless designs based on SWLS without compromising the functional accuracy. Our work is relevant to applications such as audio coders, decoders and video encoders where NMMs are frequently applied with limited bit sizes. Our study also sheds light on the sensitivity of hardware efficiency to design parameters and provides insights into the optimal configuration of sensitive coefficients for improved hardware efficiency. Our study has further extended the application of NMMs to complex scenarios such as large-scale NMMs with thousands of terms and high-bit lengths over 14 bits. Our research assesses whether the Earth's radio activity could be caused by particles emitted from primordial black holes. The rate at which these black holes consume matter from the surrounding environment is significant, leading to a theory that they could be responsible for the phenomenon of (mini-)shell shocking. A population of these black holes is believed to exist, with some estimates suggesting they could comprise up to 10% of the total stellar mass density in the galaxy. A key aspect of our research is the emission of $e^+e^-$ pairs near the Schwarzschild event horizon, resulting in a high-energy burst that could be detected as radio signals when annihilated matter falls towards the black hole. Initially, we determine the rate at which these black holes should occur based on the overall number density of matter in the galaxy, and find that this rate is significantly higher than standard astrophysical sources. However, we also account for various factors that could reduce this occurrence rate, including the black holes' original formation as neutron star binary mergers, and the rate at which they would consume matter from the surrounding environment if they existed in the galaxy's disc. Ultimately, our findings suggest that these black holes could be responsible for a significant background radio signal, with levels as high as 10^-3 Kerr electromagnetic bursts per year per gram of galactic material, and that further investigation is needed to determine their role in the phenomenon. The temporary increase in radiation as matter approaches the event horizon, combined with a potential population of these black holes, leads to a unique setup with numerous observational consequences, and we use this theory to explain various phenomena, including short-duration radio signals, and the temporary increase in radiation as matter approaches the event horizon. Additionally, we explore the potential for these black holes to be detected through radio spectroscopy, and find that certain experimental designs could be modified to detect these rare events. Finally, we utilize our model based on these black holes to estimate the extent to which they could contribute to the diffuse background radiation across various energy scales, and find that their contribution is significantly higher than standard astrophysical sources above the energy threshold of 10 MeV. As a result, we propose that these rare events could be responsible for a significant component of the diffuse background radiation across various energy scales. This paper presents the Virtual Protected Framework, a modern, high-performance, and energy-efficient processor architecture designed for extremely secure computing environments. The VP-F framework incorporates advanced, hardware-enabled obstacle protection at multiple levels within a standardized pipeline sequence to safeguard against malicious programs and side-channel attacks. Each stage in the pipeline is engineered to safeguard against specific types of threats through an innovative obstacle protection method, which leverages the Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) protection offered by modern General-Purpose Processors (GPPs). This approach, integrated into a standardized five-stage pipeline, delivers efficient and robust protection against diverse security risks. Furthermore, our study, conducted using the VP-F platform, demonstrates substantial performance improvements over existing obstacle protection methods in both encrypted and decrypted environments. This pioneering work lays the foundation for a novel, hardware-enabled obstacle protection technique, enhancing both security and processing efficiency in future computing systems. In particular, we explore the integration of this framework in blockchain-based applications, an area where we suspect this technology to be particularly useful in the future. Our research focuses on a distinct problem by considering it for constrained inputs, specifically those with certain defined limitations in their incidence matrices. We've developed an innovative approach for semantic segmentation, facilitated by hyperspectral images, which can replace the need for labeled data in the training process of a semantic segmentation model. By taking advantage of the enhanced features provided by hyperspectral images, we've designed a model that outperforms other methods, achieving a 44.3% pixel-level accuracy on the Cityscapes dataset benchmark. Notably, our model's performance excels, particularly in categories that were previously underperformed, such as 'parking' and 'bus'. By integrating a bi-directional encoder and an extended decoder, our model, called HEBS, showcases outstanding efficiency, consisting of multiple compact modules, totaling 13 successive operations, thereby securing a significant computational advantage. Consequently, our model's feature extraction efficiency is significantly boosted. Extensive visual studies demonstrate the abilities of HEBS in effectively capturing detailed high-frequency components and robustly segmenting diverse urban scenes, encompassing intricate architectures and vibrant vegetation. Moreover, a comparative study in various settings, including scale factors and image resolutions, consistently showcases the superior performance of HEBS over other baseline models. Lastly, the compatibility of HEBS with other widely-used semantic segmentation methods has been verified, thereby paving the way for numerous possible modifications to these methods. The proposed model offers an attractive alternative for a wide range of tasks in semantic segmentation. Comprehensive source code and results can be accessed at https://github.com/IndigoPurple/HEBS. The coronal mass ejection-driven shock wave, triggered by solar wind interactions with Earth's magnetic field, has been studied through numerical simulations in three parts: a global three-dimensional MHD model, a solar coronal heliosphere model, and a kinetic Vlasov model. By integrating these simulations in a sequence, researchers were able to examine the effects of shocks on the solar wind and Earth's magnetic field, particularly with respect to the phenomenon of solar wind acceleration in the heliosphere, which has been a topic of debate. Model coupling showed that the magnetic field's energy growth in the heliosphere was consistent with observations, and the results implied that the solar wind acceleration could be attributed to the interaction with planetary magnets, including Earth's, in a broader context. Furthermore, the simulation outcomes suggest that the acceleration of solar wind protons proximal to Earth's magnetic field may be attributed to angular momentum transfer from geospheric particles, rather than planetary interaction alone. This study provides new insights into solar system interactions and the processes governing the heliosphere and its connection to Earth's magnetosphere. Finally, the results imply that solar system isolation due to a planetary boundary may be a misleading concept, and planetary interaction can actually influence the surrounding interplanetary medium, especially in terms of magnetic field coupling and particle transfer. The study also highlights the importance of considering cosmic context and angular momentum transfer mechanisms in understanding shock waves and solar wind acceleration. The code used in this research is available for public use through the http://sol.gong.ucla.edu/portal/Code.html website. Future work will involve further modeling of solar wind protons within kinetic frameworks and the application of co-smoking gun techniques to evaluate theoretical models and observations consistently. Key words: solar wind, acceleration, planetary interaction, shock waves, kinetic Vlasov model, heliosphere, coronal mass ejections, angular momentum transfer, cosmic propagation, solar wind protons, kinetic heliosphere, heliosphere simulation, co-smoking gun technique. Notably, the research reveals that the acceleration of solar wind protons can be attributed to two processes: the interaction of planetary magnets and angular momentum transfer from geospheric particles, which is a previously unappreciated mechanism. The study also implies that solar system isolation due to a planetary boundary may be a misleading concept

In a standard RAM model with cell content initialization and unlimited-sized integers, we establish a theory explaining which algorithms can be performed within a constant number of steps $k$ and with at most $c$ memory accesses. This results in a theoretical bound of $c\geq k$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that $c$ is equal to $k$ under two distinct conditions: when the algorithm utilizes $k$ steps of execution and memory accesses are free, or when the algorithm requires $k$ memory accesses and execution is free. Combining these findings yields the conclusion that an $f(k)$ step algorithm using $k$ steps must also require $f(k)$ memory accesses using $k$ steps. Building on this, we derive a general method for determining the time complexity of an algorithm executed on a RAM with unlimited-sized integers, which applies to a wide range of operations including multiplication, division, modulo operations, and square root functions. Ultimately, we prove that these operations can be performed within a constant number of steps $k$ and with at most $k$ memory accesses only when the inputs fit within a polynomial range of size $O(k^c)$ for a given exponent $c$. Finally, we present an application of our theory to prove lower bounds for a comprehensive list of problems. These include approximate $k$-clique problems, partitioning problems, and other partitioning-related problems. The derived bounds are precise and offer the best known results, surpassing all previously established limits. For example, we prove that finding a $2/3$ clique in every $3$-partite graph requires more than $k$ steps, a more precise lower bound than what was previously known for $k$ steps. Similarly, we establish that partitioning the vertices of a $k$-clique into two groups to make both groups $k/2$ cliques is impossible in less than $k$ steps. These and other detailed examples are provided in the paper along with further verification that the derived bounds are tight in every case. The proposed approach offers a unified valve to measure time complexity, providing a precise evaluation of the time required to solve a given problem. The only input information needed for this evaluation is whether the problem can be solved within a constant number of steps $k$ and with at most $k$ memory accesses, a condition we refer to as $k$-feasible. The time complexity of a given program can be determined as $f(k)$ if the program is $k$-feasible

To facilitate effective session-based suggestion, we should consider two essential factors: relevance and diversity. To improve relevance, we focus on crafting suggestions with high likelihoods of being clicked. Conversely, to achieve diversity, we aim to suppress frequent item interactions. Notably, existing recommendation models overlook the interplay between relevance and diversity. In this work, we introduce an innovative two-stage framework, self-guided graph co-training, to harmoniously integrate relevance and diversity. The framework comprises two core components - session-based graph attention network and item interaction-guided graph attention network - working in tandem to enhance both suggestion quality and diversity. The former generates initial suggestions, then leverages user behavior within each search session to guide the second model in identifying under-interacted high-quality items. In turn, the latter utilizes the session-based graph attention network's output to enhance the first model's performance. Through joint training, the framework enables the two models to complement each other, ultimately yielding a distributed set of suggestions that consider both relevance and diversity. In our experiments, our approach demonstrates superior performance over prominent baselines on two established datasets, achieving an average 0.44 and 0.35 improvements in click-through-rate and diversity, respectively. Notably, the framework surpasses state-of-the-art session-based recommendation models while achieving a comparable outcome in terms of relevance. In a real-world setting, our approach also demonstrates a significant 11.2% and 10.6% increase in average session-based suggestion quality and diversity, respectively. The code and data used in this study can be accessed via the GitHub repository https://github.com/Chen-543/SBGCR. Furthermore, a pre-trained model is available at https://github.com/Chen-543/SBGCR/tree/main/model_pretrain. In addition, we have released the dataset preprocessed in Python via the link https://github.com/Chen-543/SBGCR/tree/main/dataset_preprocessed. This data release facilitates easy access to the pre-processed data, enabling other researchers to build upon this study. The empirical analysis and findings illustrate that considering diversity in session-based suggestion enhances its overall quality when compared to models prioritizing relevance alone. Moreover, we have analyzed the established datasets used in this study, revealing a notable absence of diverse items in search sessions and the frequent interaction with top-ranked items. These findings validate the approach of addressing relevance and diversity concurrently in session-based suggestion. In various object classification tasks, particularly in visual cognition and artificial intelligence, the role of recurrent neural networks (RNNs) is increasingly acknowledged. Unlike traditional feedforward networks, RNNs are capable of harnessing object features at different scales and levels, ultimately leading to better classification performance. This study aims to uncover the underlying processing strategy used by RNNs in object classification. Utilizing a controlled dataset with explicitly defined category and non-discriminatory attributes, we observed that RNNs trained on object classification exploit these attribute categories to optimize processing and improve classification efficiency. Notably, the temporal dimension was found to be effectively utilized by the RNNs in integrating attribute information. This work provides the first evidence of RNNs relying on pre-existing category structures, thereby extending the scope of RNNs beyond those trained on sequential data. Instead, these results suggest RNNs can adapt to various data types and exploit pre-existing structure in the information being processed. Overall, this study offers a deeper understanding of the role of RNNs in object classification, aiding in the development of future datasets and data types designed to effectively utilize the temporal processing capabilities of RNNs. Finally, this work has the potential to further illuminate the cognitive mechanisms underlying object classification in the human brain. All code used to simulate the data and analyze the results can be accessed at https://github.com/JulianTassa/OrthogonalObjectAttributes_RNN. This study is a continuation of previous research on the cognitive biases influencing object classification in the human brain, as detailed in a recent review by Rahtz et al. (2020) and Gaurino et al. (2022). Additional information on this topic can be found in Tassa et al. (2022). Experimental data discussed in this study is available for download at https://neurobias.ugent.be/objectattributes/. The UGent Neural Cognition Unit kindly facilitated access to the experimental data. Despite numerous studies on non-Hermitian topology, the influence of correlations remains a significant unknown factor in topology-induced phenomena. Our research demonstrates that inter-electron interactions can drastically alter the point-gap topology in one-dimensional systems, as seen in a modified version of the non-Hermitian Peierls model. We simulate two distinct scenarios: one with independently moving electrons and another with correlated electrons in a same-spin paired state. Notably, our results show that the correlation between electrons significantly alters the point-gap topology, changing it from a quantized charge transfer in the independent electron system to a non-quantized charge transfer in the correlated electron system. Our study reveals that the point-gap topology is sensitive to the specific many-body effects emerging in interacting systems, as the emergence of a Kondo lattice is sufficient to eliminate the topological charge transfer. Our discoveries provide valuable insights into the role of correlations in non-Hermitian topology, encouraging further exploration of the interconnected roles of interactions and driving fields in non-Hermitian topological systems. Furthermore, our research has real-world applications, as interactions are present in many systems, such as those described by the non-Hermitian Hubbard model. Based on our analytical findings, we predict that the absence of independent electron mobility would convert any point-gap topology into a bulk band structure, while correlations could still induce zero-dimensional localized states and alter the electron density in the confined region. Our predictions may be verified through experimental observation using scanning tunneling spectroscopy or other techniques. Ultimately, our research lays the groundwork for the utilization of point-gap topology to manipulate electron mobility in novel materials with correlated effects, thereby opening the door for innovative applications in quantum technology and related fields. Additionally, our study highlights the distinct topology-induced phenomena resulting from independent electron mobility and correlations, thereby differentiating them from one another. In this regard, we propose that correlations can be viewed as a unique mechanism for controlling electron mobility, as opposed to the driving fields traditionally used in the study of non-Hermitian topology. Furthermore, our research indicates that correlations can be utilized to'switch on' quantum conductivity in specific regions of a metal surface, thereby expanding our understanding of quantum transport and the design of efficient metal-based quantum devices. Lastly, our study demonstrates that the surface conductivity due to correlations can coexist with non-Hermitian-induced currents, thereby exhibiting complementary behaviors, as observed in the surface charge density and current density distributions displayed in our figures. Ultimately, our discoveries are expected to foster further research in the interconnected fields of quantum

The constructed sets meet the requirements of Golay complementary sets, with one set's elements being non-primitive, while the remaining three sets have primitive elements. The proposed sets serve as a foundation for developing Golay complementary sets of larger sizes, with potential applications extending to differential sets and squares. Moreover, these pair-wise complementary sets can be utilized in the creation of Golay complementary sets with fivefold, sixfold, and sevenfold combinatorial symmetry. The developed sets exhibit a high level of efficiency in their element distributions. Specifically, the distance between any two elements within each set is shown to be greater than or equal to the size of the set's smallest circle divisor, with this minimum distance achieved by the set's elements being within the same circle. Additionally, the proposed sets exhibit a high level of arithmetic operations simplicity, rendering them computationally efficient. The set's non-primitiveness property can be bypassed by utilizing a rotation of the set's elements, thereby producing a set with purely primitive elements. The general methods used for constructing these pair-wise complementary sets can be adapted to create numerical grids with a high level of symmetry, which can further be modified to generate numerical sequences exhibiting similar properties. The developed sets may also be directly utilized in the construction of differential sets and squares, thereby simplifying their creation process. Lastly, these pair-wise complementary sets can be employed in the construction of squares with fivefold, sixfold, and sevenfold combinatorial symmetry, thereby simplifying their construction process. Through these analyses, we have determined the Higgs boson's width, and also constrained its interaction with high-energy vectors, including a set of limits in model-independent scenarios. By combining on-shell and off-shell production projections, we have established the most stringent constraints to date on the Higgs boson's width, with its value estimated to be less than 0.246 TeV (at 95% confidence level). Additionally, we have obtained a set of precise constraints on the Higgs boson's interaction with high-energy vectors, with their strengths quantified in terms of momentum transfer Q and photon pseudorapidity |η|, spanning a wide range from 20 GeV to 200 GeV and -2.4 to 2.4, respectively. Further, we have found that the Higgs boson's interaction with high-energy vectors is generally consistent with the Standard Model predictions, with deviations not exceeding 65% in any given scenario. Several breakthroughs in solving various important problems efficiently have been achieved through soft optimization (SO) techniques, which can be easily adapted to tackle other challenging issues. Despite several available implementations, designing an SO library remains an underexplored area in research. To fill this gap, we present an open-source framework for developing various SO methods efficiently. Our proposal includes a comprehensive so-called LibOPT, which is based on Python and C++ to ensure maximum flexibility. LibOPT is designed as a modular, multi-objective optimization library, allowing it to be extended with different SO methods efficiently. We establish a formal framework for the Scott framework of PCF within univalent type theory, without relying on choice principles.  To achieve this, we define a type theory specifically tailored to describe domain theory, which we demonstrate is equivalent to a known domain theory known as cpcf.  Building on this, we form the type theory's lifting domain, allowing us to prove that it satisfies the necessary properties for the Scott framework.  Notably, the key zero-difference property hinges on univalence.  Although we focused on developing a pure type theory, the results enable constructing a denotational semantics for PCF, and we show that it is equivalent to a standard semantics for the language.  The new Scott framework provides a natural means for defining and reasoning about partiality in univalent type theory.  It turns out that the chosen domain theory results in a natural encoding of booleans as a pair, rather than a single unit type, which we show yields a simpler semantics.  The work should contribute to expanding the repertoire of type theories that can be used for denotational semantics.  It may also serve as an inspiration for other applications of univalent type theory, including programming language design and proof-assistant development.  The full proof has been formalized in Coq and is available at https://hal.inria.fr/hal-03339533. This research introduces an algorithmic method for text summarization that employs a graph-based strategy, specifically designed for concise document comprehension. Unlike existing approaches that rely on pre-existing graph structures, this technique constructs a node-weighted graph from a dataset of source text articles, with each text partitioned into equal components, to facilitate the extraction of key information. This paper introduces an innovative Framework for Term Prediction, FTPTP. It's a two-part system that learns from context-specific data in two ways: first, by analyzing instances of knowledge units in various contexts, and then by identifying similar situations that contain the predicted knowledge unit. The framework is comprised of two key models: the Knowledge Base Model and the Situation Model. The Knowledge Model leverages Bayes' theorem to determine the probability of a knowledge unit given a context, while the Situation Model trains a classifier to recognize instances of knowledge units in different contexts. The framework can be adapted to address two common challenges in knowledge unit prediction: sparse data and false positives. Our experiments on two large datasets demonstrate that the FTPTP framework significantly enhances the accuracy of traditional Bayes' rule-based term prediction models. The framework achieved a 14.72% relative improvement in F1-score on the Wikipedia dataset and a 8.09% relative improvement in F1-score on the Knowledge Graph dataset. The predicted knowledge units also demonstrated high relevance and coverage, with 97.46% and 98.63% of predicted knowledge units correctly identified on the Wikipedia and Knowledge Graph datasets, respectively. The predicted knowledge units also showed a high level of semantic similarity with the actual knowledge units, with a mean cosine similarity of 0.485 on the Wikipedia dataset and 0.441 on the Knowledge Graph dataset. The FTPTP framework can be applied to diverse datasets and knowledge-based models, such as Naive Bayes, with good results. We have developed a Tsallis form of holographic dark energy (HDE) model with a new variable, called dark vitality, which originates from the Quintessence framework. A possibility of considering space-time fill energy as a complex field has been introduced. By applying the Randall-Sundrum I model, where the Friedmann-Robertson-Walker metric is used, we derived the model's equations of motion in the low-energy limit and determined the existing conditions for which the model's dynamics are governed by the Tsallis form of HDE model. Further, we analyzed the cosmological parameters, such as the deceleration parameter, the density parameters, and the Efstathiou parameter, in two scenarios. One scenario assumes that the real and imaginary components of the quintessence field are not interconnected, while in the other scenario, the imaginary component is connected to the real component via an equation that we formulated. Through this analysis, we concluded that the imaginary component of the quintessence field plays a crucial role in understanding the phases of HDE and, therefore, is an essential component of the model. Based on this understanding, we predicted the phase transition time for the model and found that it occurs approximately $2.14\times10^3$ Gyr ago. Additionally, we found that the model is in the phantom phase, which is in accordance with recent cosmological observations. For the sake of completeness, we presented the variation of the deceleration parameter with the dimensionless variable $\ln a$ and found that it is consistent with the prediction made by Berman in 2002. Finally, we compared the performance of the model in predicting the Hubble parameter with the observations and found that the predicted values of the Hubble constant by the model match with the observed value. Based on this comparison, we estimated the model parameters, namely the non-extensive frustration and the fractal frustration parameters, using two different methods, and found that their values are in the range $0.5895\leq q_0\leq0.5898$ and $10^{-30}\leqk_0\leq10^{-29}$. Therefore, the model is compatible with the observation of the Hubble constant. Finally, we concluded that the model, which is based on the Tsallis form of HDE with a new variable, called dark vitality, offers an excellent explanation of the present cosmological scenario. Furthermore, as the on-shell parameters vanish (massless limit), our method exhibits a seamless transition to the standard Pauli-Villars scheme, making it an effective method for both massive and massless scenarios. This research examines the possibility of forming composite stars, consisting of deconfined quark matter and neutron matter, governed by the Sigma-omega-rho model for quarks and the MIT and NJL models for various quark concentrations. To investigate this, we analyzed the bulk properties of the quark matter in its ground state, specifically the energy density, pressure, and bulk modulus as a function of the alphas quark concentration, and also computed the speed of sound within the matter. Our results show that quark matter with concentrations below 10% can exist in three distinct states - condensed, mixed, and deconfined - whereas the deconfined state dominates for concentrations above 10%. Additionally, we found that the pressure of the quark matter increases with the concentration of the quarks, and that the speed of sound within the matter is significantly subsonic. Our findings indicate that the boundary between neutron matter and quark matter is strongly dependent on the quark concentration in the latter. Utilizing the thermodynamic properties of both types of matter, we identified the potential existence of composite stars, consisting of a neutron core surrounded by quark matter, and also uncovered possible possibilities for three-star configurations consisting of a neutron core, quark matter, and nucleon matter. Our research presents a new perspective on compact stars, with the potential to be tested through the analysis of future gravitational-wave data. Our study also highlights the potential links between quark matter, nucleon matter, and liquid stars, prompting the need for further investigation. Our analysis further reveals that the mass radius slope of the compact star can be positively influenced by the presence of quark matter, and that this effect can be significant at a 95% confidence level. Our research further examines the behavior of beta-decay processes within quark matter, comprising various quark concentrations, and shows that these processes are possible in quark matter, and that they significantly affect the energy balance of the matter, and force quark matter to condense into a more stable state. Our research also reveals that quark matter with high quark concentrations are resistant to radial changes, and that this phenomenon is accompanied by a significant increase in pressure within the matter. Furthermore, we found that quark matter with high quark concentrations have a tendency to collapse under external forces. Our study also presents new perspectives on the nature of quark matter, and that quark matter is weakly interacting, and composed of omega and rho mesons, and that the Sigma model is not applicable to quark matter

Recent studies on oscillators have successfully applied the concept of
nonlinear dynamics to gain insights, but the application of this approach to
understand the behavior of laser-cooled atoms in complex optical structures is
still an unresolved issue. Our research investigates the thermodynamic properties
of a system consisting of $N$ interacting bosonic atoms within an array of
dissipative optical lenses, where the interaction is controlled by a optical
magnetic field. Our findings reveal that the system exhibits distinct thermodynamic
characteristics, such as a vanishing heat transfer and a specific heat capacity,
in the long-term steady-state regime. Furthermore, we computed the steady-state
correlations and entanglement of the atom field in the dissipative array and
evaluated their reliability by assessing the convergence of the correlation
functions and entanglement as a function of array size and phase space resolution. 
Our research shows that the thermodynamic properties of the system can be
quantitatively explained by fractionally integrating the open dynamical system,
which bridges the gap between nonlinear dynamics and the underlying quantum
dynamics. By identifying the terms that dominate the thermodynamic properties and
isolating the contributions from individual units in the array, our study
provides a valuable framework to understand the discrete building blocks of
complex optical structures and enables their systematic analysis and characterization. 
Lastly, the application of our analysis could pave the way for a novel approach
to understand and manipulate the behavior of cold atom systems and could be
extended to other dissipative systems like superconducting qubits and cavities.

The thermal Hall response, determined by $\sigma_{HT}$, serves as a thermal counterpart to the electrical Hall coefficient, $\sigma_{Cz}$. While both coefficients share a common origin in their respective conductivities, their values behave differently in response to the application of an external force. For instance, although $\sigma_{Cz}$ maintains its proportionality to charge conductivity, $\sigma_{HT}$ demonstrates a divergence from its thermal conductivity counterpart, $\sigma_{Cz}$. Additionally, we observe that $\sigma_{HT}$ fails to exhibit a correlation with $\sigma_{Cz}$ in scenarios featuring convection-dominant heat transport. Furthermore, we note that $\sigma_{HT}$ may not adhere to Einstein relations, particularly not the local Einstein relation, under non-zero spatial inhomogeneities. Finally, we discuss the possibility of effectively isolating $\sigma_{HT}$ in experiments by selecting specific spatial patterns and offer a possible interpretation of our findings through the salting of liquid helium. The latter could potentially serve as an experiment to determine $\sigma_{HT}$. This work showcases the unique properties of $\sigma_{HT}$, offering new perspectives on heat transport in systems with spatial gradients. In turn, this unique characteristic may provide fresh insights into understanding general thermal Hall phenomena. The proposed ideas for potential experimental verification may pave the way for future research in thermodynamics. Previous initiatives for creating treebanks in Hebrew, initiated in 2009, have been restarted with an updated approach. This new project, started in 2018, is based on Rawlinson's treebanking guidelines and benefits from the existing resources and knowledge gained from the earlier efforts. This domain-specific and English-inspired UD Hebrew treebank combines the best aspects of both traditions. Despite Hebrew being a Semitic language with a distinct character, and given the scarcity of scientific studies on it, the project includes advanced annotations, such as Masmid's morphological analysis and BDB's lemma data, as well as comprehensive annotations for sentences containing ambiguities. The new treebank consists of 6,564 sentences from the Tanakh and 14,601 sentences from modern Hebrew texts, distributed across 37 domains, making it the largest and most diverse Hebrew UD treebank available. Leveraging a range of leading algorithms for parsing and evaluation, the results show that the current best UD Hebrew model achieves an F-score of 43.4% on the new treebank. Furthermore, the researchers conducted a range of exploratory evaluations to understand the challenges of parsing different domains in Hebrew and the potential benefits of using contextual information in natural language processing tasks. The new Hebrew UD treebank, along with its accompanying models, is accessible via Zenodo at the link https://zenodo.org/depositories/1399198/depositories/fc7f4e. For technical information and documentation, please visit the project website at https://hebrew-ud.github.io. Additionally, the team has established a GitHub page (https://github.com/hebrew-ud) for the project, where researchers can collaborate and contribute to the initiative. The UD Hebrew community welcomes collaborations of various kinds. If you are interested in participating, please don't hesitate to reach out to Hebrew-UD@lists.uni-linz.ac.at. This project explores the possibility of creating a voice without prior knowledge of the speaking voice, its pronunciation or intonation patterns. We investigate whether a model can learn to generate speech using only raw audio and a transcription system that identifies fundamental speech units and their patterns. Ultimately, this goal aligns with creating a voice system for endangered languages. Our approach involves using a pre-trained neural network to identify speech units and their patterns, which are then represented through a set of broad linguistic categories. The results show that a significant portion of speech synthesized using this approach is intelligible and semi-reliable, achieving a level of complexity similar to that of standard voice synthesis systems. However, the overall quality remains limited, primarily due to the coarseness of the transcription system. To improve the synthesis quality, we propose modifying the transcription system to provide more detailed information about speech units and their patterns. Additionally, we observe that the synthesis process can be improved by incorporating prior knowledge about the speaking voice. The findings of this project suggest that creating a voice without prior knowledge of the speaking voice is feasible, but improving the synthesis quality beyond a basic level requires incorporating prior knowledge. Therefore, a possible middle ground between complete knowledge and none is possible. We demonstrate that a system with limited knowledge can achieve a higher synthesis quality than one without any knowledge. Optimizing multi-agent motion in various domains can be challenged by detecting feasible and efficient trajectories in high-dimensional joint state-space. Traditional planners using black-box optimization methods often result in a phenomenon called 'optimization-induced terrorism,' where nearly optimal solutions exhibit small changes in value, but considerable changes in feasibility. To address this issue, a novel multi-stage approach combining convex programming and data-driven approximate relaxation is proposed for optimizing multi-agent motion. This method first derives upper and lower bounds for agent positions through data-driven McCormick envelope relaxations based on accurate collision detection and efficient graph construction. These relaxed bounds accelerate convergence to a viable trajectory by eliminating unnecessary variables and reducing dimensionality. Additionally, the method optimizes and re-assigns bounded variables at each iteration, outperforming traditional methods that fix variables throughout the optimization process. As a result, this method generates high-quality trajectories with minimal deviations in feasibility, demonstrating superior performance in simulation and experimental evaluation compared to standard optimization-based planning methods. The method achieves speed-ups of up to 3 times in simulation and 1.8 times in real-world testing, with improved feasibility and reduced terrorism scores. The proposed method is a versatile and general approach that can be applied to a range of optimization problems and its source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ramnathv/mccormick_plan. Experimental data, including videos of the method in action, can be found at https://ramnath-v.github.io/mccormick_plan. The method could also be used in areas such as autonomous driving, where optimizing multi-agent motion can be challenging and detecting feasible trajectories is critical for ensuring safe and efficient travel. For example, this method could be applied to optimize the movement of various agents, such as vehicles and pedestrians, within a complex network of roads and pathways, while taking into account various priorities and constraints, such as maximum allowed velocities and close proximity to each other. The proposed method is a valuable tool in such applications and its public availability and public demos allow for easy replication and understanding of its performance. However, our research reveals that the production of these particles is not solely dependent on the vitality but is also influenced by the flow rate of the system, especially the puller component. A higher flow rate is found to increase the production of high-energy particles, and this effect is more pronounced in systems that have a higher puller component. This research uses the hydrodynamic model and two different types of initial states to study these phenomena, specifically the default state from the PHENIX collaboration and a state with enhanced puller components. This paper presents an approach to simultaneously controlling the performance and limitations of nonlinear systems subject to constraints. Building on existing research into optimal control theory, this framework seeks to balance multiple objectives, including a desire for the system to operate at its limits, known as performance limits, in addition to conventional objectives such as minimizing cost and maximizing output. These multiple objectives are formalized within a single framework known as the equilibrium-regulated system, which incorporates sensitive variables indicating when performance limits are being approached. Necessary and sufficient conditions for solving this problem are developed within the framework of geometric optimal control theory, which also provides a method for solving the problem directly through the use of sensitivity-compatible trajectories. This approach is illustrated with two examples, including one in space which operates under a budget in orbit around Mars and another regarding the operation of a robot arm. In both cases, the proposed method enables the calculation of optimal trajectories that take into account both performance and limitations, in addition to conventional objectives, in an equitable manner. It is shown that accounting for equitable regulation improves the quality of the obtained trajectories when compared to ignoring performance limits, in favor of a more comprehensive approach. As such, this contribution has the potential to enrich the design and planning of controlled systems, particularly those in complex and challenging environments, by incorporating performance limits and sensitivity to equitable regulation. Building on this research, it is envisioned that equitable regulation will become a standard tool in the design and planning of controlled systems, enabling a greater range of optimal trajectories to be taken into account in the future. Keywords: Optimal control of nonlinear systems, equitable regulation, performance limits, geometric optimal control theory, sensitivity-compatible trajectories. Sciences and technology disciplines: Aerospace engineering, mechanical engineering, robotics, systems engineering, computer science. Application domains: Mars rover, robot arm, spacecraft, satellite, rocket, Earth rover. Research techniques: Geometric optimal control theory, sensitivity analysis, Mars simulation, robotic arm simulation. Key concepts: Performance limits, equitable regulation, sensitivity-compatible trajectories, geometric optimal control theory. Achieved results: Obtained new results in the field of optimal control, particularly regarding the application of equitable regulation to nonlinear systems under constraints, with related conditions and algorithms. Developed new approaches: Formulation of the equilibrium-regulated system and the calculation of sensitivity-compatible trajectories. Addressed previously unresolved issues: Incorporation of performance limits and sensitivity to equitable regulation in the design and planning of controlled systems. Illuminated new aspects: The potential benefits of equitable regulation, particularly regarding trajectory selection, in contrast to conventional approaches that may operate sub-optimally.

We introduce an innovative research direction in object recognition, focusing on accurately determining an object's pose and shape from partially accessible sensory data. Our study begins with a realistic assumption that certain critical aspects of an object are unknown. As a result, we propose the resilient object pose estimation challenge, which aims to predict an object's orientation and position relative to a standard reference frame, while also accounting for potential variations in its overall shape. Moreover, in situations where sensory data is incomplete, we consider the problem of ideal object recognition, which seeks to identify an object's class, as well as its intrinsic shape characteristics, given limited keypoint data. Our work initiates a comprehensive study on resilient pose estimation and ideal object recognition, offering theoretical analyses and practical observations, as well as presenting the ResPoseCk dataset, a large collection of 3D object models with varying poses and shapes. Our research demonstrates that, even with limited and imperfect sensory data, resilient pose estimation and ideal object recognition are achievable with appropriate loss functions and models, as evidenced by our proposed approach, which achieves an accuracy of 86.69% on ResPoseCk. Our study aims to contribute to the advancement of resilient systems in object recognition and provide valuable insights into ideal object recognition. The proposed approach, as well as the ResPoseCk dataset, are made available for public use. The dataset can be accessed at https://xiezhengdiao.github.io/ResPoseCk/. For the one-parameter Cauchy distribution, constructing intervals and squares of confidence, at least asymptotically, becomes extremely difficult due to the absence of parameter estimation by maximum likelihood. In this research, we develop an original method for obtaining confidence intervals and squares of order n, at least asymptotically, without requiring additional parameters such as l1-regularization or bootstrapping. The proposed method demonstrates strong consistency for both the interval and square, and we also establish the order of these confidence intervals and squares. The results show that they are almost optimal and cannot be improved upon, and this is verified through practical examples and simulations. The method can also be extended to fit the two-parameter Cauchy distribution by treating one parameter as a known value, and this modification is included in the paper. The research provides a new and efficient approach to constructing confidence intervals and squares for the Cauchy distribution, and it is suitable for a range of statistical applications. To determine which high-energy collider is best suited to resolve the question of possible instability in the Higgs sector, we analyzed theoretical and experimental aspects. Based on current theoretical knowledge, we identified potential signs of such instability, such as large additional Higgs bosons or significant cubic Higgs couplings. To quantify these signs, we used comprehensive studies from the Helac On the Fly framework, incorporating latest SM calculations. The findings were then evaluated against the detection capabilities of proposed colliders, including CLIC, FCC-ee, and LHC with its various energy upgrades, as well as the HL-LHC. The analysis demonstrated that linear colliders offer the best prospects to investigate the instability in the Higgs sector, especially by examining the production of rare three-body processes at $\sqrt{s} = 3$ TeV or by leveraging resonance production at $\sqrt{s} = 100-1000$ TeV. In contrast, the HL-LHC may reach detection limits for certain unstable scenarios, though it will require thorough analysis of the Higgsstrahlung process at $\sqrt{s} = 14$ TeV. The investigation also revealed that a collider energy of $\sqrt{s} = 5000$ TeV would be needed to confidently detect instability in the Higgs sector, especially in the most extreme cases, such as highly coupled additional Higgs bosons. Ultimately, this study underscored the significance of completing the planned research programs at CLIC and FCC-ee to fulfill the objectives of the Strategy for a Sustainable Culinary Particle Physics. Additionally, we emphasized the necessity of undertaking in-depth theoretical investigations into the underlying mechanisms of the instability, its possible connection to particle scale new physics, and the role of resumation in correcting the SM instability, particularly around the Z-boson. Furthermore, we stressed the importance of incorporating genuine SM states into the search for instability, especially in connection with the process of Higgs boson production via heavy-quark loops. The study therefore provided an in-depth analysis, relevant both theoretically and experimentally, of the quest to understand the stability of the Higgs sector, as well as the construction of the collider chain to accomplish this endeavor. Lastly, we noted that this study could be adapted with modifications to investigate similar instability concerns affecting other particles, such as the W-boson, though the specifics would necessitate different analyses. A new, robust method is proposed to analyze time-resolved data by leveraging trajectory optimization techniques. Conventional approaches focused on inverting data from time-series measurements typically utilize continuous or discrete dynamical models. Despite their strength in long-term dynamics, these models may falter when directly applied to short time-frames, leading to unstable solutions. On the other hand, trajectory-based approaches can effectively handle both short and long time-frames but may yield nonsensical trajectories in the presence of large errors. This work demonstrates that by reformulating the traditional inverse problem through forward-optimization in a trajectory framework, we can safely analyze time-resolved data while ensuring robust and continuous solutions. Our method is not only versatile but also versatile, allowing it to incorporate a wide array of continuous and discrete models, as well as operate seamlessly with various performance functions that assess solution quality. To showcase the strength of this approach, we successfully applied it to determine asteroid ephemerides and the spectral properties of pre-main sequence stars. Additionally, we highlight that the underlying optimization problem may have multiple local minima, which can be critical in understanding the coexistence of different states in biological, astronomical, or other types of dynamic systems. By choosing the solution that best balances model accuracy and physical plausibility, we can gain valuable insights into the underlying physics of the system being studied. Our code is publicly available and can be accessed at the designated website. Future research will focus on developing novel algorithms to identify the diverse local minima of the optimization problem, thereby uncovering and comparing different solutions to the inverse problem at hand. Future work will also be focused on developing novel formulations of the optimization problem that directly incorporate the diverse local minima, thereby providing a more comprehensive range of solutions to the inverse problem at hand. We hypothesize that such an advancement in trajectory-based models will open up new avenues for analyzing dynamic systems where the coexistence of different states is known to occur, such as star formation (e.g., multiple protostar states for a given parent star), animal behavior (e.g., resting and feeding modes for a given animal), or human decision-making (e.g., different action plans for a given choice). Ultimately, we expect that future work along these lines will not only strengthen our understanding of dynamic systems generally but also reveal new and unexpected insights into the underlying physics of the system being studied. Predicting future actions in video clips is a challenging task known as future action prediction (FAP). Deep future action prediction models that use future frame generation (FFG) to forecast video clips beyond their known frame sequence achieve high performance levels. Nevertheless, these models are difficult to train due to the need to synch the generated frames with the real ones across different frame indices. To address the FAP problem, a new model called Feature Mapping RNN (FM-RNN) is introduced, which uses a radial basis function kernel to transform the video's spatial and temporal features into a higher-dimensional feature space. FM-RNN predicts future actions by calculating the inner product of this transformed feature space with class templates. FM-RNN is an efficient model that does not generate frames and can be trained quickly, as the prediction of future actions is independent of the frame indices. FM-RNN achieves better performance than the current state-of-the-art deep future action prediction models that use future frame generation. FM-RNN achieves an 8.53% Mean Absolute Error (MAE) on Zhongshan + Yale action dataset which is an 8.61% improvement compared to the current state-of-the-art deep future action prediction models. Additionally, FM-RNN outperforms state-of-the-art models on other benchmark datasets by achieving 6.22% and 3.64% improvement in terms of MAE on UCF101-24 and UCSD-TVlocator datasets respectively. FM-RNN's code and data can be found on this GitHub repository: https://github.com/ChunyuYou/Feature_Mapping_RNN. FM-RNN has been successfully applied to future action prediction on video clips of car drivers, hospital patients, and other individuals, demonstrating its general applicability to diverse future action prediction tasks. On April 12, 1985, a powerful and bright explosion occurred on the surface of the star AD Leo, erupting at L$_v$ = 31.6 km/s and lasting for several weeks. This event was observed in multiple wavelengths and led to a 0.2 mag increase in the star's visual brightness. We studied high-resolution spectra of the star captured during and after the eruption, analyzing observations taken just two days after the eruption and comparing them to modeled spectra obtained through 3D non-local thermodynamic equilibrium (3D NLTE) models. These models were developed using the STARBOX code and were specifically created to replicate the chemical abundance and distribution in the star as observed in the spectrum. By utilizing the spectrum of a cooler, inactive twin star along with the abundance of metals in the solar system, we were able to construct the 3D NLTE models. These were then used to generate synthetic spectra in the 3200-4000 A wavelength range with a resolution of 12,000 and a line spread function width of 1.3 km/s. The results of our analysis revealed that the expanded photosphere and moving material from the eruption reached speeds of 100-200 km/s two days after the eruption, covering a surface area corresponding to roughly 5% of the star's visible disk. The hottest moving material was found to have a temperature of around 8000 K, while the cooler, 5500 K material had a much smaller velocity of around 20 km/s. This is consistent with the observed changes in the star's near-ultraviolet brightness and temperature. The models we constructed also allowed us to estimate the energy released by the eruption as 1.5 x 10$^{43}$ erg/s, with a large fraction of this energy self-absorbed within the expanded photosphere.
