We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors, enabling the deformation theory to be formulated through the use of spinors and Dirac operators. We establish that the space of infinitesimal deformations for an instanton is equivalent to the kernel of an elliptic operator. With this approach, we prove that abelian instantons exhibit rigidity, and subsequently apply these results to define the deformation space of the canonical connection on nearly G2-manifolds with a normal homogeneous structure of seven-dimensional algebraic Lie group G2. We further calculate the cohomology of this Dirac operator, establish the deformation space of the canonical connection on nearly G2-manifolds with a Euclidean action, and derive an explicit formula for the space of infinitesimal deformations for instantons on nearly G2-manifolds with a vector cross product. We conclude by reconstructing the deformation theory of instantons on compact torseiform manifolds with a maximum G2 action. In addition, we enhance the scope of this paper to include degeneration of instantons in the context of degenerating nearly G2-manifolds with control, which serves as a foundation for future research in this area. The content of this paper contributes to two distinct areas of research - the mathematical theory of supergravity and the geometric investigation of non-complex, 7-dimensional manifolds that admit a parallel G2 structure. We have intentionally written the paper with overlapping applications to both theories in order to facilitate mutual cross-fertilization. However, in order to maintain clarity and avoid duplication, the introduction primarily focuses on the research questions of geometric investigation, while the body of the paper delves into both theories. A detailed summary incorporating both theories can be found in the conclusion of this paper. Neural network-based encoders play a crucial role in representing the state of a point cloud in a compressed format, facilitating downstream tasks with improved efficiency. However, current methods employing traditional point cloud transformers struggle to leverage the geometric properties inherent in point cloud data, leading to subpar performance. This issue can be addressed by integrating a geometrically-aware transformer perception module, specifically designed for point cloud structures, into a compressed encoder architecture. The proposed TPC module incorporates several innovative features: (1) a custom coordinate transformation system to prioritize local neighborhood interactions over global correlations, (2) a unique data smoothing step to preserve the distinctness of nearby points, and (3) a set of strategically selected permutation matrices that prioritize the exchange of feature vectors between neighboring nodes. Experimental evaluations confirm that the TPC module outperforms state-of-the-art methods in various point cloud-related tasks. Additionally, the proposed method's design flexibility allows it to be applied to a range of tasks beyond the scope of this study. The code for this research is openly accessible on GitHub. We investigate medium access control in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks with a new 1-PAM FMCW protocol, allowing us to analyze its performance under ALOHA and CSMA access methods. A mathematical model is developed to simulate slotted ALOHA access and a Markov chain is created to analyze CSMA access. Simulation results show that while SLSA access minimizes the probability of packet collisions, it results in a lower overall throughput than CSMA access. However, with the addition of a simple back-off mechanism to our SLSA access mechanism, we achieve both reduced collision probability and high throughput, demonstrating a optimal solution. Additionally, we propose a novel back-off strategy for CSMA access that dynamically adjusts its back-off time based on the network's current utilization, balancing collision probability and throughput efficiency in both SLSA and CSMA access scenarios. Our findings provide valuable insights for designing efficient medium access control mechanisms for FMCW radar networks. Experimental validation of our theoretical model is conducted using PyCW, an in software FMCW radar platform. This research paves the way for the optimization of medium access control in radar networks over wireless channels. Temporal knowledge graph inference focuses on predicting time-specific relationships between entities. Current approaches, such as based on recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and attention, have limitations in handling limited episode data and are difficult to adapt and apply across different datasets. In response, we introduce a new set of challenges, denoted as the TimeLink challenge, aimed at developing effective methods for temporal knowledge graph inference. We present a model that ranks episode samples based on their scores, and to address data limitations, propose using a two-component representation of entities: a model-agnostic set of latent factors and a narrow set of ranks that can cross-learning with the model's parameters. Through experiments on three datasets, we demonstrate that our approach surpasses state-of-the-art models, and our open-source toolkit includes 17 rival models for temporal knowledge graph inference. We further conduct a thorough analysis of our model and the ranking challenge, highlighting the benefits of using the time-conditional epistemic Hamiltonian for temporal knowledge graph inference. As such, we refer to the version used here as the time-conditional epistemic Hamiltonian for ranking (TCHR), which offers a more stable and versatile solution. The toolkit and more information can be found at https://github.com/kailinzhao/TDH-R. Keywords: TimeLink, Temporal knowledge graph inference, Rank-based model, Low-rank representation, Model-agnostic latent factor model.

The problem of distributing N jobs among M nodes, each with C resources, under a batch size of B, when using dynamic scheduling, is equivalent to solving a generalized version of the Bin Packing Problem. This leads to the concept of using a partitioned array to store job states and defining partition boundaries as we need to manage shared resources. Consequently, the number of partitions is adjusted according to the number of nodes available. Consequently, the problem of allocating jobs to nodes is reformulated as a problem of dividing a single array among the array's partitions, and an efficient array division method is developed and proven to work correctly, allowing us resulting in O(n) time complexity. This is further demonstrated through the development of an efficient dynamic scheduling algorithm, also proven correct and efficient. This approach is then applied to create an accurate simulation of a real-world distributed system, and the performance is measured in terms of mean array size and mean batch size under a batch size of 64. It is observed that when mean array size exceeds a batch size of 64, mean batch size decreases, confirming theoretical expectations. Moreover, when mean array size is less than a batch size of 64, mean batch size remains at 64, and both mean array size and mean batch size remain consistent with previous findings. Ultimately, mean batch size remains at 64 plus the difference between mean array size and 64 multiplied by 64 divided by mean array size. This research is presented at the 2024 Cyber Defense Research Conference. Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach that leverages time-series data to define meaningful groups within these systems by focusing on the impact one element has on another. Our method, IBIC, incorporates an influence measure that reflects the statistical connection between two elements, enabling the identification of clusters through their inherent dynamics. To test the efficacy of IBIC, we applied it to both a synthetic network and the Cambridge grid power system, showcasing its ability to define clusters based on the dynamic characteristics of these systems. Our results highlight IBIC's superiority over traditional clustering methods, demonstrating the potential for IBIC to improve reliability in power systems by identifying and isolating faulty sections. Furthermore, IBIC's flexibility and performance make it an suitable tool for applications in various domains. A detailed explanation of the approach, along with the used code, is available online at https://github.com/amiramini/influence-based-clustering. IBIC has been successfully demonstrated on different datasets, and our research shows its ability to identify relevant clusters based on dynamic influences, rather than static characteristics. This is particularly useful in domains such as medicine where correlations may not necessarily imply causation, and the ability to measure influence accurately can break down complex problems. In the future, we aim to expand IBIC to tackle challenges in systems with high dimensionality and those governed by non-linear dynamics. Additionally, we are exploring its application to problems in personal behavior networks and drug action mechanisms. These areas, coupled with the efficacy demonstrated so far, make IBIC a versatile approach with vast potential applications. To test the efficacy of IBIC in personal behavior networks and drug action mechanisms, we are currently working on collecting data from these systems and developing a dataset that combines these time-series data with relevant attributes of the elements involved. In addition to these efforts, we are also examining the performance of IBIC on datasets with high density and those governed by non-linear dynamics. We will examine three philosophical approaches - Carnap-Hilbert, Kripke, and Steiner - as they pertain to Leibnizian infinitesimal calculus. Although these approaches were initially discussed in relation to real analysis, we will adapt them to focus on calculus with static lawlike statements, emphasizing the distinct nature of infinitesimal entities. Our analysis will highlight the differences and similarities among these frameworks as they relate to Leibnizian calculus. Furthermore, we will argue that the Carnap-Hilbert framework is particularly suitable for developing the fundamental principles of Leibnizian calculus. Additionally, we will derive within this framework a formal system for Fregeized Leibnizian calculus, and demonstrate that this formal system is compatible with the Frege-Burgess method of second-order logic. Our derivation of Fregeized Leibnizian calculus also addresses potential concerns regarding the paradoxical implications of infinitesimal entities, demonstrating that these concerns can be resolved in a manner analogous to the resolution of paradoxes in integers and rational numbers. Finally, we will defend the use of infinitesimal entities as a legitimate means of exploring the nature of calculus, and argue that this approach is essential for gaining a deeper understanding of the underlying philosophical principles. In conjunction with this, we will suggest that the Carnap-Hilbert framework, the Kripke account, and the Steiner account can be viewed as distinct methodologies for examining the nature of infinitesimal entities, and that these methodologies have distinct cognitive merits. Ultimately, the choice of an account depends on one's particular research objectives and the manner in which one chooses to interpret the fundamental principles of Leibnizian calculus. If one prioritizes consistency then the Carnap-Hilbert account is the most suitable choice. Conversely, if one prefers an account that incorporates a semantic intuition then the Kripke account or the Steiner account may be more appealing. Lastly, if one wishes to understand the philosophical underlying principles of Leibnizian calculus in a manner analogous to the underlying principles of integers and rational numbers then the Carnap-Hilbert account is the most suitable choice. In conjunction with this, we suggest that the Frege-Burgess method of second-order logic, in conjunction with the Carnap-Hilbert account, provides a comprehensive framework for examining the nature of Fregeized Leibnizian calculus. Using an accurate model of intergalactic matter, researchers have generated large-scale HI intensity maps on backgrounds with known cosmological properties. These simulations inform predictions for upcoming large-scale experiments such as DELPHI and other similar projects. This study examines two key factors that affect predictions: how accurately these maps align with the smoothed 3D HI distribution, and how effectively these maps remove non-relativistic foreground emissions. Numerical simulations indicate that large-scale HI fluctuations are consistently represented across various smoothing scales, spanning several thousand kilometers. However, a significant discrepancy arises at smaller scales, where predictions based on observed galaxy distributions significantly diverge from the true HI values. This discrepancy is largely attributed to the incomplete removal of foreground emissions in upcoming experiments, leading to a substantial bias in predicted HI power spectra at smaller scales. This study emphasizes the need for higher-resolution simulations that can account for the inherent uncertainty in predicted HI power spectra at scales less than 10 million kilometers. Additionally, this study reveals that utilizing cross-correlations with other observed signals can significantly mitigate the uncertainties at smaller scales, reducing the predicted bias to less than 10%. This study lays the foundation for future predictions with similar experiments, incorporating their distinct characteristics and limitations. We examine how the concepts of autonomy and infiniteness relate to each other, and highlight cases where infiniteness can provide a beneficial aspect, even in tasks such as solving equations.  Ultimately, this framework allows us to reinterpret fundamental ideas in mathematics, including the circuit model of computation, through a more abstract lens.  This new perspective enables us to ask previously unconsidered questions, such as: Can advanced mathematical concepts, such as topological properties, be understood as forms of operators that are capable of providing value?  Are there distinct categories of operations that are capable of producing different amounts of value?  This research has only just begun to scratch the surface of these possibilities. One major limitation of existing recommender systems lies in their failure to adequately provide personalized recommendations to users with diverse preferences and varying scopes of engagement. While model-based methods excel in addressing the broadness issue, they often neglect to present relevant recommendations to users with narrow interests. In contrast, systems that rely on user-generated content face challenges in guaranteeing the quality of such content and often produce subpar search results. This paper introduces an improved hybrid recommender system designed to surpass the shortcomings of individual methods. By integrating the strengths of contextual information-based and behavior-oriented approaches, our framework offers enhanced search outcomes and a higher level of personalization for users with a range of profiles. An empirical evaluation of our framework, using real data from the MovieCe recommendation system, demonstrates its superiority over other systems in terms of both recall and precision. Furthermore, a comprehensive analysis of user-generated content reveals the significant impact of system-driven features on overall quality. Notably, our framework has been successfully implemented in the actuality of MovieCe, where it has led to notable enhancements in system metrics. The presented work is expected to contribute to the advancement of recommender systems, while also serving as a useful reference for developers seeking to improve their existing systems. We establish that certain symmetric random matrices are B-free if and only to what extent they are free of type B, and we derive conditions under which certain random matrices with independent entries can be considered B-free. Additionally, we prove the existence of orthogonal polynomial systems for Wigner matrices, provided they are B-free. Our work relies on the concepts and techniques from free probability theory, probability theory, and functional analysis. We also discuss the relevance and applications of our findings. We demonstrate that our results can address questions regarding the spectral distribution of matrices with vanishing mean, particularly for those with vanishing mean and non-vanishing second moment. Our study also encompasses the broader context of matrix mean and skew-free projections, and we examine the relationships between being B-free, being free of type B, and being purely free of type B (PF-type B) for rectangular random matrices, and we explore the connections between being B-free and the indices of negative definiteness and pseudo-definiteness for specific symmetric random matrices. A key aspect of concurrent systems revolves around identifying the timing properties that can be verified through the system's execution sequence, whether timed or untimed. Although certain properties are inherently verifiable when the system is untimed, similar verification becomes impossible if timing is considered. In this context, we revisit three system characteristics: whether they can complete, whether they can get stuck, and whether one task can prevent another task from initiating. We explore their equivalents in both timed and untimed systems and provide a new condition that distinguishes between these properties in timed systems, along with an algorithm to verify this condition. This condition reduces to a well-known condition for untimed systems, thereby offering a simplified verification method for those cases. We also examine system properties where a task can prevent another task from initiating and provide an algorithm to verify this condition in both timed and untimed systems. Lastly, we outline specific challenges that arise when handling timing-specific complexities. We demonstrate that deciding whether a timed system can get stuck is actually a decidable task, unlike its untimed counterpart. This achievement, however, comes with a cost - the verification algorithm requires an exponential amount of time, a notable deviation from its untimed counterpart which can be verified in linear time. We present two distinct conditions that distinguish between these properties in timed systems, however we chose not to present them as algorithmic solutions but rather theoretical distinctions. This achievement, however, comes with a cost - the verification requires knowledge of when the system transitions, an aspect that is often influenced by the scheduler. We present a novel way to overcome this obstacle by formulating two distinct conditions that capture the essence of when a timed system can complete or get stuck, solely based on the system's transition structure without requiring knowledge of when the system transitions. This, in turn, offers a way to verify whether a timed system can complete or get stuck, along with providing an algorithmic solution that runs in linear time. We present in-depth characterization findings of the GRAVITY chip camera, which are key to understanding the performance of the instrument during parabolic flights with the Ground-Based Astronomical Test Telescope. The tests revealed minor discrepancies between the predicted and measured behavior of the telescope's point spread function. The results, based on 464 images collected over four flights with a total of 11.5 hours of usable exposure time, revealed a mean residual error of 0.94 ± 0.19 millarcseconds. The images themselves exhibit a signal-to-noise ratio of 100 to 300, primarily limited by the noise in the GRAVITY chip output. The in-flight graisms were found to be sufficient for purposes of astronomical research, though it was discovered that the graisms still possess inherent asymmetries. Our analysis suggests two possible sources of this asymmetry, namely it could stem from inherent asymmetries inherent to the GRAVITY chips themselves or from differences in the focal plane geometry of the telescope. Ultimately, the in-flight graisms were found to be capable of resolving a separation distance of 98 milliarcsseconds at a 30Hz sampling rate over the course of four test flights with the GBAT. A detailed breakdown of the capabilities and characteristics of the GRAVITY chip camera are included in the accompanying detailed paper. We examine $k$-Center variants in graphs with limited doubling or freeway dimension. Our study focuses on the Capacitated $k$-Supplier with Outliers problem and establishes both time-efficient algorithms and optimal solution values for both doubling and freeway graphs. Our work contrasts these results with the capability of having constant-factor solutions for $k$-Center on such graphs. We suggest the Capacitated $k$-Supplier with Outliers problem as a more challenging variant that yields fractional values proportional to $\Omega\left(\frac{\log k}{\log \Delta} \right)$ when considering a $\kappa$-doubling graph with $\Delta$ vertices. Moreover, we demonstrate that this problem offers an alternative formulation, which has an optimal value proportional to $\Omega\left(\frac{\log k}{\log \kappa} \right)$ when applied to a $\kappa$-freeway graph. We propose the suggestion that finding constant-factor solutions for the Capacitated $k$-Supplier with Outliers problem on $\kappa$-freeway graphs might be impossible. We provide an approximate 3-approximation algorithm that can solve the Capacitated $k$-Center problem with outliers for $\kappa$-freeway graphs. We suggest the possibility that solving the Capacitated $k$-Supplier with Outliers problem could be equivalent to solving the Capacitated $k$-Center problem with outliers, which might yield an approximation ratio proportional to $\Omega\left(\log \frac{k}{\epsilon} \right) $for $\epsilon$-fractional solutions. We offer an approximation algorithm that has an approximation ratio proportional to $\Omega\left(\frac{\log \kappa}{\log \frac{k}{\epsilon}} \right)$for fractional $\epsilon$-solutions. We demonstrate that our 3-approximation algorithm can be efficiently implemented using a linear programming relaxation and can solve the Capacitated $k$-Supplier with Outliers problem with a time complexity proportionate to $kn^6$. Furthermore, we propose an efficient algorithm that can solve the Capacitated $k$-Supplier with Outliers problem with a time complexity proportionate to $kn^3$ for input graphs that have a fixed diameter. In many algorithmic contexts, it is sufficient to find approximate solutions that satisfy certain criteria with high probability. This probability is measured in relation to the total number of possible outcomes, and the tolerance for error is indicated by a parameter called $\sigma$. For the specific task of solving systems of polynomial equations, algorithms must be able to accurately solve systems of degree $\tilde{O}(\sigma^{-n})$ where $n$ represents the number of variables. Notably, if $n$ is equal to 1, researchers have developed an algorithm capable of solving equations of nearly quadratic nature within a time frame of $\tilde{O}(\sigma^{-2} \cdot \log \sigma)$. This innovation has led to a corresponding reduction in the exponent of a previously established lower bound under specific assumptions. This paper presents an algorithm that, given a degree $d$ and desired error tolerance $\sigma$, is capable of solving systems of $k$ polynomial equations in $n$ variables within a time frame of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(2^{O(n\log d)} \cdot \sigma^{-d} \log \sigma)$. This technique may have further applications in other algorithmic contexts. Finally, this paper establishes a corresponding lower bound under certain assumptions, leading to a quasi-polynomial gap between currently established upper and lower bounds for this task. The spectrum is investigated using the framework of in-medium Cornwall-Jackiw-Tapp model for ρ-mesons. Our findings show that both the transverse and longitudinal modes of the ρ-meson experience a decrease in mass as the chemical potential increases, with the rate of decrease being faster in the longitudinal mode. We investigate the problem of scale estimation in large graph communities that have been affected by malicious entities. Our research demonstrates that it is possible for individual nodes within these communities to estimate their size without relying on a central authority or consensus among nodes. Our method does this while accounting for the potential for malicious nodes that may attempt to mislead other nodes with false information. Assuming that a significant majority of nodes within the community function properly and malicious nodes behave rationally, our algorithm achieves accurate scale estimates while remaining robust against a limited number of malicious entities. To our knowledge, this study represents the first instance in which a scale estimation algorithm has been developed in the context of graph communities that have been affected by malicious entities. Additionally, we evaluate the performance of our algorithm through analytical analysis as well as simulations that compare its effectiveness against a theoretical baseline that assumes an unreliable failure model. Results indicate that our algorithm surpasses the baseline in both cases. Our findings have implications for the development of reliable scale estimation algorithms in graph communities affected by malicious entities. This revised version includes supplementary materials with a simulated annealing approach that maximizes our algorithm's accuracy in a limited number of iterations, as well as additional statistical analysis and improved simulation results that confirm our algorithm's effectiveness in a more limited model that involves malicious nodes that may behave differently than a rational malicious entity. Developing initial data for numerical relativity remains challenging, particularly when creating enhanced models of physical phenomena in numerical relativity. We introduce a novel approach, using a combined iterative Lagrange multiplier method (CLMM), which facilitates the rapid preparation of high-precision initial data for various spacetime configurations. CLMM optimizes a modified Hamiltonian constraint within the C00-4 link variant of the Conformal Transverse Traceless (CTTT) method. This advancement is an extension of the CTTK method, incorporating a conformal metric and a constrained 3-metric obtained from an inverse problem. We find that our technique produces accurate solutions for various scenarios, including isolated and binary black hole systems, by resolving the Hamiltonian constraint precison and demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach. Furthermore, we have implemented the CLMM technique in the publicly available GIMIC code and made the initial data set described in this paper available under a free license at https://doi.org/10.6087/c19d57607f. In addition to contributing to the existing toolset in numerical relativity, we have evaluated the computational efficiency of our approach, striking a balance between runtime and accuracy. We have observed that our technique offers a significant reduction in runtime compared to other methods, with minimal loss in accuracy. Specifically, our tests have shown that we can prepare initial data at an unprecedented frequency for sensitive parameters, thereby addressing a longstanding limitation in numerical relativity. In particular, we have focused on model enhancements such as the "mass-asymmetry" parameter, ranging from 0 to 0.25, and has found that our technique surpasses other methods by preparing initial data at an unprecedented frequency for sensitive parameters. This achievement has significant implications for theoretical and phenomenological modeling in numerical relativity. To facilitate widespread adoption, we have made the initial data set described in this paper available under a free license at https://doi.org/10.6087/c19d57607f. Additionally, the GIMIC code used to generate the results has been modified and made available at https://github.com/pdCCTTK/pdCCTTK/tree/CLMM. Furthermore, we have maintained a public repository of initial data, hosting the results at https://doi.org/10.6087/c19d57607f. To make the initial data set more accessible, we have assigned unique identifiers to each data set, spanning from 2021001 to 2022000, and detailed information on dataset attributes can be found at https://doi.org

We introduce a comprehensive framework for labeled distillation called PILE, which combines multiple teachers' prediction outputs and corresponding ground truth labels to create accurate student models through a simple iterative approach. The framework consists of three key components: pairwise comparison, iterative aggregation, and model updating. First, we perform pairwise evaluations of different teaching methods to determine their strengths and weaknesses, which are then aggregated to create a more effective training signal for the student model. Next, we iteratively adjust the student model based on the training signal, adjusting its confidence levels and prediction outputs until convergence. Finally, we update the student model to maximize its performance. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of PILE, which outperforms existing methods on several benchmark datasets and educational platforms. For example, on the DMD dataset, PILE enhances model accuracy by 3.6% compared to sole multi-teacher distillation without labels. Our code can be accessed at https://github.com/IndigoPurple/PILE. Ji et al., 2022, inspired us to devise PILE. We are grateful for their work. However, our framework differs from model distillation in the traditional sense, which typically involves reducing the complexity of a complex teacher model to a simpler student model. Instead, PILE involves collective distillation, which involves adjusting both the student and teacher models to better match the ground truth labels. Our framework is also distinct from other labeled distillation methods due to its iterative aggregation mechanism, which involves updating both models iteratively. PILE has several key advantages over existing multi-teacher distillation methods. Firstly, it is simpler and more robust. Secondly, it is effective even when there is only one teaching method available. Lastly, it outperforms existing methods on various benchmark datasets and educational platforms. Our results show that PILE can enhance model performance by up to 4.3% compared to sole multi-teacher distillation without labels. We conducted an ablation study to confirm the efficacy of PILE. Our results indicate that iterating both models (i.e., using both the student and teacher models) is essential for achieving high accuracy, as evidenced by the fact that testing both models (i.e., using both the student and teacher models) performed significantly better than using either model alone (with a 4.3% improvement). We attempted to mitigate the risk of overfitting by incorporating regularization but found that it did not significantly improve model performance. Therefore, we excluded it from our final model. Our results show that PILE can be successfully applied to various benchmark datasets

A linear system with multiple equations is examined, where the coefficients of the solution vector are constrained to lie within a bounded range. We demonstrate that a unique solution exists for this system when the number of equations exceeds a threshold related to the constraints, and provide an approach to obtain this solution. This problem has analogous applications in compressive sensing, matrix rank minimization, and low-rank matrix recovery. To prove our result, we rely on principles from category theory and metric geometry to establish a continuous connection between problem parameters and solution vectors. Additionally, we show that varying the system's coefficients continuously can lead to continuous variations in the solution vector. This enables us to conclude the existence of a continuous path between any two optimal solutions that correspond to different system parameters. However, this property does not necessarily guarantee the uniqueness of the solution for the original problem with its specific coefficients. An example is given to illustrate that optimal solutions may not be unique, even in this scenario. We also consider a related problem where the system's coefficients are chosen uniformly at random, and show that a unique solution exists when the number of equations exceeds a threshold that is proportional to the constraints and the minimum value of the system's coefficients. This result generalizes the findings of previous studies that investigated the uniqueness of solutions under uniformly distributed random system coefficients. Furthermore, we propose that our theoretical analysis, which involves studying the geometry of the constrained coefficient range, may provide insights into the continuous nature of the solution set and offer a potential explanation for the observed trend. Lastly, we explore the relationship between our theoretical findings and the asymptotic results of previous studies that investigated the uniqueness of solutions under both uniformly distributed random system coefficients and non-uniformly distributed system parameters. Furthermore, we propose that our proof methods, which rely on principles from category theory and metric geometry, may provide an alternative approach to obtain these asymptotic results. Additionally, we suggest that our results may be generalized to investigate the uniqueness of solutions in the continuum for the moment relaxation problem. This could be achieved by relying on principles from category theory and metric geometry to map the linear system to a metric space, and then obtaining a continuous representation of the solution set. We focus on a specific transport operator and show that the traditional approximations fail by more than expected when the operator's divergence and curl exceed a certain limit. This issue persists in even the simplest of scenarios, namely when transporting a constant vector in a quadrilateral element. To resolve this issue, we propose two methods of correction: one involves combining neighbouring elements to achieve a higher-order approximation, while the other involves introducing stabilising terms to punish inaccurate transports. We demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods through numerical experiments. Nonetheless, it's worth noting that our proposed methods do not offer optimal performance when the transporting operator is smooth. This alternative method is based on a curved Raviart-Thomas approximation and is presented here for the first time. This technique has several benefits, including improved data diversity and simplified model design. However, training deep neural networks in a distributed environment is complicated by the difficulty in replicating model parameters, especially when working with large datasets and complex models. To overcome these limitations, we have developed an approach called regional reviewer training (RRT), which utilizes model partitioning and data resampling to ensure consistent results across different distributed models. This is achieved by identifying potential boundaries within the data and splitting the models accordingly, then combining them with sampling techniques to refine the outcome. Our experiments using CNN and RNN models demonstrate that RRT can achieve comparable accuracy to traditional methods, while also allowing us to determine the optimal model partitioning strategy. Additionally, we have observed significant improvements in training efficiency with a small increase in memory usage, thus enabling a faster and more stable model-training process. Our work has addressed the problem of achieving consistent results in model-parallel training of deep neural networks, and has shown that RRT is an effective approach to this challenge. The code used in this research study is publicly-accessible through GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/jaimesk/Regional-Reviewer-Training. This public repository includes the code used to replicate the results presented in the research, and may be utilized by developers and researchers to implement the RRT algorithm. Our evaluation has shown that RRT is a versatile approach, and we anticipate that it will be useful in a variety of deep neural network training applications. The main advantage of RRT is its ability to achieve high training efficiency while minimizing the memory usage, thus enabling a faster and more stable model-training process. The success of RRT has paved the way for further research into the development of new algorithms that can significantly improve the training efficiency while making minimal changes to the model structure. Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has garnered less attention than its two-dimensional counterpart. In this research, three-dimensional chaotic scattering is studied by applying it to a non-mixing system where the limit of conservative dynamics serves as a point of reference. When a conservative limit is achieved, the stable manifolds surrounding a temporary island of stability intersect to form a Wada basin of attraction. Reducing a parameter in a dissipative system causes these Wada basins to shrink, and as a result, their boundaries intersecting points increase. Conversely, increasing a parameter in a dissipative system causes these Wada basins to expand, and their corresponding stable areas within the chaotic set grow. These findings can be attributed to the behavior of a particle within the chaotic set as it undergoes conservative dynamics during its escape, and subsequently becomes trapped in a stable area within the chaotic set. In order to analyze this phenomenon, the system's conservative and dissipative dynamics were studied using the LKT method and a second-order correlation function, respectively. Utilizing three-dimensional visualization, the consequences of feeble dissipation on the conservative and dissipative dynamics of a quasiperiodically forced H\'enon-Heiles model were observed. In this model, feeble dissipation results in the creation of Wada basins of attraction near a temporary island of stability, and as it increases, these Wada basins expand and the areas surrounding the chaotic set grow. These observations present a distinct theoretical understanding of three-dimensional chaotic scattering, and offer a unique perspective on the conservation of particles within a system by utilizing feeble dissipation to analyze the escape rates and patterns within a chaotic set. In this study, the system's ability to maintain particles through feeble dissipation was evaluated, and the impact of feeble dissipation on three-dimensional chaotic scattering was analyzed while maintaining a conservative limit. Interestingly, increasing feeble dissipation results in the growth of stable areas within the chaotic set, and as it reaches a point where particles within the set become nonergodic and ultimately confined to a limited region within the set. Ultimately, this research offers a distinct understanding of three-dimensional chaotic scattering, and presents a unique perspective on feeble dissipation where particles within a set become trapped and conserved in a limited region within the set. Moreover, this research presents an unusual perspective where feeble dissipation results in the confinement of particles within a set by increasing the stable areas within the set, and as it reaches a point where particles become nonergodic and trapped in a limited region within the set

Investigating the thermodynamic properties of Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes through their adiabatic processes reveals that their critical stability is tied to the cosmic censorship hypothesis. Adding a complex scalar field to these black holes leads to a phase transition, causing them to lose stability under specific conditions. This loss of stability results in an increased minimum temperature in the black holes, which can only be avoided if they adhere to the weak cosmic censorship hypothesis. The implications of this outcome suggest that quantum gravity may impose an additional constraint on the scalar field's coupling strength in nature. Furthermore, this research sheds new light on the relationship between the thermodynamic phase transition and the cosmic censorship hypothesis. It demonstrates that this phase transition can be viewed as a phenomenon that violates the strong cosmic censorship hypothesis in these Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes. However, this violation is mitigated by the hypothesis's weak form, indicating that its consequences are temporary and ultimately resolved. Moreover, this research clarifies the link between the charging process and the black hole's critical stability, which is a key aspect of the weak cosmic censorship hypothesis. Using numerical examples, this research verifies its findings on the critical stability of these Reissner-Nordström anti-de Sitter black holes under specific conditions. The outcome of this investigation suggests that the validity of the weak cosmic censorship hypothesis in these black holes is tied to the minimum value of the scalar field's coupling strength. When the scalar field's coupling strength falls within a certain range, these black holes can lose their charge, leading to a state of instability. However, this loss of charge is temporary and is eventually reversed, resulting in a state of thermal equilibrium. Based on these findings, this research concludes that the strength of the scalar field plays a critical role in the cosmic censorship hypothesis, which is a key aspect of quantum gravity. In the earliest stages of a star's formation, it's surrounded by an envelope that contains solid particles. As the star forms, its radiation affects these particles, resulting in the diffusion of particles both towards and away from the star's heat source. Eventually, large solid particles that can absorb starlight easily will be pushed far away from the star. Large solid particles play a significant role in reducing the intensity of starlight reaching the planet formation region, thereby impacting Earth's biosignature potential. Conversely, particles with smaller sizes are more easily pulled towards the star and ultimately end up in the star itself. In the simplest case, gas particle interaction is governed by a thermodynamic equilibrium, yet observations suggest that particles are always larger on the star-side of the planet-forming disk, indicating that equilibria are rarely achieved. Even when equilibrium is reached, particles in the disk's inner layers will continue to be driven towards the star, driven by variations in the star's luminosity over time. This leads to a reduction in the disk's inner regions' ability to support life with a habitable climate, due to a lack of high-frequency IR emission. Meanwhile, particles on the star-side of the planet-forming disk will continue to evolve, impacting the star's surface as they abrade the photosphere and create the conditions for stellar halos and dust clouds. Ultimately, this process influences the star's overall luminosity and radius, while also regulating the star's surface sc scattering and absorption of light. Research into star formation must consider the interaction between radiation and solid particles, rather than just gas, in order to fully understand the star's formation and evolution. This research reveals that particles in the disk around these stars are always larger on the star-side, indicating that the star's emission has broken the symmetry of the disk, with the star's energy affecting the solid particles. This phenomenon is seen in the disks around both young and mature stars, as well as those stars that are often observed to have exotic properties, such as binary stars and stars in circstellar environments. This research demonstrates that the star's emission has a significant impact on the solid particles in the disk, ultimately creating differences between the disk's inner and outer regions, while also regulating the star's surface activity and radius. To investigate this, we analyzed the publication titles from the arXiv database over the past 28 years, utilizing a statistical model that measures the intricate structure of scientific research output. Our analysis reveals that the consistency of particle physics data, when subjected to the same constraints as human language, is remarkably high, exceeding 80% in the past decade. This consistency is notably resilient to different models of grammatical complexity. However, when we expanded our evaluation to the more fundamental theory of quantum gravity, the coherence of predicted results significantly dropped, below 50%. Ultimately, this study underscores the notion that physical truths can be unearthed from data through an objective analysis that adheres to universal principles of simplicity and ease of processing. Furthermore, the consistency of these results presents a compelling case for a new paradigm in the underlying structure of physical theories known as the Unveiling Program. While the time frame for this breakthrough to occur is difficult to predict, the consistency of our analysis suggests that the Unveiling Program has the potential to significantly advance our knowledge of physical theories in the near future. This, however, poses a challenge: how can we effectively create and utilize a wide range of satisfactory solutions? To address this issue, we investigate how phenotype variety within multi-solution optimization evolves and is utilized in four major approaches – multi-objective optimization, Pareto-founding, risky optimization, and probabilistic model-assisted optimization. Through a comprehensive analysis, we identify common strategies used to promote and explore phenotypic variety, as well as their respective benefits and limitations. Based on this examination, we propose several key insights that can aid researchers and engineers in designing their optimization frameworks, ultimately leading to better performance and more versatile solutions. Our study also paves the way for future research, suggesting that comparing various approaches to optimizing phenotypic variety could yield valuable practical outcomes. At the core of our investigation is the underlying assumption that a wide range of satisfactory solutions offers various benefits, although this premise could be contested if the number of satisfactory solutions is limited. Therefore, the suitability of our analysis also depends on the specific context and goals of the optimization problem at hand. Our work does not address cases where the goal is to explore as many satisfactory solutions as possible; instead, we focus on scenarios where phenotypic variety is aimed to enhance and manipulate already satisfactory solutions. A new proposed method called the "cluster-sturdy" estimator addresses this challenge by incorporating two well-established meta-analytic estimators, the Hunt-Chen and the Condence-Paulo estimators, to facilitate a reliable estimation of correlated effect sizes in the context of mixed-effects meta-analysis. The proposed estimator offers the following advantages: it is always positive definite, includes a robust estimation of mean effects, and through simulation, demonstrates robustness to heterogeneity and outcome dependency. Moreover, this new approach offers a suitable alternative when effect sizes vary significantly or outcomes are dependent. The method can be utilized by adding just one new equation to the existing Hunt-Chen and Condence-Paulo estimators and through simple simulations, the method has shown better performance. Finally, the method was successfully tested on real-world data from two consecutive studies that estimated the correlation between outcomes of the antiviral therapy for chronic hepatitis B treatment. The proposed approach provided a reliable estimation of the effect size under various scenarios. A multiple-time-step integration technique is also introduced to efficiently handle distinct time steps in a unified simulation, paving the way for future research into more intricate collision models. Ultimately, this study aims to enhance our understanding of collision dynamics in particle-resolved simulations. The proposed method has been successfully validated and is now available for use in the OpenFOAM CFD library with an open-source implementation. High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault-tolerant storage systems that can withstand hardware failures.  Failure recovery in such systems involves copying data to a replacement unit and re-establishing consistency, which poses a problem for energy-inefficient memory used in high-performance computing.  Since hardware costs have outpaced the need for multiple copies of data, this work explores the concept of algorithmic fault recovery for systems using less expensive non-volatile memory.  By leveraging the properties of non-volatile memory to reduce the need for data replication and increase efficiency in failure recovery, this research presents an algorithm that enables fast and efficient failure recovery while minimizing energy consumption in large-scale high-performance computing systems.  Through simulation, this study evaluates the performance of this algorithm under various failure rates and compares it to current methods, showing that it results in significant reductions in access latency, disk usage, and overall energy consumption.  Furthermore, this algorithm has been shown to work equally well for applications using complex data access patterns, leading to ongoing research into its adaptation for use with more complex algorithms.  Ultimately, this study suggests that this algorithmic approach to fault recovery could be a valuable resource for maintaining the efficiency of high-performance computing systems.  Due to the limitations of traditional fault recovery methods, this work has yet to fully utilize the properties of non-volatile memory, and algorithmic fault recovery may provide a way to unlock this potential.  In particular, this algorithm has potential applications in systems using near memory, where data is stored in non-volatile memory located close to the central processing unit, and could lead to significant improvements in efficiency.  Therefore, this study is just the beginning of ongoing research aimed at fully leveraging the capabilities of non-volatile memory.  This could enable near memory, a form of storage that reduces data access latency by storing data within the system itself. Studies of the $J/\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) suppressions in Pb-Pb collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV have been carried out using data collected with the LHCb detector. The investigation, which focuses on the $J/\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons produced in collisions at 5.02 TeV, confirms previous findings on $J/\psi$ suppression in Pb-Pb collisions at 2.76 TeV. The analysis computes the $J/\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) suppression ratios, $I_{\rm AA}$, and determines the prompt and nonprompt contributions to the former. The investigation finds that 60% of the $J/\psi$ suppression belongs to nonprompt mesons. The study also seeks to understand the $J/\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) nuclear modification factors using a model based on in-medium energy loss in a nuclear environment. The $I_{\rm AA}$ for $J/\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons in 0-30% central Pb-Pb collisions ranges from 0.60 at 8-12 GeV to 0.18 at 20-30 GeV, and from 0.46 at 8-12 GeV to 0.12 at 20-30 GeV, respectively. The study also determines the $I_{\rm AA}$ for $\psi$(2S) as 0.25, 0.18, and 0.06 in 0-30%, 30-50%, and 50-100% Pb-Pb collisions, respectively. The data are consistent with the model's prediction for the effect of the medium on $J/\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) formation. Additionally, the research presents $I_{\rm AA}$ for $J/\psi$ and $\psi$(2S) in Pb-Pb collisions as a function of rapidity, $y$, and finds that the suppression increases by 0.04 (0.006) per unit of negative rapidity for $J/\psi$ ($\psi$(2S)). The study also examines how $I_{\rm AA}$ changes with $p_{\rm T}$ and finds that the $J/\psi$ suppression deepens by 0.05 (0.08) per GeV from 8 to 20 GeV.

Our research reports on the initial findings of a study examining the intra-band polarization variability from a distant supernova remnant, specifically Cassiopeia A, over a roughly one-year period, facilitated by the IXPE mission. This is a pioneering observation in the X-ray band and the first to document polarization fluctuations associated with a supernova remnant on a timescale of months. During our studies, Lexis-Crossi statistics revealed a significant level of polarization (greater than 3 sigma) in a 13-17 keV energy range, especially within a region called the "north-east hotspot." Following an in-depth analysis with a model-based fit, we were able to deduce that the polarization level in this region varies, reaching as high as 13% in a 13-17 keV energy range. Our study further uncovered evidence of a rotating magnetic field, with a rotating period lasting between 3.2-4.2 years, and a magnetic field angle of about 45 degrees. This discovery is also supported by previous studies on the region's rotation period and structural patterns. Through further investigation using a grid search method, we were able to extract physical data including a uniform magnetic field strength of approximately 0.35 Gauss and a particle energy loss rate of about 0.56 MeV cm^3 s^-1 in a 13-17 keV energy range. Our study also sheds light on the underlying physics of a region within Cassiopeia A known as the "north-east hotspot," revealing variable polarization and a possible electron-positron wind interaction. This discovery is also indicative of a region in a supernova remnant undergoing rapid acceleration, a phenomenon also observed in other supernovae remnants and pulsar wind nebulae. Our study offers a new observational perspective on the region's physical conditions and can potentially aid in understanding the underlying physics of a region within Cassiopeia A and similar supernovae remnants, while also providing a reference point for future studies on high-energy astrophysics. This research is expected to be expanded upon with the launch of the NICER mission, enabling researchers to monitor the region for a longer duration and with greater sensitivity. A well-known problem posed by Paul Erdos concerns identifying the minimum-sized set of integers containing integers with the lowest possible total sum that also guarantee the existence of a pair of integers with the highest possible total sum that differs by a given sum target (mod some number n). Erdos initially suggested using 2t+1 numbers, and offered a 2t-category proof that using 2t integers is enough in general. However, he also suspected that the 2t-bound could be achieved directly. Our research explores various versions of this problem, particularly where the integers in the set are chosen uniformly from a given range. In one such scenario where the range is all integers up to 2t-1, our findings show that the 2t-bound is achievable directly using a simple argument. In another scenario where the range is all integers up to N, our research indicates that the 2t-category proof provided by Frankl and Rödl can be applied directly. In yet another scenario where the range is all integers up to even numbers, an alternative 2t-category proof has been proposed. Furthermore, our research also explores some generalizations of these problems. Proximal optimization is a technique that has recently been adapted into various forms of non-smooth optimization methods. One such method, the proximal gradient method, can be seen as introducing a small amount of "heat" or regularization to the optimization process. In our study, we examine how this type of optimization relates to a generalized notion of Newton's method, and derive a rule for determining a suitable step-size that ensures self-concordance, a parameter that quantifies the smoothness of the optimization problem. We subsequently establish a generalized criterion for self-concordance based on the curvature of a manifold, and demonstrate that proximal optimization can be used to generate a sequence of points on this manifold that converge to a geometric or algebraic limit that depends on the specific manifold and its self-concordance curvature. We also propose an algorithm for identifying a manifold and its self-convergence curvature, and test it on simple examples. Lastly, we investigate the topological properties of the resulting manifolds and their algebraic structures. Our study provides a framework for using proximal optimization not only as a tool for solving optimization problems, but also for generating and understanding complex geometric and algebraic structures. Additionally, under certain conditions, proximal optimization can be seen as sampling points from a manifold, and our study can be seen as an algorithm for defining a manifold based on these sampling points. Our work combines elements of optimization, differential geometry, algebraic geometry, and topological invariants, and provides a new and innovative approach to these fields. We also investigate the applications of our methods in other fields, such as statistics, machine learning, information theory, and quantum mechanics. We demonstrate that proximal optimization can be used to extract information from quantum states, and explore the resulting geometric and topological structures. Our study provides a new framework for understanding the interplay between optimization, geometry, and physical systems. In particular, we investigate the proximal optimization of Schrödinger liapunov functions, and generate a sequence of points in phase space that converge to a geometric or algebraic limit. The accuracy of cross-matching techniques in astronomy is severely hampered by the inherent difficulties in pixel-to-pixel variations within CCD images, making it challenging to compare pixels between different datasets. Nevertheless, this issue could be addressed through the adoption of adaptive techniques that align images based on photometric rather than spatial correlations, thereby unleashing the potential of photonic-based data reduction methods to compare pixels across images. Utilizing an image dataset derived from the OmegaCAM telescope at the ESO's VLT, we explore the application of an adaptive algorithm of mean-local-standard-deviation and its modified version, along with a neural network-based method, to compare pixels across images, revealing that both methods yield more accurate results than traditional spatial alignment techniques. Furthermore, the phonic nature of these solutions enables them to scale efficiently to larger datasets, making them highly suitable for astronomical cross-matching tasks. Our research finds that the modified mean-local-standard-deviation method produces results comparable to those achieved by a deep learning approach, indicating that the problem might not necessitate elaborate neural networks, and rather, a simplified photonically-motivated approach could be an effective solution. Ultimately, the implementation of these methods has shown great promise to accelerate and improve the accuracy of sparse and abundant photometric catalog cross-matching in the coming decades, given the expected growth in datasets. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/astrophotonic/ML_CMCMS.git. (This article is the first in a series of four that utilize the astrophotonic approach).

The increasing use of Electronic Health Records leads to extensive data creation, enabling researchers to build various healthcare-related models. This study focuses on developing an attention-based graph neural network to predict the efficacy of combined medications. Our analysis reveals that current work on graph neural networks falls short due to overreliance on oversimplified graph creation methods, neglecting the resulting network's connectivity and hindering model performance. To address this, we introduce a detailed approach for creating a comprehensive drug interaction network that captures nuanced information from existing literature. When applied to PREDICT-DB, a large dataset containing 251,514 medication pairs, our model yields outstanding predictive results, surpassing state-of-the-art performance while providing clear interpretations. Moreover, our proposed method surpasses baseline models in accuracy when tested on real-world hospital data, demonstrating its practical value and clinical relevance. To ensure transparency and trustworthiness, we also conduct thorough evaluations, including model feature importance analysis, exoplanation, and empirical evidence verification. Our work offers a valuable contribution to the healthcare machine learning community, providing an exemplary case study on graph neural networks that can be adapted to various other healthcare-related prediction tasks. The proposed algorithm and code are freely accessible under the MIT License at the GitHub repository: https://github.com/predict-db/medscore. Additionally, the drug interaction network is available at: https://predict-db.org/drug-interaction-network. Finally, the predicted medication pairs are displayed on an interactive dashboard at: https://predict-db.org/predict. Please contact Dong (Alexander) Yang at dongyang@uoguelph.ca for further information. The predicted medication pairs can also be downloaded from the PredictDB platform. Our work is dedicated to developing transparent, explainable, and compassionate AI solutions for real-world healthcare problems and uses PredictDB data, an extensive dataset containing hospital medication data. Our research offers valuable information to healthcare professionals and can aid in making data-driven decisions when prescribing medications to patients. Although our work focuses on a combined medication scoring task, the proposed method has vast applications in other prediction tasks, such as understanding complex human relationships, analyzing text conversations, and generating engaging stories. In the future, we plan to expand our research to other prediction tasks within the PredictDB platform while ensuring that our models remain transparent, explainable, and compassionate. To facilitate reproducibility, we provide the code and data used in this study at the link: https://github.com/predict-db/medscore. Our work is dedicated to developing AI solutions for real-world healthcare problems

The proliferation of autonomous vehicles (AVs) worldwide has led to a surge in research into improving safety through the detection of road hazards. Present-day systems, however, are hindered by their national bias, caused by being trained on data from a single country and expecting to perform well in other countries. This challenge can be addressed by developing a single, universal model capable of identifying road hazards across different nations. In an effort to drive this research forward, we present a large, comprehensive dataset known as RHD, comprising over 21 thousand high-quality images of road hazards collected from three nations (the US, Australia, and the UK). This dataset serves as the foundation for a nationwide transfer learning-driven approach, in which we evaluate the potential of pre-trained models from various networks on three tasks: road hazard classification, localization, and segmentation. Our experiments reveal that, through transfer learning, AVs can be protected from national biases, and a more comprehensive range of high-level features can be learned, resulting in significant performance gains. Specifically, our results show that, by employing transfer learning, the accuracy of AVs in identifying road hazards can be elevated by 6.3%, their localization of these hazards can be improved by 0.9 meters, and their segmentation of these hazards can be augmented by 10.3%. Ultimately, our work presents a significant contribution to the safety of AVs by demonstrating that, through transfer learning, these technologies can be insulated from national biases and deliver superior performance. All our code and the RHD dataset are openly available at https://github.com/Auie-UIIT/RHD. This research is the product of an academic study. Imitation learning can be difficult in new areas of study due to a lack of expert demonstrations.  While collecting demonstrations in a new domain can be costly and time-consuming, finding relevant examples in a related field is often feasible.  Expert demonstrations from a related field, such as driving tasks, may not directly apply to a new area, such as navigation.  This research focuses on imitation learning for unstructured new areas using demonstrations from related fields with related tasks.  A key challenge is transferring task-related skills from the demonstrations while discarding task-unrelated skills.  To address this, we developed a method that separates relevant and irrelevant skills in the related field and adapts them separately to the new area.  To achieve this separation, we used an autoencoder to isolate task-related skills in expert demonstrations and developed a conditional behavior network to perform both new area tasks and related field tasks after observing the separated skills.  Experimental results on simulated datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of this method.  In future research, we plan to test this method on more complex real-world datasets. A vast majority of early star formation's total stellar mass is thought to be generated through a supernova's rapid conversion, yet the supernova's influence on the formation of new stars remains unclear. In our study, we simulate the intense magnetic fields produced by a supernova and its effect on collapsing molecular clouds, specifically around a Population III protostar. Using two-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations with electrodynamics, we examine how magnetic fields of varying intensity and orientation affect star formation. As a reference, our model mimics the natural turbulence experienced by collapsing clouds. In regions where magnetic fields are relatively weak, our results show intense rotation and disk fragmentation, consistent with predictions based on instability analysis. However, when we introduce magnetic fields ten times stronger, as expected from a supernova's effect, rotation disappears and the cloud collapses directly into the protostar. In another scenario, when the magnetic field's direction matches the angular momentum's direction, we observe the formation of a smaller, highly magnetic star and a surrounding disk. In situations where the magnetic field's direction contradicts the angular momentum's direction, we discover an irregularly shaped structure formed around a smaller, highly magnetic star. In all cases where magnetic fields have a significant impact, we notice the elimination of disk fragmentation, suggesting that intense supernova-produced magnetic fields can prevent the formation of new stars in regions surrounding Population III protostars. Therefore, we speculate that such magnetic fields may contribute to the late onset of second-generation star formation. Additionally, we propose that highly magnetic planets could provide a suitable environment for the late-stage supernova-affected star formation's remaining material to fall into. In these extreme conditions, it is possible that late-stage supernova-affected star formation's remaining material could yield exclusively first-generation objects. Finally, as a result of late-stage supernova-affected star formation, the material essential for both first- and second-generation stars becomes inextricably linked. Consequently, we contend that it would be impossible to accurately assess the unique properties of second-generation stars while they are still in their early stages. In a scenario where magnetic fields have a significant impact, as happens with Population III protostars, it is possible that all stellar objects ultimately produced by supernova-affected star formation would ultimately belong to the same generation of stars, as they derive from the same massive star. Association rules analysis involves examining transactions that combine products. Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a set of association rules, and denote the support and confidence associated with each rule as $(\mathit{Sup}), (\mathit{Conf})$. We can view association rule analysis from several standpoints, and these perspectives can be tied to the concepts of deduction frameworks and bases for association rules. A deduction framework is a structure consisting of a set of predicates and a collection of formulas constructed using logical operations. Bases for association rules are minimal subsets of transaction data that enable the derivation of the rules via certain queries. In this study, we focus on time-series transaction data and active rules with a fixed confidence level, and we investigate the problem of identifying the smallest transaction bases that can generate the active rules. We can represent transaction data as a first-order structure, and its theory consists of conditions that reflect the transactions' combinations of products. A deduction framework is said to be generated if its membership in the theory can be verified. We prove that generated deduction frameworks have equivalent query capabilities to the original structure, and we can derive the active rules within them. We also establish a relationship between the concepts of bases and deduction frameworks, and under certain conditions, we can find the smallest transaction bases that can generate the active rules by limiting the search to the deduction frameworks. The study presents theoretical connections between replication, deduction frameworks, and bases for association rules, and it addresses the related problem of identifying the smallest transaction bases that can generate the active rules. Experimental findings demonstrate that the performance of our approach surpasses that of the standard method that searches the entire transaction space. The study concludes with suggestions for further research. The study's findings can be found at: https://github.com/keqiang2014/Association-Rule-Bases. The connection between mental wellness and criminal behavior within the justice system is a well-established issue. Research has demonstrated that people convicted of crimes are more likely to suffer from mental illnesses, such as depression and anxiety. This correlation raises questions about the effectiveness of compulsory therapy for improving mental wellness in this population. Using a longitudinal dataset from the National Survey of Health and Aging, we examine how voluntary participation in therapy affects the mental health of convicted individuals. Noting that treatment is often coerced, we employ a difference-in-differences method to separate the impact of treatment on those who would have sought treatment voluntarily. Our analysis suggests that treatment has a positive effect on reducing symptoms of depression and anxiety, although the effect diminishes over time. Additionally, we discover that the positive impact of treatment is more pronounced in those suffering more severe mental health issues, and that treatment appears to lower the likelihood of reoffending, with the effect increasing over time. This study highlights the potential of treatment to improve mental wellness and reduce crime, while also emphasizing the need for research on the long-term effectiveness of treatment in addressing the complex relationships between mental health, crime, and the justice system. Ultimately, our findings suggest that even when treatment is coerced, it has a lasting impact on the mental health of convicted individuals. This study offers crucial insights for policymakers seeking to address mental wellness and crime, while also illustrating the capabilities of treatment to improve mental health in this sensitive and often stigmatized population. Radio maps are being considered as a promising solution to make wireless network planning more efficient by using a virtual interface to navigate through a target area. To create these maps, drones equipped with multiple radio frequency interfaces are used to collect data in real-time as they fly around. We investigate the effectiveness of radio maps in simulating channel behavior and predict their performance when used in area coverage scenarios with the help of these drones. Our research reveals that radio maps may not always be a suitable option, particularly when operating in dynamic environments and with limited drone visibility. Furthermore, using radio maps alone is not enough to deliver accurate results in scenarios requiring deep network penetration. To address this issue, we use a design approach that combines radio maps with machine learning models to compensate for each other's limitations, ultimately yielding an average error rate of less than 10% in area coverage calculations. The effectiveness of our approach is showcased through extensive field trials conducted in an outdoor environment. Overall, our contribution will help researchers better understand the strengths and limitations of radio maps, ultimately leading to the development of more accurate spectrum exploration tools. To facilitate future research, we are making our source code available. Additionally, key findings from our study are being presented at an IEEE conference. Several studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of data enhancement techniques, particularly label noise, to improve model performance. In this research, we investigate whether these techniques can be effectively applied to real-world applications involving existing data and provide new insights on their use. Through comprehensive experiments, we examine the use of label noise to enhance training data for both speech recognition and translation models. In addition to establishing a baseline, we also explore the potential of using pre-trained models to exploit the information present in enhanced datasets. Our results indicate that weak label noise can be beneficial, and combining it with strong noise yields better performance. However, direct use of strong noise on existing data is not advisable due to the risk of degradation. Conversely, strong noise can be safely applied to data generated from pre-trained models, leading to significant performance gains. This gives us the opportunity to utilize these models in a new light, as data generators for large-scale language models. Ultimately, the optimal approach involves a combination of weak label noise applied to existing data and strong noise applied to data generated from pre-trained models. This methodology can serve as a comprehensive data augmentation strategy, enhancing existing datasets and data sources. Code and models are available for reproduction of our results.

Consider two distributions, denoted as $F$ and $G$, with parameters $\theta_i$ and $\lambda_i$ respectively, where $i=1,\dots,n$. We investigate estimating the average of a mixture of these parameters when individual observations or samples from $F$ are available, under the assumption that $\theta_i$ and $\lambda_i$ are independent and normally distributed with known means and variances. Notably, we find that the mean of this mixture equals the mean of $G$ plus a known linear combination of the means of $F$ and variances of $F$ and $G$, and similarly for variances. These relationships enable us to construct an efficient estimator of the mixture variance based on a single observation from $F$ and known parameters of $G$. Furthermore, our results lead to a testing procedure for identifying components of mixtures, and provide bias-corrected estimates for the parameters of $F$ when they are congruent. Ultimately, our research contributes insight into the behavior of sample variances under changing population means, revealing cases where sample variances are minimal at the population mean and identifying conditions under which sample variances are maximal, minimal, or equivariant. Our research has practical applications in assessing the homogeneity of non-normal populations. Notably, our findings are illustrative of the additive principle under specific assumptions, and its counterpart, the multiplicative principle, which governs the behavior of certain statistical estimators. Our research also touches on the additive principle, providing novel contributions to the field. Achieving one-sided differential privacy involves maintaining dependent characteristic confidentiality by limiting the exposure of certain properties. We introduce a new framework, called dependent characteristic confidentiality, and within this structure, we develop a method to make reliable inferences about population characteristics while ensuring that sensitive dependent characteristics remain private. This framework serves as a necessary condition for one-sided differential privacy, and we further illustrate its significance through a real-world example. Moreover, we present a method to make reliable inferences about population characteristics while ensuring that sensitive dependent characteristics remain private, and this method serves as a necessary condition for obtaining a simplified version of one-sided differential privacy, known as characteristic-sensitive differential privacy. We demonstrate that our framework has practical applications in the fields of epidemiology and statistics, and we showcase its efficacy in an empirical study involving the simulation of private data. We also offer an analytical evaluation of the effectiveness of this framework in maintaining dependent characteristic confidentiality while ensuring that population inference remains reliable. These additional findings were the result of an in-depth examination of the properties of Mittag-Leffler functions and polynomials as well as the fractional integral and differential operators. - The application of this operational calculus to a broader range of distributional equations

- A more comprehensive exploration of the properties of Mittag-Leffler functions and polynomials
- A more general approach to solving complex-valued distributional differential equations and systems
