Automating the inspection of training data to identify problematic examples and data sets within multi-stage machine learning processes is a critical challenge. To address this issue, we have developed a systematic approach to diagnose issues arising from individual data instances or groups of data sets. Our method calculates the significance of each data instance or group based on the contribution they makes to the model, using a value representation for significance that can be translated into the Shapley value framework. This allows us to generate a comprehensive spectrum of instance significance, from the most influential to the least significant, by computing standard Shapley values or their variants for groups of data sets. To efficiently handle large datasets, the significance of individual examples can be estimated in parallel, while the significance of non-uniform groups of data sets can be approximated using Monte Carlo simulations. The proposed algorithm is demonstrated to be effective in a simple model and also in a full end-to-end machine learning pipeline, encompassing data preprocessing, feature selection, model training, and model testing, in three real-world scenarios. The results show that our approach can automatically identify problematic data instances and groups, which are often small in number, and that it outperforms existing diagnostic methods in several aspects, including efficiency, stability, and model quality. The effectiveness of the approach is further illustrated with detailed debug reports that highlight issues arising from individual data instances or groups of data sets and provide suggestions for data curation practices. The code to reproduce the results is available for download. With further refinement, this algorithm has the potential to support advanced data diagnostics in a variety of machine learning applications. The underlying algorithm is a general solution that is compatible with any machine learning algorithm and data sets, and it is also compatible with automated machine learning frameworks. Furthermore, the algorithm is inherently designed to handle multi-stage machine learning processes, including pipelines with multiple stages, and it can be extended to support diagnostic services in other domains. The approach is primarily designed to promote data curators, data scientists, and other machine learning professionals to view data debugging as an ongoing process that requires attention at various stages of model development and testing. By computing instance significance, data curators can monitor diagnostic information and become aware of issues arising from individual data instances or groups of data sets, which can be used to guide data curation activities, such as data normalization, feature engineering, model retraining, and model reconfiguration. This approach leads to a discovery of interesting patterns and relationships among geometric shapes of various dimensions. These curves serve as fundamental building blocks for studying the interactions between geometry, statistics, combinatorics, and topology. This study provides an in-depth examination of how high pressure influences the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn, an antiferromagnetic compound with a triangular structure. Theoretical models predict that when exposed to pressure, Mn$_3$Sn undergoes a stable transformation into a hexagonal structure, facilitating easier doping. We experimentally investigate this process, using a non-linear Hall resistivity to assess the antiferromagnetic parameters and thus the structural properties of Mn$_3$Sn. The measurement results indicate that as pressure increases, the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn undergoes a significant enhancement before eventually decreasing beyond a critical pressure of 5 GPa. In contrast to standard Mn$_3$Sn, a pressure of 7 GPa is required to induce a complete hexagonal structure, suggesting that our research can serve as a hallmark to identify this phase transition in Mn$_3$Sn through an anomalous Hall effect perspective. Furthermore, our research explores the underlying mechanism behind the increased anomalous Hall effect at lower pressures and the decreased effect at higher pressures. The findings suggest that both pressure-dependent features are caused by distinct features in the electronic properties of the two structures, resulting in a Hall effect response that is highly sensitive to pressure. The conversion of Mn$_3$Sn from a semimetal to a metal under pressure also contributes to the changes in the anomalous Hall effect, as demonstrated in this study. The research offers a means to control the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn through pressure-induced structural modifications, opening up the possibility for identifying other pressure-dependent antiferromagnets with similar properties. The study also highlights Mn$_3$Sn as an ideal test subject for investigating the connection between ferromagnetism and the anomalous Hall effect, as evidenced by experiments using a quantum sensor. The research provides a fundamental understanding of how high pressure influences the electronic and magnetic properties of Mn$_3$Sn, shedding light on the underlying physics behind the resulting phenomena. The research offers a means to regulate the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn by using external pressure, inducing a complete transformation of the material's electronic and magnetic properties. The study could serve as a significant reference point for investigating the synthesis of other hexagonal metals using high-pressure techniques and the resulting modifications to their anomalous Hall effect. The research could also facilitate the development of new technologies using Mn$_3$Sn and similar materials, as well as Hall effect devices that can function at high pressures. Given a hyperbolic 3-manifold with a specified Euler characteristic, we develop methods to determine the range of variations in its Thurston norm. This applies to tight contact structures, of which there can be multiple on a single 3-manifold. We establish that the minimum and maximum values of a tight contact structure's Euler characteristic and the norm of its convex contact structure are all related to the characteristic's value. This holds true for all hyperbolic 3-manifolds with a specified Euler characteristic, and our results are consistent with Libarle's previous findings for minimal Euler characteristic 0 manifolds. We expand upon Libarle's work, obtaining similar findings for all hyperbolic 3-manifolds with a specified Euler characteristic, and our results are accurate to a factor of 16. Next, we define new properties for links, denoted F+ and F-, and prove that they are both invariant under complete deformation. We establish that a manifold is homotopy equivalent to a circle if and only if a specific convex contact structure has an Euler characteristic of 0. Finally, in the appendices, we provide a comprehensive overview of previously unpublished results, and we reevaluate the previously established upper bound of 16, achieving a much tighter upper limit of less than 1.25. Additionally, we provide an explicit formula to calculate the Euler characteristic of a specific class of closed, oriented 3-manifolds. This formula is based on the number of twists in a specific type of link, and it allows us to reevaluate previously established bounds. Ultimately, our results provide further insight into the characteristics of hyperbolic 3-manifolds, and their properties under various contact structures. These findings also shed light on the characteristics of both left and right invariant parts of a tight contact structure. The properties of these parts are closely related to those of the underlying hyperbolic manifold, and our results provide a thorough understanding of their relationships. In the process of developing these theorems, we also proved several nontrivial lemmas that may be of independent interest. These include a formula to calculate the Euler characteristic of a specific type of map, and a nontrivial inequality involving the characteristics of both the original and reversed versions of a closed, oriented 3-manifold. These findings demonstrate the connections between the characteristics of both a hyperbolic 3-manifold and its reverse, and highlight the relationships between the characteristics of both the original and modified versions of a tight contact structure. We propose an entropic method to quantify directional emission in microcavity lasers. This approach uses the volume of far-field emission as a metric, enabling simple calculation via far-field images or simulations. The entropic method offers two advantages: it can determine symmetry breaking without calculating emission patterns, and it remains unbiased towards any fitting parameters or assumptions. Furthermore, this hypothesis-free method remains invariant under coordinate transformations, ensuring its physical relevance. By applying this approach, we investigate the effect of two common design techniques used to enhance directional emission: the shape of the microcavity and the placement of apertures. Our results demonstrate that the entropic metric provides a clear indication of emission directionality, thereby facilitating a quicker and more efficient design of microcavity lasers with the desired properties. This research combines theoretical framework and numerical simulation to illustrate the efficacy of the entropic method in analyzing directional emission in microcavity lasers. The findings present a new tool for designing microcavity lasers with low polarization and high directional emission. These designs have significant practical value due to their versatility in integrating optical systems and the potential to increase optical transmission efficiency. The entropic method could be applied to other anisotropic systems and offers a unique tool for evaluating emission properties. The research presents a new perspective on analyzing anisotropic emission and opens the door for further development with exciting research possibilities. Our research focuses on the stability of cryptocurrencies based on their use as a medium of exchange. We start by examining the ideal level of stability, which we consider to be the case where the price of bitcoin remains steady over time. However, since this is not a feasible goal, we explored the next best option – logarithmic stability. This approach is grounded in economic theory and takes into account the underlying characteristics of a medium of exchange, which necessarily involves price fluctuations in the long run. We demonstrate that two factors significantly influence the stability of cryptocurrencies: the rate at which new units are created and how transactions are verified. Building on previous studies, our analysis reveals the conditions under which cryptocurrencies can function as efficient media of exchange and provides a theoretical basis for evaluating stability. This concept is further developed to assess the stability of other cryptocurrencies, including ethereum and ripple, in addition to bitcoin. Our results show that these cryptocurrencies do not meet the criteria for logarithmic stability, which may have implications for their potential as long-term means of exchange. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the proof-of-work system used in bitcoin is actually a significant advantage in achieving stability. We conclude by highlighting the importance of logarithmic stability for the long-term survival and adoption of cryptocurrencies. Given the current market conditions, where investors primarily focus on short-term and long-term price predictions, the concept of stability in cryptocurrencies is inherently linked to their potential as means of exchange. Thus, achieving logarithmic stability becomes a crucial goal for the sustainable development and widespread acceptance of cryptocurrencies. The solar system's outer atmosphere, spanning from the Sun to about 36 astronomical units, experiences a unique environment governed by magnetohydrodynamics and high-energy particle fluctuations. As the solar wind enters the Alfvenic zone, it enters a state of turbulent instability, primarily driven by compressive waves rather than rotational ones. The nature of this compressive turbulence remains unclear and varies depending on the scale and location within this region. The Magnetospheric MultiScale mission has allowed researchers to study turbulent dynamics and energy transfer in the Alfvenic zone and its interaction with the solar wind's magnetic field. Analyzing data from the solar wind, researchers have discovered that pressure fluctuations exhibit an almost Gaussian distribution, but with a bias towards lower pressures, indicating non-thermal energy transfer. Utilizing the spacecraft's potential detectors, they re-processed the data into velocity distributions, revealing a bi-modal structure that matches a broad spectrum model. This study presents fresh perspectives on the solar wind's turbulent dynamics, providing evidence of a cascade effect from larger scales to smaller ones. The findings also suggest a link between the solar wind's velocity and magnetic field strength, as well as the ion scale and sub-ion scale of these instabilities. The research offers a new understanding of the solar wind's dynamic behavior, paving the way for future research into the Alfvenic zone's dynamics, including the interaction between magnetic fields and turbulent flows. In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are commonly limited by the coherence time, typically measuring in hundreds of attoseconds to few femtoseconds. This research investigates the potential to circumvent this time constraint through self-destruction of macropulse modulation, a concept yet to be explored in full potential. We utilize a multi-energy-model to simulate an undulator-based nonlinear self-amplification scheme, combining this with detailed macropulse modulation implementation. Our findings demonstrate the possibility of generating attosecond pulse trains in the XUV and soft X-ray regimes, with a significant increase in pulse duration if modulation depth is high. We identify a viable regime for this approach, with a hopeful promise for generating attosecond pulses in the hard X-ray region. Ultimately, achieving such short pulse durations will have far-reaching implications for the fields of high-field physics, biological imaging, and nonlinear spectroscopy. Presented here are detailed numerical data that support the findings of the study. The data consists of various fields that describe the temporal and spectral characteristics of pulses produced by the proposed modulation scheme. The include pulse amplitude, wavelength, temporal FWHM, temporal RMS duration, temporal duration based on spectral resolution product, and relative pulse stability. Additionally, the data includes coefficients defining the tapered macropulse modulation in the undulator. The data can be accessed at https://dx.in.cnki.com/front/article/information?id=GSN-111610-101. Additionally, the data can be accessed via: 10.17632/4xkz747z9x.

A numerical model that incorporates viscous forces into a two-layer channel flow is developed, assuming the presence of shear and no lateral flow between parallel layers. The model is validated through comparison with existing experimental and numerical data obtained under non-viscous conditions. It is observed that when the ratio of viscous forces to inertial forces is low, the model matches experimental data very closely. However, as the ratio increases, deviations between the model and experimental results become more pronounced, especially in the experimental regime characterized by high shear rates and weak pressure gradients. It is found that if the assumption of parallel flow layers is not met, the model overestimates the width of the shear zone by a factor of 1.5 to 2.5. A simplified analytical model that accounts for both inertial and viscous forces is developed, demonstrating that the latter dominates the former in a specific parameter range. The results suggest that if the assumption of negligible lateral flow between layers is not met, the model overestimates the width of the shear zone and the rate of eclogitization (D/D0) by a factor of 1.5 to 2.5, which is particularly significant in a specific parameter range of Nn=0.01-0.1. The study concludes by noting that while the assumption of parallel flow layers is reasonable under low viscous regime, it may lead to inaccurate results in a more complex flow environment. Therefore, caution should be exercised when applying the physical optics model without thoroughly assessing the flow conditions. The model presents an effective solution for estimating layer thickness in cases where viscous and inertial forces are equally dominant. Additionally, the study's findings can contribute to a better understanding of geological processes such as eclogitization and ultrahypersubduction. These interpretations are based on a comparison with numerical simulations from the iDynAMo project. A corresponding code is included in the repository to replicate the results. To address the issue of electoral manipulation through the manipulation of voting district boundaries, our research focuses on an existing heuristic for detecting gerrymandering and proposes an innovative method based on the heat diffusion approach. The goal is to develop an automated technique that can accurately determine whether a district map is unfair. We began by applying the FS algorithm to analyze mock temperature distributions and established that it effectively detects uneven heat spreads. However, the FS algorithm's reliance on the finite element method limits its feasibility as a detection tool. Building on this foundation, our team developed an improved heat diffusion method utilizing spherical harmonics, thereby creating an innovative heat diffusion approach. This novel method facilitates detecting gerrymandering in voting district boundaries and enables the calculation of a score indicating the level of electoral manipulation. We tested our approach on actual US district maps from 2011 and simulated temperature distributions, achieving promising results. Ultimately, this research enables the use of the heat diffusion approach as a reliable indicator of gerrymandering. While there are similarities with existing detection methods, our approach offers distinct advantages, primarily due to its reliance on the PH method rather than the FS algorithm. Consequently, this research contributes to the ongoing pursuit of an automated gerrymandering detection technique. We make the PH method and our test maps publicly available to support future research on this problem. To succeed in visually navigating an unknown space, a robotic agent must balance active exploration with task-driven focus. Conventional approaches typically separate these components, but this research proposes a more integrated solution. By utilizing a predictive model to estimate the robot's state from its sensor observations, the research develops a novel task-driven objective function that measures surprise based on the state's unpredictability. This objective function is optimized through a reinforcement learning process that can adapt to various sensing modalities. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in unknown environments through a comparison with leading navigation methods that emphasize exploration or focus. The research also demonstrates its ability to transfer to deep learning models and navigate scenarios involving real-world robotic platforms, such as Pepper and RoboThor, successfully. In accretion scenarios where a jet or outflow forms, researchers hypothesized that material extracted by feedback mechanisms could lead to a disk instability, potentially explaining outburst cycles in black hole X-ray binaries. To examine this idea, we investigated the impact of Bondi mass reduction rates and observed limits on these rates in various astrophysical contexts, discovering a stringent bound of $a_{\rm max} \approx 0.66$ for the accretion disk's inner boundary. Our findings suggest that any instability triggered by feedback should manifest within a timescale of hours, contradicting the hour-to-day timescales often seen in black hole X-ray binaries. Therefore, we propose that the mechanisms forming outflows in these binaries might operate at a level where they can't be seen in high-energy spectra, but a more in-depth study of AGN outflows is needed to confirm this conclusion. Additionally, we observed that a step-function model for the Bondi mass reduction rate fits the data better than a linear model. We suggest that further research should focus not only on understanding outburst mechanisms but also on the role of outflows in maintaining equilibrium in accretion disks. We present several open questions. We used existing data from Cyg X-1 to establish a baseline understanding of accretion dynamics in the metallic regime, but we encountered a limitation - our model depends on the metallicity of the disk for accurate calculations of Bondi mass reduction rates, a factor that remains unknown. Furthermore, we identified four features in high-energy spectra that don't fit our model and could be attributed to mechanisms other than Bondi mass reduction, and we found that our results are consistent with a disk that is partially Comptonized. We used existing data from HST to examine photospheric parameters and observed limits on Bondi mass reduction rates in the visible regime, discovering a timescale of hours for any instability triggered by feedback mechanisms. Our findings suggest that this timescale could be universal, and we propose several tests to confirm this conclusion. Finally, we used existing data from radio observations to examine Bondi mass reduction rates in the kinetic energy regime, discovering a timescale of days and suggesting that any instability triggered by feedback mechanisms should manifest within this timescale. Our findings imply that feedback mechanisms could be constantly extracting and redistributing energy within accretion disks on a daily basis. Although this hypothesis remains unverified, we present several open questions and propose that future research should focus not only on understanding outflows in the radio regime but also on the role of feedback mechanisms

We examine the formation of heavy black holes in metallic-poor nuclear star clusters, focusing specifically on regions of less than 10 pc in dense stellar aggregates. Our study reveals that HBSH formation, resulting from the merger of neutron stars in these areas, generates the majority of gravitational waves within a frequency range of 20-104 Hz. The predicted gravitational wave events from such sources within the first gigayear of the universe's history, prior to the cosmic dark ages, significantly exceeds the anticipated rate of observations by the LISA telescope. Under the assumption that dark compact remnants maintain their current spatial distribution among low-metallicity nuclear clusters, LISA is likely to observe tens of thousands of events from HBSH mergers in its initial year of operation. The peak frequency of these gravitational waves will range between 10^-2 and 10^-1 Hz. The analysis also indicates that the rate of gravitational wave detection by LISA is largely unaffected by limitations in resolving closely packed sources, but may vary depending on criteria used to identify low-metallicity nuclear clusters within dense stellar aggregates. The study further estimates that, in the initial two years of operation, LISA is likely to observe hundreds of thousands of gravitational wave events from the mergers of neutron stars and black holes within galactic nuclear clusters, producing a substantial enrichment of signal power in the frequency range of 10^-1 to 10 Hz. The analysis suggests that the majority of this gravitational wave activity originates from nuclear clusters surrounding low-mass galaxies, and that the rate of detection is primarily governed by the characteristics of these dwarf galaxy systems. These incidents not only reduce the reliability of the energy infrastructure but also increase maintenance costs. Validating the causes of incidents in power distribution systems is often challenging due to the difficulty in obtaining precise data on weather conditions and other factors. This research proposes an innovative method that uses smart meter data to effectively identify incidents in power distribution systems. The approach relies on a data-driven approach rooted in statistical analysis to pinpoint incident-related anomalies in the energy consumption patterns of customers. To refine the results, the system uses an advanced algorithm that minimizes noise and provides a clear picture of the incident's impact on energy consumption. Our proposed method has been tested on actual data from a real-world power distribution infrastructure consisting of 12000 customers. The results demonstrate its ability to accurately identify incidents while filtering out irrelevant information. The system is comprised of two main components: the Incident Detection Unit and the Confirmation Reconciliation Mechanism. The former relies on a complex algorithm that uses multiple criteria to pinpoint unusual patterns in energy consumption, while the latter uses a different technique to validate the results and eliminate potential false positives. The integration of these components through a data-driven approach enables the system to provide a clear confirmation of incident causes while ignoring background noise. The system has been evaluated using actual data from a real-world infrastructure consisting of 1280 customers. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform for assessing the capabilities of language models, as they can engage in text-based interactions mimicking real-world conversations with a clear indicator of success: achieving the desired outcome, or the 'goal'. Previous research has shown that language models perform well in these games, but achieving the goal often proves difficult without conducting extensive search within the game environment. This search process raises concerns about the safety of relying on language models in practical applications. To mitigate these concerns, we propose an innovative approach that combines language model predictions with a novel quantification method for measuring probability distribution similarity. This quantification enables the efficient selection of the top model predictions using a nearest neighbor data structure, allowing us to process millions of data points per second. This speedup empowers language models to achieve the goal in text-based games by filtering out unnecessary predictions, a feature we demonstrate using the TextWorld game. Our research demonstrates that by enhancing the decision-making process of language models, we can significantly scale up their capabilities and successfully complete a variety of challenging text-based games. The TextWorldExpress framework is open-source and available on GitHub. Experiments are conducted using the T5 model. The text-based game used in this research is TextWorld. Although the perfect topological insulator has a 0d Z2 number, the presence of external flaws can alter this property, resulting in a 1d Z2 number for the bulk. To assess the 1d Z2 number, we use an approach that relies on the non-zero homogeneity of the fermionic zero-mode bundle following the reduction of its 2d structure to a 1d framework. Consequently, we determine the 1d Z2 number by examining the 1st homology group's non-trivial characteristic feature in the reduced bundle, which indicates a divergent fermionic zero-mode density along the boundary, ultimately failing the topological insulator's bulk-boundary correspondence. Consider the scenario where $p \geq 2$ and $\alpha, \beta$ are real numbers with $\alpha < \beta$. Let $A_{\alpha,\beta}$ denote the sector $\{z \in \mathbb{R}^2 : \arg z \in (\alpha,\beta)\}$. This paper focuses on finding p-harmonic functions in $A_{\alpha,\beta}$ that are symmetric across the real axis and equal to $|z|^p$ at the boundary. We derive an equation that approximates these functions at the origin and demonstrate that this equation converges to a specific function, which we call $K_p(z)$. Notably, although $K_p(z)$ may be undefined for certain values of $p$, it converges to a specific function, which we call $K(z)$, for all $p \geq 2$. To solve this problem, we use a combination of variational methods and fixed-point theorems. This study has several applications, including deriving approximations for p-capacity in sectors and extending a theorem initially proved by Eremenko and Taurmanen. As an interesting observation, we note that $K_p(z)$ may not exist for certain values of $p$, yet it converges to $K(z) \approx 0.5 + 0.39i$ for all $p \geq 2$. For example, in the case of $p=20$, $K_{20}(z) \approx 0.5002 + 0.3901i$, while in the case of $p=2$, $K_2(z) \approx 0.4998 + 0.3988i$. All of these results suggest that the limit as $p \to \infty$ of $K_p(z)$ is $0.5 + 0.39i$. This study also demonstrates that the function $K(z)$ is a non-degenerate $p$-harmonic function in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Therefore, the principal result of this study is that the function $K(z)$ can be expressed as a solution to a specific p-harmonic equation for all $p \geq 2$. This result is equivalent to the formula $K(z) = \frac{p}{p-2} |z|^{p-2}$. This study also includes a technical appendix, which proves some general results on the existence and uniqueness

Extreme environmental fluctuations have far-reaching effects on ecosystems and the surrounding coastal areas.  Research into these events has historically been hindered by a lack of simultaneous, high-quality data from multiple locations, which are essential for understanding the spatial distribution of these phenomena.  A new method incorporates Bayesian predictive peaks into a multi-dimensional spatial model, allowing it to identify and prioritize locations where joint data would be particularly useful.  These "hotspots" are predicted based on existing relationships between environmental variables and are weighted according to the expected return on investment if joint data were collected there.  In various scenarios, this proposed approach effectively prioritizes locations where joint data would be most valuable, and can be utilized through an interactive interface to guide researchers collecting field data in high-resolution formats.  This is particularly relevant for research into extreme events in oceanic environments, where a simulated example involving ocean currents and wave patterns is provided.  The proposed technique is referred to as multiPEAK.  Further details on this can be found in a separate document.  The code used for this research is accessible via github.com/edgarpaul/PEAK. To study Higgs boson generation at the LHC using the matrix element technique, we examine collisions between protons and a Higgs boson pair in the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel. The matrix element method focuses on selecting events that best match the predicted $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ phenomenon at the LHC, based on the distribution of event kinematics. Two distinct approaches were used to compute the matrix elements and determine the event classification. The first approach relied on an amplitude-based method, while the second used a particle-level description. We evaluated the effectiveness of the matrix element method in reducing $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ event contamination and identified a $p_T$ threshold for the central $\textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}$ pair that significantly improves this reduction. Additionally, we assessed the matrix element method's ability to optimize Higgs boson pair detection at the LHC by leveraging the matrix element technique. Our study showed that this approach significantly boosts $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ event detection rates, with a notable increase of over two orders of magnitude at specific $p_T$ thresholds. Furthermore, using the matrix element method, we found that the LHC can potentially detect Higgs boson pairs at thresholds two orders of magnitude lower than previously estimated. The matrix element technique's ability to optimize detection is due to its ability to efficiently eliminate irrelevant $\textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}$ event contributions and focus Higgs boson pair analysis on the most relevant kinematic regions. The increase in detection thresholds in the absence of this technique is primarily attributed to efforts to minimize $\textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}$ contamination through other methods. Our study also examined the effectiveness of two distinct Monte Carlo event generators - MadGraph and Herwig - in computing the matrix elements

The creation of rocky exoplanets is a focus area for research in the field of planetary science.  An important goal of this area of study is to gain a thorough understanding of the chemical compositions of the interior sections of terrestrial-type exoplanets as they form.
  We conducted an extensive analysis of the chemical compositions of 31 stars that host terrestrial planets similar in size and composition.  Using a reliable spectral modeling approach, we were able to accurately determine the abundance of key elements in the stars within a precise margin of error.
  An analysis of our results against synthetic evolutionary models revealed that the stars we studied had a consistent enrichment pattern in the core and a uniform depletion pattern in the envelope.  This pattern indicated that the core of these stars is made up primarily of iron, with a small amount of magnesium, and that the envelope is mostly composed of silicon, with oxygen, nickel, and sulfur.
  A comparison of our measurements with the abundances in the solar system showed that the stellar values match the solar values within a consistent margin of error.  This consistency is evidence of a similar planetary structure in our solar system and the systems we studied, with rocky exoplanets that are similar in composition and size.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have become a preferred method for wireless localization based on channel state information (CSI), utilizing raw CSI to learn location-specific features from acoustic signals. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of DNNs heavily relies on data quality and adequate training data, which can be challenging and costly to obtain, particularly in new and untested environments. Our research introduces an innovative approach called attention-enhanced CSI, an attention mechanism integrated with the DNN, that enhances its generalization capabilities and adaptability to various environments. An internal attention module is applied to focus attention on the most relevant acoustic signals and their corresponding CSI, thereby optimizing channel feature extraction and reducing dependence on extensive training data. The proposed attention-enhanced CSI scheme demonstrates superior performance and robustness compared to conventional DNNs, with a notable enhancement of 8.6%, 10.3%, and 12.6% in 70%, 85%, and 95% training data scenarios, respectively. Additionally, it is noteworthy that this method yields superior results under data-deficient conditions. The computational efficiency of this scheme has been ensured by carefully selecting the feature representation of CSI and acoustic signals, thereby enabling real-time deployment on typical hardware, making it a practical solution for localization applications in resource-constrained environments. This paper launches a comprehensive investigation into various types of modal logic, with the aim of linking them to established topological frameworks. The underlying strategy is to examine which properties of these frameworks can effectively support the modal logic underlying any given model. The study begins by reviewing and reinterpreting the connections between different topological structures, with a particular focus on crisp topologies in the context of classical logic. Specifically, it demonstrates that both the internal logic and the algebraic semantics of a commutative ring are inherently first-order, with this first-order model being equivalent to the standard model when the initial assumptions are met. This initial chapter serves as a foundation for more in-depth analyses in subsequent papers. By examining high-order logic in relation to topological structures, the study establishes a series of key results that can be utilized to prove both conservativity and decidability in various extensions of modal logic. Moreover, it explores the implications of using different topological structures to define a modal logic's underlying algebraic structure, with a particular focus on multivalued modal logic. The study identifies two distinct topological frameworks that can effectively be linked to multivalued modal logic: multivalued topological Kripke semantics and multivalued ring-based semantics. Multivalued topological Kripke semantics can be refined into two separate forms, with both forms being capable of representing the same linguistic expressions. Furthermore, it proves that multivalued ring-based semantics is conservatively extendable to first-order algebraic semantics. The study also delves into the specific case of fuzzy logic, with both fuzzy topological Kripue-Kripke semantics and fuzzy ring-based semantics serving as possible representations. By examining both fuzzy topological Kripke semantics and fuzzy ring-based semantics, it proves that both can effectively be interpreted in their respective standard models. Moreover, it proves that fuzzy ring-based semantics is conservatively extendable to first-order algebraic semantics. Finally, the study analyzes both local cleavage theory and global cleavage theory, with a particular focus on their connections to topological structures in both commutative rings and hyperreal fields. By establishing a series of key results, it proves that both local and global cleavage theories can be reduced to a singular definable formula in the context of commutative rings, with this further proof expanding into hyperreal fields through the use of bad members. Ultimately, the study sets the stage for a comprehensive investigation into various types of modal logic by linking them to established topological structures in both commutative rings and hyperreal fields.

which inherently comes with various forms of uncertainty. This formal structure is mirrored 
in the field of machine learning, specifically in model evaluation and interpretation. While 
general concepts of uncertainty are well established, the literature lacks a unified framework 
for describing and quantifying uncertainty in relation to inference. We introduce a standardized 
approach to categorize and compare different uncertainty methods across various scientific and 
machine learning settings, encompassing 14 distinct techniques represented in the journal's special

Scientists use computer models to study real-world phenomena on a specific time interval, but often these models rely on external references, which can be difficult to replicate exactly. This is known as an inverse issue, causing model estimation to be complicated. By treating the reference data as a collective property of the models, a new approach, Multiple Contour Estimation (MCE), offers a reliable method for resolving this issue. In this study, we demonstrate the utility of MCE on a computer simulation model with time-dependent outputs. Due to its versatile formulation, MCE can be applied to a range of model types, as illustrated using a case study based on a well-known jet engine model. Overall, MCE provides a useful tool for scientists to bridge the gap between model reference and observation. This approach offers a valuable contribution to the field of computer model validation. MCE is an open-source software, accessible through http://mce.pw. Additionally, a detailed description of the model used in this research is available at https://model-portal.eu/model/eng-jet-engine-1.0.2. AI systems designed to operate in harsh environments must be capable of withstanding potential attacks on their training data.  In situations where some of the training data is suspect and may be compromised, developing robust models is crucial, especially in fields like computer vision.  Research has shown that relying on global information in models can make them more resilient to tampering with the training dataset.  However, this increase in resilience comes at a cost – these models are harder to damage than before, but also lose some of their ability to learn from specific, targeted samples.  In this context, we explore the use of regional information in models as a potential way to improve their ability to utilize local queries.  Our experiments in computer vision have shown that regional information can aid models in learning from partial queries, and we have developed different types of regional queries that can be effective in various scenarios.  While initial studies have shown that regional information can be beneficial, the impact of multi-headed queries – where models utilize information from various sections of images – is still unclear.  We have found that multi-headed queries are not the most effective way to utilize regional information and that other approaches, such as regional attention, are more practical.  Additionally, we have devised a method to gradually introduce regional information to models while mitigating any performance decline.  Through our research, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of regional information in enhancing the resilience of models to data tampering.  Our findings also offer practical guidance on the implementation of regional information in models to maximize their resilience.  In contrast to existing research, our approach focuses on local information in models and can be easily adapted to various settings.  We have also developed and will soon release a new dataset containing images that have been manipulated for research purposes.  Our dataset is designed specifically for research into image classification and tampering and can be used to study the effect of gradual data manipulation on model performance.  This phenomenon, known as data shift, is an area of ongoing research.  Our work offers insight into the potential causes and our approach can be adapted to various research areas that may be affected by data shifting problems in the future.  In particular, our study has shown that regional information can aid models in performing better in data shifting scenarios, and this is true across different types of manipulated images.  We have tested our approach in model training and confirmed that regional information can significantly improve model performance in areas with limited data, a phenomenon that may be attributed to regional information aiding models in learning from partial queries. By comparing various methods of determining star formation rates (SFRs) in galaxies at specific distances, we found that different techniques yield consistent results for SFRs beyond a certain threshold of observed emission. However, these methods disagree for galaxies with lower emission levels. As more sophisticated modeling becomes available, using techniques like template fitting for spectral energy distributions (SEDs), we observed an increase in predicted SFRs for galaxies with lower emission levels. Furthermore, these calculations often yield negative SFRs for galaxies with the weakest emission, which is unsustainable. We propose using a reliable SFR indicator, such as the $Br\gamma$ line, to benchmark against SFRs derived from more complex modeling, revealing their inconsistencies, especially for galaxies with low emission levels. Finally, we note that using strong $Br\gamma$ observations as a benchmark produces a consistent distribution of SFRs across different galaxy types, regardless of whether or not complex modeling is used. This result implies that using $Br\gamma$ observations can help identify galaxies that are problematic for SFR estimation using more complex models, potentially indicating where these models fail or need revision. By re-examining the SFR calibration for these models using $Br\gamma$ observations, we observed an increase in consistency, but a discrepancy still remains for certain galaxies. Hence, we suggest further investigation into the properties of galaxies that cannot be accurately estimated for SFR using complex models, which may hold important clues for understanding galaxy evolution and energy production. This study presents an innovative approach to generating synthetic speech at varied lengths, inspired by a statistical model that forms speech as a result of selecting median vocabulary based on frame-to-word alignment probabilities. Building upon this idea, two non-statistical methods for producing synthetic speech at different lengths have been developed. The first method involves sampling vocabulary at a median rate, while the second method uses an algorithmic process akin to a searching mechanism. These two methods are compared in terms of their coherence with human speakers, and system evaluations confirm that both methods excelled in generating synthetic speech within specified lengths. Moreover, our analysis suggests that the median-driven approach is more effective than a corresponding statistical method in creating synthetic speech with consistent lengths. In addition, a sample of both mediated and algorithmically derived sentences from our experiment's data is made available online. This paper was initially presented at the 80th IACSP conference, held in Shanghai, China.

When combining datasets, the risk of overfitting increases, and model selection becomes more complex. Additionally, many deep multimodal learning techniques employ model-specific representations, limiting their effectiveness. In real-world applications, it is often difficult and time-consuming to tailor models to a particular dataset. The unified framework's capabilities were further demonstrated by extending it to handle non-K-fan datasets, and the results indicate a significant improvement over baseline models. The global WhatsApp crisis began in 2019-2020 when several countries experienced widespread misinformation spreads within local communities via the app, particularly concerning viral myths linking COVID-19 origins to conspiracy theories. In an effort to combat this issue, WhatsApp introduced several measures to limit message sharing. The primary goal of this study is to assess the impact of these changes. By collecting and analyzing public WhatsApp chats in India, our research investigates two primary aspects: the overall effect on misinformation circulation and the diverse messages exchanged among users. Our findings indicate both a decline in forwarded messages and a decrease in the spread of conspiracy theories related to COVID-19, primarily resulting from high-ranking users promoting publicly available news content. Conversely, the majority of regular users continue to engage with misinformation, highlighting the challenges in ensuring app users become reliable news sources. Our research outcomes support the WhatsApp initiative and suggest further optimization strategies to enhance the app's misinformation mitigation capabilities. Furthermore, our analysis provides valuable insights into understanding the spread of social misinformation within private online communities. The combined approaches of social science and natural language processing used in this research yield valuable insights into examining app or platform features and their effectiveness in combating misinformation. Moreover, our investigation contributes to understanding the ongoing global WhatsApp crisis and offers concrete recommendations for feature design and optimization to combat misinformation within private online environments. The code used in this research study is publicly accessible via a GitHub repository for reproducibility purposes. The purpose of this research was solely to examine public messages on WhatsApp, specifically in India, with the aim of understanding the impact of WhatsApp features on misinformation spread. We analyze a general branching population where individual lifetimes are independent and identically distributed with arbitrary distributions, and individuals give birth to new ones at random times following a Poisson process independently from each other. It's assumed that every individual has a set of randomly assigned alleles at random independently, and we consider a large population where the population size grows indefinitely, and show that under these conditions, the distribution of allele frequencies converges uniformly across all generations to a stable frequency spectrum. This stable frequency spectrum can be represented as the sum of two components, where the first is a straightforward calculation of visible genetic data, and the second is significantly more complex and represents genetic information that is invisible due to coalescence events in the population's history. We develop a mathematical formula for calculating this invisible genetic information, and demonstrate that it converges to a specific constant times the logarithm of the population size in the population's late stages. This constant is determined by the average rate at which population members coalesce over time, and we show that it is directly proportional to the average time between successive coalescence events in the population's history. This stable frequency spectrum, and information about allele frequencies, can be utilized to create effective methods of estimating the rate at which population members coalesce over time, and in doing so create a powerful tool for measuring genetic diversity in branching populations. Estimates of this rate can be made under two different scenarios - with knowledge of the population's generation history, and in situations where the population's generation history is unknown. When the population's generation history is known, we can precisely calculate the rate at which population members coalesce over time by taking the inverse of a specific mathematical expression which represents how often individuals coalesce relative to the population's generation size. When the population's generation history is unknown, we develop a method of estimating the rate at this rate by taking the inverse of a specific mathematical expression which represents how often individuals coalesce relative to the population's size at the time they first appear in the population. Extending previous research, our analysis explores the impact of novel investment strategies introduced at different times on existing agent-based portfolio management methods. Our findings indicate that the introduction of new strategies generates significant short-term profits, prompting a shift towards novel tactics. However, once agents adapt, their performance matches that of the existing strategies. The duration between the introduction of new strategies and their integration varies depending on several factors, including the type of adaptation and the size of short-term gains. The research also reveals that certain types of novel strategies are more popular than others, with the most widely adopted generating shorter-term profits. On one hand, waiting for others to adopt new methods may result in missed short-term gains. On the other hand, early adoption may lead to significant short-term losses. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the most profitable approach is one that combines continuous innovation and regular updating of existing methods. Electrostatic gating limits the flow of electrons in integrated circuits. Another potential means of information transport, magnons derived from spin waves in magnetic materials, is typically resistant to such gating. However, we have found that by using a superconductor with a strong spin-orbit interaction, we can achieve significant amplification of the magnon transmission through a proximity-induced effect. This technique offers a new means of controlling magnons and developing novel data storage and processing technologies. It also presents an unusual opportunity to experimentally observe the Beth-Hamilton anomaly, a phenomenon that occurs when magnons within a material couple with quasiparticles in a nearby superconductor, giving rise to counter-intuitive transmission patterns. Our method for gating magnons may be incorporated into existing systems and used to develop cutting-edge technologies in magnonics. Furthermore, we have explored an old idea for controlling magnons through a two-layer structure comprising a ferromagnet on top of a superconductor. Although this setup fails to significantly gate magnons, it does exhibit an interesting connection to the Beth-Hamilton anomaly and may have a role in developing novel devices that combine electrically induced magnon gating with generation and detection mechanisms. To facilitate experimental observation of the latter setup, we have provided an detailed analysis of the conditions necessary for the gapping of magnons in this structure. These conditions could be met by using materials with specific material parameters, such as nickel ferrite used in the first example, or those possessing high gapping fields, such as YInMn. Ultimately, we have presented two unusual means of controlling magnons - one of which is based on using superconductors with strong spin-orbit interactions, and another one, a long-established concept, which might rely on high gapping fields or unique magnetic materials. These approaches could be combined to develop innovative technologies based on magnonics. The widespread use of machine learning in audio classification has led to significant challenges in handling diverse datasets, limited labelling, and model deployment complexities. Recently, distributed learning has been explored as a viable solution to tackle large-scale audio classification issues, but it still presents two major hurdles: ensuring model generalization across different data distributions in a distributed setting, and effectively learning new classes not encountered during training. To address these challenges, a new approach is proposed that utilizes a unified model for multi-task learning, a theoretical understanding of model generalization through maximum entropy regularization, and a novel two-stage learning method via conferencing and adaptive averaging. This approach is successfully tested on two open-access tasks, including zero-shot learning of novel acoustic events and improvement of existing classes in music instrument classification, demonstrating up to 13% improvement in accuracy over conventional methods. The development of a distributed deep learning framework for open-source use is also outlined to facilitate future research and applications. Creating high-dimensional entangled quantum systems, specifically Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states, has become more achievable with the advancement in experimental technology. This has shifted focus from detecting entanglement to understanding its characteristics, particularly its multidimensional nature. We aim to address this through a proposed method for quantitatively analyzing correlations within high-dimensional entangled states, much like in the standard logarithmic negativity measure. This approach involves using a logarithm of the hyperbolic number and derived logarithmic hyperbolic entanglement of the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state. As this method applies to any high-dimensional entangled state, it is expected to be a valuable resource for scientific research, facilitating a deeper understanding of quantum systems and experiments. We will demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to two entropy-based methods for generating high-dimensional Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states, specifically the recursive projection method and the dual boson sampling approach. These implementations highlight the versatility of the proposed concept, encompassing various types of high-dimensional entangled states, including those that may exhibit non-classical properties such as hyperentanglement and high-dimensional entanglement of multiple particles. The proposed framework will enable researchers to compare and characterize different high-dimensional entangled states using a standardized quantitative metric. This, in turn, is expected to contribute to the advancement of high-dimensional quantum technology and contribute to the evaluation of future experiments. Finally, we will outline the feasible experimental procedures for creating high-dimensional Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states using integrated boson sampling systems and propose future developments to enhance its effectiveness. These include utilizing broadband sources, expanding to entanglement of multiple particles, and employing true dual racah structures within high-dimensional quantum systems. The incorporation of these advanced ideas will significantly expand the logarithmic hyperbolic entanglement of the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilberg state, making it potentially applicable to the optimization of future high-dimensional quantum systems. To achieve this, one can leverage the duality between the recursive projection method and true dual racah structures, notably in the context of multiple particle entanglement. This connection, rooted in hyperbolic geometry, offers a profound understanding of high-dimensional quantum systems and may provide the key to unlocking further advancements in high-dimensional quantum entanglement. This could potentially involve true dual racah structures that may enable researchers to access previously unattainable levels of high-dimensional entanglement, notably without relying on logarithm of the hyperbolic number methods. We will examine this possibility in more detail

Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology has gained attention for improving the performance of wireless systems, particularly in areas with intense signal blocking. However, the efficient operation of an IRS system relies on the precise calculation of the IRS channel, user channel, and IRS positioning. Given the complexity and high computational demands of these requirements in large-scale systems, an optimized approach is needed to facilitate real-world implementation. This paper presents a novel method for simultaneously estimating IRS and user channel and positioning parameters in single-carrier systems, using an iterative least-squares algorithm and minimum entropy decoding. The results show that this approach can significantly reduce computational complexity while achieving nearly optimal performance. The complexity of this method scales linearly with system size, making it more efficient than other methods that have higher order complexity. The study also provides a deep learning-based solution for estimating IRS and user channel and positioning parameters, using a CNN model that achieves comparable performance to the iterative method. A key finding of the study is that CNN models can be trained offline and then applied online, eliminating the need for iterative processing in real-time transmission. The study conducts a thorough analysis of these solutions and finds that the iterative method and CNN models can be combined to achieve nearly optimal performance in real-world systems. The results show that this combination can achieve nearly the same performance as exhaustive search while reducing computational complexity. The study also provides a comparison of different solutions and shows that the iterative method and CNN models can be scaled to handle large-scale systems, achieving similar performance to exhaustive search. The results further show that CNN models can be used in conjunction with iterative methods to achieve nearly the same performance as exhaustive search while reducing computational complexity. The study also observes that iterative methods can be used to accelerate the convergence of CNN models, and proposes a scaling technique for CNN models based on iterative methods. The results show that this proposed technique can achieve nearly the same performance as exhaustive search while reducing computational complexity. The study also evaluates the performance of these solutions under different scenarios and finds that the iterative method and CNN models can be combined to achieve nearly optimal performance in these scenarios. The results show that the performance of these solutions deteriorates as the system size increases, but the iterative method remains a better choice due to its lower computational complexity. The study also assesses the numerical performance of these solutions and finds that the iterative method and CNN models can be combined to achieve nearly optimal performance in these assessments. This study analyzes patterns among COVID-19 news coverage, infection rates, and fatality numbers across 393 U.S. metropolitan regions, leveraging data from two sources: a COVID-related news dataset spanning January 2020 to April 2021, and the COVID spread data from The New York Times and CDC. Our investigation focuses on how news coverage in each region compares to national trends, and whether there's a correlation between local COVID coverage and infection/death rates. To control for regional variations in population, demographics, and income, we utilized a set of socioeconomic indicators. Our results show that areas with higher COVID news coverage experienced decreased infection rates and mortality rates relative to low news coverage areas. Moreover, there's a statistically significant link between local COVID news coverage and national death rates. Additionally, our investigation reveals that areas served by newspapers that maintained their employment and publishing stability during the crisis tended to receive more COVID-related coverage, and, as a result, experienced lower infection and death rates. Our findings imply that robust local news media plays a critical role in combating the pandemic. Our study offers empirical evidence that supports the continuum theory, and provides quantitative data to inform the understanding of the link between news coverage and pandemic progression. Our analysis also highlights the significance of local news media in informing the public about the pandemic, and emphasizes the need for a well-functioning media ecosystem to mitigate the pandemic's adverse effects. Our research may contribute to the development of theories that explain how news coverage affects COVID-related metrics, and sheds light on the potential consequences of the media decline observed in recent years. Our data can serve as a reference for researchers who conduct studies on the spatiotemporal patterns of COVID news coverage and the associated infection and death rates across different metropolitan regions. Our work may also be utilized by policymakers and public health officials to make informed decisions based on an in-depth analysis of COVID-related news and the region-specific infection and death trends. Our study involves two distinct datasets: news coverage and COVID spread. Our initial findings reveal that areas experiencing earlier COVID-related news coverage tended to experience higher infection and death rates. We hypothesize that this outcome may result from a self-reinforcing cycle in which areas affected by the pandemic first receive negative news, which then fuels public fear, exacerbating the pandemic's spread. Our analysis also shows that regions with more robust local news media coverage experienced lower infection and death rates, and highlights the significance of local media in combating the pandemic. We develop a novel theoretical framework to examine how traditional recurrent neural networks and their transformer counterparts learn to count in sequence. Our approach utilizes a random memory matrix that simulates the internal workings of these networks. Our results indicate that the diagonalization of the random memory matrix plays a crucial role in accurate counting, and that the presence of a dominant eigenvalue significantly impacts this process. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the internal state vectors following the diagonalization can be arranged in a hierarchical order, which in turn enables sequential counting without the need for explicit weight updates. Our findings are substantiated through extensive experiments involving both synthetic and real datasets, and our analysis offers insights on the characteristics of the memory matrix that facilitate successful counting. Our empirical observations suggest that networks with specific memory properties are more likely to exhibit robust counting capabilities even in the presence of adversarial attacks. Our research contributes to the understanding of the underlying mechanics of modern neural networks and may lead to the development of enhanced memory designs to boost counting performance. The source code for this research is available at https://github.com/jbmeier/counter-rnn. The dataset used in this research can be accessed through https://doi.org/10.13140/3.0.89219/90664. The empirical data collected during this research, in addition to the analysis, can be found at https://doi.org/10.13140/3.0.89219/90664.

An additional option, Cuckoo Filters, has also been suggested, but it too has its drawbacks. Both of these solutions create problems of false positives and, in the case of Cuckoo Filters, additional issues of data overwriting. To address these concerns, a new solution, Xor Filters, has been developed. By using only insertion operations, Xor Filters can achieve similar levels of efficiency and accuracy as Bloom Filters with Chaining, or in some cases, even surpass them. Additionally, Xor Filters can be used to develop approximations of limited-space databases, accurately filtering out entries that contain specific modified elements. Further development of Xor Filters has led to the creation of Xor Filters Extended, a variant that can efficiently remove entire prefixes from keys. This has ultimately resulted in the creation of Bisect Filters, a solution that combines the efficiency of Cuckoo Filters with the accuracy of Bloom Filters, all while achieving compact results similar to those of Bloom Filters with Chaining. This approach avoids issues typically encountered with realistic image feedback by utilizing simplified proxy gradients within simulated environments. In real-world scenarios, proxy gradients are eliminated through the use of actual gradient information, thereby refining the agent's path selections. Our results demonstrate improved performance in exactly one out of two out-of-the-box evaluations. Deepfake creation and detection continue to evolve, with research demonstrating significant progress in both areas. Despite advances, detecting deepfakes remains a difficult task, particularly when encountered for the first time or in scenarios where visual cues are limited. There is a pressing need for more sophisticated deepfake detection techniques that can accurately identify both visually and semantically manipulated content. To address this challenge, this study presents an innovative approach to deepfake detection, leveraging a unique training method and a cutting-edge, unconstrained media dataset for evaluation. The method has been created in conjunction with an innovative method for generating highly realistic deepfake content that can pass undetected even when analyzed by state-of-the-art deepfake detection models. The method does not rely on any additional labeling and can operate effectively in low-resolution, low-quality, and compressed video environments. The generated content includes a range of novel combinations of AF and BF attacks, making it an invaluable resource for enhancing deepfake detection models. The method has also enabled the development of a highly accurate deepfake detection model, achieving a remarkable mAP of 0.2405 on the UFBD4K dataset. The creation and detection methods will be publicly available upon publication, facilitating further development and advancement in this critical area for research. The accompanying code and dataset can be found at https://github.com/AK-99/UnconstrainedDeepfakes. The dataset will also be released through CVF upon publication. The method has been successfully demonstrated on HF and BF attacks, with performance enhanced by an average of 10% compared to existing deepfake detection models. The development of this approach will contribute to further research in this area, enabling more accurate deepfake detection and facilitating ongoing advancement in deepfake creation and detection. The method has been thoroughly evaluated and shown to perform effectively under a range of different metrics, with results presented here. The method does not rely on pre-trained models, instead utilizing self-supervised learning to develop the method, with training and testing conducted on the UFBD4K dataset. The method does not utilize any additional information or support, instead relying solely on the deepfake content for training and evaluation. The method does not depend on state-of-the-art deepfake creation models, instead using a standard AF model for comparison, with results demonstrating the method's performance against a range of different deepfake creation techniques. The method does not depend on AF content alone, instead using a range of different deepfake creation methods, including BF attacks, to develop the method, with results demonstrating the method's performance against novel content.

The presence of a subsurface liquid water ocean in a exoplanet can be inferred through transit spectroscopy by analyzing the absorption of metals in the visible light spectrum. This method relies on the dissolution of these metals in an ocean, which is only possible if the ocean is connected to the planet's degassing process. Planets with this characteristic transit signatures typically have smaller or comparable hide-and-seek ratios when compared to Earth. In contrast, planets with these characteristic transit signatures that have a larger hide-and-seek ratio than Earth are likely composed of a small liquid water ocean encapsulated in a rocky layer, which is connected to the degassing process. This is a more common phenomenon among 0.1 to 0.3 Jupiter-mass planets that are capable of supporting life. Our research shows that smaller or comparable hide-and-seek ratios are typical among the planets in this category, and we have identified three planets that are particularly notable - K2-18 b, PH2- b, and GJ 139 b - which have the distinct transit signatures and are also small enough to be candidates for supporting life. Our research also demonstrates that more advanced telescopes will be able to detect larger and more massive objects such as super-Earths and mini-Neptunes with the distinct transit signatures, which could further expand our knowledge of the distinct transit signatures. Finally, our research shows that future telescopes will be able to detect thousands of planets with the distinct transit signatures, which could further our understanding of the distinct transit signatures. Additionally, sub-Jupiter-mass planets with the distinct transit signatures are composed of a small liquid water ocean encapsulated in a rocky layer that is connected to the degassing process. Our research shows that future telescopes will be able to detect thousands of planets with the distinct transit signatures. This extensive array of detectable planets with the distinct transit signatures is a key result that indicates the vast possibilities for discovering more planets with the distinct transit signatures. These discoveries will contribute to our understanding of how the distinct transit signatures are formed and maintain their state. This knowledge will also help us find other indicators of subsurface liquid water oceans that are disconnected from the degassing process, which could further our search for life in the universe. We investigate the learning capabilities of spiking neural networks using the backpropagation through time algorithm, specifically adapting it for use with continuous-time activation functions. Our study reveals that using a continuous activation function leads to ill-conditioned weight updates, resulting in extremely large weight changes required to implement learning. To resolve this, we develop a biologically plausible spike-rate dependent learning rule from the original algorithm. Our results indicate that a certain level of spike noise must be tolerated to enable learning, and we experimentally verify that our proposed learning rule enables SNNs to learn complex temporal patterns in a self-supervised manner, significantly outperforming the original algorithm in both training efficiency and stability. Notably, our learning method excels in learning long-term sequences compared to alternative methods, such as actor-critic algorithms, as exemplified by our experiments involving learning a binary piano sequence. Our study demonstrates the development of a biologically feasible spiking neural network capable of learning complex temporal patterns in sequential data, thereby enabling self-supervised learning of long-term sequences. Although this capability comes with the caveat of requiring spike noise during training, our results indicate that this level of spike noise is within the range observed in natural neural activity. Therefore, our study suggests a potential pathway to enable spontaneous learning in artificial neural systems modeled after biological brains. System adaptation or improved performance using the minimum amount of relevant information is the primary goal, guided by principles of optimality. This work introduces a general framework for identifying and addressing shifts in complex systems that operate under conditions of partial observability. We develop an innovative solution based on the concept of an Adaptive Partially-Observed Change Detection (APCDD) model, utilizing an advanced nonlinear observer that integrates an optimal predictive model and a novel action of adaptive isolation. Through theoretical analysis, we prove that the APCDD model offers predictive performance that is equivalent to performance achieved with complete information, under specific conditions that rely on system parameters and a measuring sensor. As a result, the APCDD model is capable of adapting to changes in the system and its observer, as well as detecting and separating causes of disruption. These advancements are demonstrated through simulation studies that highlight the ability of the APCDD model to operate effectively in a range of uncertain environments. Our method, tailored for analyzing present-day dwarf galaxies, employs a Bayesian analysis with priors derived from similar galaxies and considers observations of multiple stars within a galaxy. Although our model assumes all stars in a dwarf galaxy formed from the same material, it does take into account contributions from globular clusters and pre-enriched gas from earlier star formations. Given a profinite group G, an action of G on a space X yields a spectrum of homotopy groups called the homotopy action spectrum of G, denoted AXG. This spectrum can be calculated using the continuous homotopy theory of prospaces and the Galois group of G, also known as the profinite group G. Defining AXG in this way allows a homotopy theory of profinite groups to be established, enabling comparisons between group homotopy theory and the algebraic structure of groups. Specifically, the Grothendieck profinite fundamental group of a space X, denoted π_1^pro(X), can be regarded as the homotopy group π_0(AXX)_{gal}, resulting in π_1^pro(X) being a profinite group with the Galois action. Moreover, the functorial properties of π_1^pro(X) can be determined, and it has been found that certain non-trivial profinite groups can serve as the profinite fundamental group of a space X. Additionally, the fact that π_1^pro(X) is isomorphic to the inverse limit of all free pro-G sets can be established, and it has been concluded that π_1^pro(X) is always profinite when X is a compactly generated topological space. A modified spectrum, called AXG^ab, can be defined for any group G acting on a space X, and it has been found that π_1^pro(X) can also be regarded as the Galois group of the abelian homotopy action spectrum of G acting on X, denoted (AXG^ab(X))_{gal}, resulting in further connections between homotopy theory and group theory. Various examples and applications have been computed to demonstrate how the homotopy action spectrum of a profinite group G can be calculated through Galois groups, and it has been found that computing π_1^pro(X) can be reduced to computing the Galois group of the homotopy action spectrum of the fundamental group of a space X acting on a pro-G set. A comparison between the profinite fundamental group of a space X, denoted π_1^pro(X), and the Galois group of the homotopy action spectrum of its fundamental group G acting on a pro-G set, denoted (π_1(G) \backslash X)_{gal}, has been established, and it has been concluded that these two groups are always isomorphic

Automatically extracting key information from visually complex documents, such as invoices, has become a major challenge in computer vision. Most previous approaches not only require a substantial amount of labeled data but also rely on a specific domain, limiting their adaptability to other document types. To address the cost associated with labeling, we propose an innovative two-stage pipeline incorporating a universal text extraction task and a downstream classification step for identifying the specific document type. This approach reduces the need for labeled data while achieving high extraction accuracy, outperforming existing methods in our experiments. Additionally, our framework allows for the extraction of relevant information from diverse documents, surpassing previous models in terms of both accuracy and domain flexibility. For example, when given an X-ray image, we can accurately identify the type of document without the need for labels, then extract text from it, and finally apply this approach to invoices, extracting important information without any additional training. Our proposed method not only reduces the expenses associated with labeling but also offers greater flexibility in handling different document types.
