The EuS/InAs interface has gained significance due to its potential to introduce magnetic properties in a semiconductor material crucial for the development of quantum devices. Using ab-initio calculations, the electronic structure of the interface was investigated across various bonding arrangements between sulfur and indium atoms. It was found that the bonding configuration significantly affects the interface states near the Fermi level, influencing the charge carrier concentration and magnetic properties. In a configuration that allows for covalent bonding between sulfur and indium, InAs tends to form a p-type dopant, whereas in a configuration that allows for ionic bonding, InAs becomes n-type. The study demonstrates that controlling the bonding configuration at the interface is essential to achieving the desired magnetic properties in the material. Additionally, the calculated energy levels are consistent with experimental findings. Based on these results, the electronic structure of the interface can be modified to introduce suitable dopants and enhance the magnetic properties of the system. Further investigation into the bonding configuration's impact on the magnetic properties and interface states is recommended. Calculations show that adjusting the position of sulfur and indium atoms significantly affects the magnetic moment and energy levels at the interface, leading to varying results. In one arrangement where sulfur is directly beneath indium, the magnetic moment is highest at the interface, whereas in another arrangement where sulfur is offset from indium, the magnetic moment is significantly reduced. Similarly, the energy levels at the interface also vary depending on the bonding configuration, with some arrangements leading to the formation of bond and anti-bond states. In conclusion, the bonding configuration has a profound impact on the magnetic properties and electronic structure of the EuS/InAs interface, making it crucial to consider these effects in future research into the magnetic properties of the system. Based on these results, it is possible that the bonding configuration could be utilized to control the magnetic properties of the system. Lastly, the mean squared displacement of atoms at the interface was calculated to quantify the dynamic interaction between sulfur and indium atoms, with results showing that the bonding configuration significantly affects the movement of atoms. In one arrangement where sulfur is directly beneath indium, the mean squared displacement is highest at the interface, whereas in another arrangement where sulfur is offset from indium, the mean squared displacement is significantly lower. Similarly, the mean squared displacement also varies depending on the position of sulfur and indium atoms further away from the interface. As a result, the electronic structure and magnetic properties of the system change significantly. Lastly, it is possible that dynamic phase transitions occur in the EuS/InAs

The convergence of deep learning models heavily depends on hyperparameters such as pruning rates during training. Unlike common methods that only consider test accuracy after pruning, we introduce ClickTrain, a highly efficient and accurate end-to-end training framework. ClickTrain allows for the continuous adjustment of weights during forward propagation, thereby enabling the optimization of dependent neurons within a dependency graph. By doing so, we achieve a significant reduction in the number of hyperparameters required, thanks to the decoupling of pruning rates among neurons in the same dependency group. As a result, the model's architecture is preserved, and inference speed is significantly boosted, particularly when multiple groups are pruned at once. ClickTrain outperforms state-of-the-art methods in accuracy and pruning efficiency, and effectively addresses challenges like non-differentiability in previous approaches, and effectively handles cases of non-uniform dependency graphs. Additionally, we propose an innovative group retraining scheme that accelerates the adaptation of pruned groups to their new boundary weights. Importantly, we demonstrate that our model can effectively mitigate the degradation often associated with pruning, and validate the effectiveness of our approach on a variety of image classification tasks, achieving impressive results superior to those achieved by the top pruning methods in both accuracy and pruning efficiency. The code for this work is available at https://github.com/yoasy/ClickTrain. Keywords: End-to-End Pruning, Deep Learning, Hyperparameter Optimization, Fast Training, High Accuracy, Fine-Grained Pruning, Architecture-Preserving Pruning.

Our investigation focuses on the structure of modal formulas in relation to their distributivity properties, and establishes a hierarchy based on the number of occurrences of modal operators. Our key finding shows that the compositionally defined modal calculus is equivalent to the compositional $\mathcal{M}$-calculus, and we demonstrate that various higher-order logic systems are at least as expressive as this $\mathcal{M}$-calculus. The 2015 detection of gravitational waves by the LIGO Virgina detection system marks a significant breakthrough. Future observations involving the collision of neutron star-black hole binaries are anticipated to yield numerous detections, making automated analysis essential to analyze all signals efficiently. We present a deep learning approach utilizing a convolutional neural network to classify binary black hole merger signals, specifically those involving a neutron star and a black hole. This study employs realistic simulated annealed likelihood events with signal-to-noise ratios greater than eight, generated by the numerical relativity code SIREN. By leveraging the real-space strain data format provided by the LIGO Open Data Archive, we overcome limitations in deep learning frameworks. Our network architecture comprising seven hidden layers successfully identifies various characteristics of neutron star-black hole binaries, and we demonstrate that it can efficiently classify signals using significantly less data compared to previous analyses. We conclude that this approach holds significant promise for analyzing future observations, and we make our code available for others to build upon. We develop a primal-dual method to find optimal policies in Markov decision processes with limited capacities. As a special case, this approach yields efficient algorithms for solving the multi-armed bandit problem with rewards and arm availability constraints. Our method can be viewed as an extension of the primal-dual technique used in linear programming to solve the multi-armed bandit problem. It involves simulating the Markov process in the epigraph of the value function and utilizing the observed sequences to approximate this function. In each iteration, a linear programming is solved to determine the optimal policy. We prove that this approach converges to the optimal policy as the time horizon increases. Furthermore, we propose a variant of our method that bypasses solving linear programming in each iteration, aiming to achieve similar performance as the time horizon tends to infinity. This approach leverages the geometric increase in visit frequencies to solve the linear programming, thus enabling its application to problems with large states and actions. In our experimental evaluations, we demonstrate that this variant yields satisfactory results, often closely matching the performance of the primal-dual method with linear programming. Our study also confirms that the choice of visit frequencies in nonlinear programming has a significant impact on the algorithm's performance, encouraging further research on frequency selection schemes. Lastly, we conjecture that our approach, when combined with any suitable frequency selection scheme, is optimal among all primal-dual methods for solving constrained multi-armed bandit problems. We substantiate this optimality claim by proving it for a significant subclass of these problems, encompassing those with reward-dependent capacities and "up-down" feasibility constraints. We test our method on a variety of real-world applications, showing that it outperforms existing algorithms and often achieves close-to-optimal performance, revealed through computational optimality proofs obtained for some problems in this subclass. In particular, our approach yields optimal policies for constrained multi-armed bandit problems with up-down feasibility, bandit problems with knapsacks, and Thompson Sampling-based choices, thereby demonstrating its general applicability to a wide range of Thompson Sampling-based policies. We propose two variants of our method to solve the general case of bandit problems with limited capacities, presenting theoretical performance guarantees for these algorithms. In our experiments, we observe that these algorithms perform exceptionally well, achieving near-optimal results, as evidenced by computational optimality proofs obtained for a subset of the tested problems. This research proposes a novel approach to recognize handwritten mathematical equations using a pre-trained Transformer model, specifically T5. In contrast to standard hand-written text recognition (HTR), which focuses on linguistic readability, the key goal of Mathematical Handwritten Text Recognition (MHTR) is to accurately capture the intended mathematical expression. Our contribution lies in adapting pre-trained Language Models, like T5, for MHTR, which has been largely underexplored previously. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach with an offline dataset, MathematicalTIMIT, an extension of the TIMIT speech recognition dataset that includes handwritten mathematical equations. Our findings show that our method surpasses the current state-of-the-art mathematical recognition techniques, benchmarked on the MathematicalTIMIT dataset. Additionally, we have released the dataset and the corresponding code to facilitate future research on MHTR. Although our method achieves exceptional results, we observed that the offline approach, which transfers a pre-trained model to a T5-like architecture, faces challenges with geometric non-linear modules, ultimately affecting its performance. Our research aims to stimulate further investigation into employing online MHTR, which is believed to yield better results, and to promote the development of a more robust, real-time MHTR model. Online visual representations of the proposed method, including demos, are available at https://mhir.org/mathematical-hir-demos/. Furthermore, the associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/mhir-tools/mhir-code. Additionally, the dataset can be downloaded from the link https://mhir.org/mathematical-hir-dataset/. We look forward to engaging with the research community on enhancing the MHTR paradigm. Please refer to the full paper for more detailed information. The full paper can be accessed at https://research.google.com/pub/pub48966.html. This study presents a novel approach to accelerate actor-critic learning using the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) technique, leading to faster convergence and improved policy performance. In traditional Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, the log-posterior in Hamiltonian Dynamics is exploited by introducing a Hamiltonian Function. This study transfers the concept to actor-critic methods, incorporating the Hamiltonian Function into the actor-critic Hamiltonian Dynamics, resulting in a more efficient algorithm. The benefits of this method are evaluated in various robotics and control tests, demonstrating faster convergence and higher cumulative rewards compared to standard actor-critic methods. The authors also investigate the benefits of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo in deep reinforcement learning experiments, comparing its performance to both Hamiltonian-free actor-critic methods and prior efficiency enhancements, such as path-length regularization. The Twin Prime Hypthesis, a longstanding conjecture, asserts that there are an infinite number of prime pairs differing by 2. Research in this field is prolific, with numerous proofs provided, although most require advanced mathematical knowledge. This paper presents a straightforward, introductory proof of the Twin Prime Hypthesis, leveraging basic principles of arithmetic to illustrate the concept. The proof relies on the Distinct Products Hypothesis, a lesser-known conjecture stating that there are an infinite number of positive integers less than sqrt(2), which can be expressed as the product of two distinct prime numbers. By applying a simple, yet effective approach, we demonstrate that the Twin Prime Hypotheses imply the Distinct Products Hypothesis, which in turn has a logical correlation with the Polya's Hypothesis. Notably, our proof avoids intricate mathematical notions, making it accessible to a broader audience. The work in this paper is an adaptation of the authors' previously published research found in the article titled "An Elementary Proof of the Twin Prime Hypothesis" (Indigo Mathematica, volume 1, issue 1). A comprehensive exploration of the connections between prime numbers is presented in this publication. Additionally, the editors of Indigo Mathematica provided an insightful analysis, revising the authors' work, which led to the development of this revised proof. The authors would like to express their gratitude to the editors of Indigo Mathematica for their scholarly feedback and guidance. The authors' work on this proof was facilitated through financial support from the Math Scholarship program. The program provided financial assistance to undergraduate students at Massachusetts Institute of Technology to explore mathematical concepts. The authors' work on this proof is an example of the program's aim to foster an environment where next-generation mathematicians can engage in mathematical research and develop their skills. This repository includes a tutorial that demonstrates how to configure and use our system, utilizing a ROS2 simulation environment and JSK Soccer Robot simulator. Our system comprises two key components: a Layered Navigation Manager and a Sonar Blend Module. The Layered Navigation Manager acts as a wrapper for existing ROS2 navigation packages, while the Sonar Blend Module fuses sonar data to provide a forward-facing obstacle detection function. This system is designed to be lightweight and adaptable, making it easily compatible with various robot configurations. We have successfully tested our system using a JSK Soccer Robot with four sonars, and have made the relevant Launch and Python files available in the repository for user convenience. Additionally, we have developed a diagnostic tool that displays a heatmap of the robot's surroundings, using a Sonar Heatmap Display Module that utilizes the Nav2 global planner's heatmap feature. The goal of the Toxic Comment Classification challenge is to utilize machine learning to recognize toxic comments on online platforms, with the specific objective of detecting aggressive content. Our team's solution, UM-IU@LING, leveraged BERT-based models and traditional machine learning algorithms to predict toxic comments. Specifically, we employed BERT-based models in both classification and regression formats, as required by the task guidelines, in addition to utilizing Support Vector Machines for the latter. Our strategy involved training a binary classifier for each class within the data, and then using a weighted voting system to determine the predicted label with the highest priority. Our approach leversaged traditional machine learning algorithms, including SVMs, to improve the model's performance. Our test submissions were based on the performance of the best-performing models obtained through 10-fold cross-validation. Our team achieved a 0.9446 F1 score using the BERT-based model, which outperformed the top-performing system in the competition, and earned second place overall in the aggressive label category. The corresponding code can be found on our umiuading GitHub repository.

Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a challenging task, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data and limited language knowledge (dictionaries and language models). While data annotation is expensive, language knowledge can be utilized to generate synthetic data, but existing approaches often fail to accurately mimic real-world labels, leading to inadequate results. A novel approach is proposed to tackle this problem, leveraging the attributes of Plastering and Pasting to complement existing data augmentation methods, addressing the need for single-image supervision in unsupervised HTR tasks. Experimental findings on the datasets, liberty mutual dataset and historical dataset from the National Library of Australia, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. It outperforms baseline approaches, particularly on the liberty mutual dataset, where its performance closely resembles that of a model with access to ground truth during training. Furthermore, it shows a significant improvement in characters, words and line recognition compared to the baseline model, with results similar to that of a model with access to ground truth on the national library of Australia dataset. While showing promising results on the liberty mutual dataset, its application on the national library of Australia dataset reveals room for improvement, especially when compared to a model with access to ground truth, indicating that the proposed method alone may not be enough to overcome deep-set biases in the dataset. Thus, a potential future direction is to investigate how the proposed method can be utilized in conjunction with other approaches to further enhance its performance. The code for this project is maintained on a GitHub repository. The liberty mutual dataset used in this research consists of a collection of forms containing various handwriting styles, which can be accessed via the repository. The national library of Australia dataset is also maintained by the repository, where users can find a wide range of historical documents and dictionaries, all annotated in the dictionary format required for this research. The proposed method is implemented using PyTorch, a popular deep learning framework. We have established a combined calculation method linking ab initio Monte Carlo and generative models for heavy nuclei. Starting from a set of calculated nuclear potentials, we generate a large database of possible nuclear configurations through the Monte Carlo method. A neural network, trained on this database, is then used to predict the relative energies of nuclei based on their respective configurations. By constraining the neural network to match observed data across a chain of nuclei, our method successfully predicts the masses of nuclei without relying on fitted nuclear potentials. This method also enables the direct calculation of energy surfaces in nuclei. Our study includes examples of applications for nuclei along the Pb chain with 2 ≤ Z ≤ 80. This method can be extended to study other chains of nuclei. Additionally, we have found that the predictions for Pb isotopes can be accurately modeled using a simple piecewise linear function, indicating that the correlations between nuclear configuration and nuclear structure are not complex. In various real-world applications, probabilistic models are employed to analyze and decision-making processes. Probabilistic circuits serve as a powerful tool for generating comprehensive probabilistic distributions; yet, efficiently ensuring coverage and representativeness, given constraints such as time or data available, remains a significant issue. Credal Bayesian frameworks offer a potential solution, allowing them to incorporate uncertainty within the modeling process itself. These frameworks treat constraints as part of the uncertainty, effectively considering all potential constraints that could be imposed. However, the frameworks face a critical challenge: ensuring model reliability, given that overly expansive sets of possible constraints can result in empty sets of valid models. Our research addresses this reliability issue by first defining a new concept - generalized constraint relaxation number (GCRR) - to quantify the impact of relaxing constraints in probabilistic circuits. GCRR measures the maximum number of removed constraints within which no invalid circuits are introduced. Our experiments demonstrate that the GCRR value significantly influences the effectiveness of Credal Bayesian frameworks, making it a crucial factor to consider in probabilistic model computation. Additionally, we introduce a novel approach - constraint relaxation partitioning - aimed at enhancing the strength of reliance guarantees within these frameworks, with our method capable of achieving optimal results in a significant proportion of the tested instances. Key parameters affecting its efficiency have also been identified and analyzed. Furthermore, we propose an algorithm for constructing the best possible reliance guarantee, leveraging our analysis to predict its performance. While this algorithm may not always be optimal, our predictions indicate that it will produce very close results to the best possible outcome in the vast majority of cases. Finally, we introduce a solution for handling an infinite number of credible Bayesian frameworks, along with associated computational complexity estimates. This solution draws from its probabilistic circuit roots and employs a novel approach to achieve efficiency. The reliability guarantees derived can be utilized to solve the issue at reduced computational complexity. Our study presents a comprehensive survey of reliability guarantees in Credal Bayesian frameworks, along with key concepts, challenges, approaches, and complexity estimates. The survey also includes several open issues, alongside our proposed solutions. Additionally, a dataset containing our algorithm's performance predictions is also provided, enabling further comparison with other possible solutions. non-zero phase. The oscillations arise due to the interplay between the 
condensate's internal phase and the oscillations of its macroscopic 
wavefunction. Our study focuses on two key scenarios: one with a weakly 
coupled condensate and another with a strongly coupled condensate. In the 
former case, the oscillations are largely confined to a narrow region, 
while in the latter situation, the oscillations spread over a broader 
area, driven by the formation of density waves. We also look into how 
internal phase fluctuations impact Bloch oscillations in both scenarios.

condensate, which may lead to the emergence of periodic density waves 
traversing the entire condensate. This study offers a comprehensive 
understanding of Bloch oscillations in superfluids, encompassing various 
excitation types. The examination of Bloch oscillations in superfluids 
opens up the possibility of exploring topological effects in quantum gases, 
potentially facilitating the realization of topological quantum technologies.

By comparing the method's results to simulations using a smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) model with varying magnetic strengths, we found agreement on the overall mass anisotropy up to a specific point but discovered that the CMZ's mass configuration might be influenced more significantly by its dynamical structure and complexity than previously thought. This implies that future studies focusing on the CMZ's mass distribution should take into account its unique morphology to accurately depict its structure. This study also paves the way for similar analyses of other star-forming regions using similar 2D correlation function techniques. Finally, this research facilitates a more in-depth exploration of the CMZ's behavior and its response to various external forces and magnetic fields, shedding light on the region's potential future evolution. This research addresses the challenge of efficient feature extraction in machine learning for identifying IoT devices based on their unique characteristics. Operating IoT devices generates time-series data features at a high rate, making real-time extraction crucial for accurate identification. Despite this, current solutions often involve offline feature selection processes that don't account for the devices' power constraints or the devices' self-discovery context. To address these limitations, this research presents a novel online feature extraction approach, called Online FE, designed to operate on IoT devices with limited resources. Unlike traditional methods, Online Fe extracts relevant features while considering the devices' power constraints and is compatible with both binary and multi-class classification tasks. Experimental results show that Online Fe achieves comparable classification accuracy to established algorithms, supporting self-discovery through bi-directional communication, while also being compatible with IoT devices' limited resources. To evaluate this, classification experiments were conducted using real-world datasets, such as IoTTrace and DeviceTrace2, on various IoT devices, including Raspberry Pi and Jetson TX2, with their power consumption considered. Analysis of the experiments demonstrates that Online Fe achieves significant reductions in communication overhead, computation cost, and memory usage, making it a suitable solution for accurate IoT device classification with limited resources. An accordion chart is a graph with a specific structure consisting of a collection of vertex-disjoint cycles in a complete graph. This graph is also known as a quartic circulant graph if the cycles within it have a uniform length. We examine the properties of accordion charts focusing on their Hamiltonicity and isomorphisms with other types of circulant graphs. Our results show that an accordion chart is Hamiltonian if it has certain cycle-free properties or when the sum of its smallest vertex degrees equals the total number of vertices. We also establish a sufficient condition for two accordion charts to be isomorphic based on their cycle structures. Besides these findings, we determine all accordion charts with four distinct vertex degrees that are isomorphic to fourth power circulant graphs. We introduce a method of constructing ViT blocks that incorporates rich information from different image scales, and propose an architecture based on the late fusion of contextual information across different feature layers. Our work presents the Steady Creator, a novel approach that bridges the gap between these models and traditional generative adversarial networks focused on semantics. The latter's performance is inconsistent due to the instability of its training process. To resolve this issue, we integrate text encoding and image decoding into a single unified generator, utilizing the diffusion process to stabilize the learning process. The Steady Creator achieves remarkable results in generative semantic modeling, surpassing previous state-of-the-art performance in the CUB dataset by a significant margin, according to mean intersection over union metric. Our model also showcases superior quality in generated birds, as evident from qualitative evaluation, demonstrating an increase of 2.5 points in visual quality score compared to the best performing model in the evaluation. Conversely, if the latter is true, it would introduce ambiguity to these theories, whose output we have plotted in relation to the invisible decay width. The alternative, that $J/\psi$ decay might involve dark energy rather than neutrinos, has also been explored, yielding a more variable set of predictions. These predictions, along with current experimental data, are displayed in a plot. Notably, this study demonstrates that the $J/\psi$ experiment has the potential to shed light on two significant, persisting puzzles in physics - neutrino coupling and dark energy - through a nuanced analysis of this particular decay. The study uses these plots to illustrate the capabilities of future experiments, such as those being conducted by the BESIV experiment.

We propose specific characteristics for these monopoles, including: they have masses similar to the proton mass; they respond to external magnetic fields but their own magnetic fields are too weak to be measured; they are stably linked to electrons; they have a specific internal structure; and they lose energy quickly. As a result of their unique properties, these monopoles settle at the center of galaxies, where they facilitate the preservation of galactic magnetic fields through interaction with electrons that accompany them. The strength of these magnetic fields, as well as the frequency at which they appear, can be quantified using specific equations. We also provide specific criteria for identifying these magnetic monopoles, both at the galactic and cosmic scales. Finally, we predict that detecting these magnetic monopoles will allow us to confirm existing theories on their behavior, while also providing new insights into their behavior at very weak magnetic field strengths. Predicting temporal and spatial variations in climate variables is crucial for multiple applications, including agricultural planning and management. In this work, we introduce a novel deep learning architecture for climate prediction, specifically designed for use in early warning and forecasting systems. Our approach combines the strengths of recurrent neural networks and attention-based models, using a shared transformer network to process multiple climate variables over a fixed spatial and temporal window. To improve modeling accuracy, we propose the use of a shifted window cross-attention mechanism, allowing our system to capture complex interactions between variables at different spatial and temporal scales. Our method is lightweight, easy to use, and efficient, with minimal computational requirements. In our experiments, we evaluate the performance of our climate forecasting model on two publicly available datasets, achieving impressive results with the shifted window cross-attention mechanism outperforming existing methods by a significant margin of 5-10%. Our model implementations and dataset downloads are available for free at https://github.com/alvachien/ClimateForecasting. Preliminary models have been deployed on AWS instance \href{https://github.com/alvachien/ClimateForecasting/blob/main/README.md}{here}. Our work follows the guidelines outlined by Kumar et al. for fair comparison in climate forecasting. In addition to presenting our model, we have also made available a wide range of hyperparameters used in our experiments, ensuring transparency and reproducibility. In brain tissue, the regulation of substance distribution is crucial for maintaining proper cellular function, particularly in neurons where excessive accumulation of certain substances can lead to cellular damage. Understanding how neurons control the transport of substances along axons is vital for comprehending central nervous system disorders characterized by demyelination and damage to peripheral nerve cells. To investigate this regulation, we're developing an optimal control approach based on partial differential equations that takes into account the complex geometry of brain tissue and axons. Our goal is to develop a comprehensive model that explains how neurons regulate substance transport, which will serve as a foundational approach for controlling substance flow in neurons. Furthermore, this model has the potential to be adapted to study substance transport in other cell types. In our presentation, we'll introduce a novel PDE-constrained optimization framework that quantifies the importance of certain substances and their roles in regulating substance transport. We'll utilize this framework to investigate the role of fast transport in regulating substance distribution in branching nerve structures, and explore its application to studying tissue regeneration in demyelinated brains. In particular, we'll focus on optimal control strategies that promote regeneration and clearance of toxic substances in peripheral nerve cells affected by cataracts. To solve these complex problems, we'll employ state-of-the-art numerical techniques and utilize a convergence-preserving exponential runge-kutta method to solve the associated PDEs. Our study offers a comprehensive approach to understanding substance transport regulation in neurons, as well as in other cell types, and has the potential to be adapted to investigate various cellular phenomena. Ultimately, this model will facilitate the development of novel therapeutic strategies for controlling substance flow in neurons and promoting nerve cell regeneration. In a phenomenon known as an intrinsic supernova, a white dwarf star collapses into a black hole through a process involving mass accretion or binary mergers. Through the use of computational models, the researcher investigates mass loss and electromagnetic emissions resulting from a 1.15 solar mass white dwarf star descending into a 1.40 solar mass black hole under various conditions of spin and binary proximity. Preliminary findings indicate that significant mass loss occurs at a distance of about two times the radius of the white dwarf from the black hole's point of impact, and that this mass loss accounts for approximately 5% of the total mass involved. Initial electromagnetic emissions are found to resemble a giant storm common in neutron star binaries, while the overall mass loss behavior exhibits similarities with both supernovae and neutron star collapses. What's more, the researcher discovers that the energy released from this star system could potentially outshine an entire galaxy. Scientific breakthroughs in various fields are significantly driven by AI-driven dataset analysis.  However, training many different types of models on various datasets leads to extensive model and memory requirements. A general-purpose, pre-trained model on a single large dataset, such as the ImageNet dataset, can weigh in at 1.3 GB, but when trained on a specific dataset, some models shrink to 10 MB or less in size.  Currently, there is no standard method for quickly identifying the optimal model configuration and its particular training requirements for a given dataset.  We propose a method, called the Dataset Particular Profiler, to help find the best model and its training settings for a specific dataset by measuring the efficiency of a pre-trained model.  We show the effectiveness of our profiler on various datasets and reveal a significant opportunity to improve AI model analysis through dataset particular profiling. The study first proves that the absence of complete subgraphs in a 4- or 5-colored graph implies its 4- or 5-colorability, and then shows that the presence of near complete subgraphs is sufficient for this colorability. We experimented with an entangled spinor interferometer, specifically a Mach-Zhender interferometer with entangled Rydberg atoms, to see how its performance might be affected. By analyzing the detection noise and considering the specific properties of the entangled state, we developed a method for modifying the input state to optimize its chances of successfully detecting a signal. This optimization strategy involves increasing the probability of finding the atoms in a specific, dimerized state, at the cost of losing some informational value. As a result, our detection sensitivity was improved, to the point where it exceeded what would be expected from either individual atoms flying through the interferometer. This technique could be applied to a wide range of devices, using a variety of entangled states, to enhance their performance and expand their capability. Deep contextualized models have significantly raised the accuracy of NLP dependencies in high resource settings. Nonetheless, their efficacy is limited in low resource settings due to the scarcity of labeled data. This challenge can be addressed by autoencoding, a method that utilizes unlabeled data for self-supervised learning, but existing approaches have been shown to degrade contextualized model performance. We introduce a new autoencoding strategy for contextualized models, one that optimizes them jointly with a dependency parser. This approach, known as Deep Contextualized Auto-training (DCA), offers an efficient solution, underscoring the importance of pretraining contextualized models with both autoencoding and dependency analysis. In our experiments, DCA achieved notable improvements over traditional autoencoding methods, particularly in resource-constrained settings. DCA's effectiveness was further demonstrated across various dependency analysis configurations and institutional RNN, Transformer, and FastTransformer architectures. The code for DCA is available in public repositories. DCA represents an efficient and robust solution for contextualized models in NLP dependencies, empowering practitioners to attain superior performance in low resource settings. DCA has shown the potential to adapt to other NLP tasks by our previous studies on autoencoding. We will test its potential on language modeling in the near future. DCA has significant practical implications, allowing contextualized models to be trained more effectively on limited datasets, thereby facilitating their application in resource-constrained NLP tasks. This is exemplified by our model's success in TagEnglish, a dataset with minimal tags and no labeled per-word annotations. Our model DCA also highlights the effectiveness of early fusion in contextualized models, autoencoding, and dependency analysis. Furthermore, DCA's performance enhancements have been demonstrated to persist in upper-level tasks, such as parsing. Thus, improving contextualized models via DCA has the potential to translate to considerable improvements in the model's performance on a variety of NLP tasks. Our model DCA can be trained with datasets of only 500 sentences, thereby exceeding its previous performance on datasets of 50k sentences. In a compound known for potential Weyl semimetal characteristics, Eu2Ir2O7 has been extensively studied but a key feature of its related series, Eu1-xBix2Ir2O7, has gone uninvestigated until now: the insulator-to-metal shift that occurs as biium is substituted into the compound. To understand this shift, the series was analyzed using HAXPES, which revealed a significant change in the band gap. This has led to the conclusion that the insulator-to-metal transition is driven by the hybridization of biium's 6s and iron's 5d orbitals. This effect is remarkably resilient to changes in the chemical composition and can be seen across the entire series, making it an exceptional phenomenon. Furthermore, the HAXPES analysis has shown that the band gap can be accurately modeled and is heavily influenced by the band structure's topology, particularly in the correlated 5d states. This has implied the presence of strong electron correlations in the system and the potential for topological phenomena to occur. Overall, the investigation has shed new light on the insulator-to-metal shift in Eu1-xBix2Ir2O7 and has provided valuable insights into the underlying quantum phenomena and band structure of the compounds in this series. The study paves the way for further research into the topological properties of the materials and their potential applications in quantum technology. A problem with this approach is that nuclear recoils on the target also cause nuclear fission, which makes it challenging to measure the light atomic particles produced. A proposed method to overcome this limitation involves measuring the Thompson scattering of electrons within the target, allowing the exclusion of nuclear recoils and thus more efficient detection of dark matter particles. In this study, we explore the effects of varying the labor parameter, which represents the strength of the particles' response to their surroundings, on the AOUP's dynamics. Our findings reveal a profound change in the system's behavior as the labor parameter shifts from a high-value regime to a low-value regime. In the high-value regime, the particles exhibit a collective freezing transition, characterized by a sharp increase in their overall polarization when near their environment's boundary. In contrast, the low-value regime shows no evidence of a freezing transition, with the polarized state relaxing more gradually. Additionally, we observe a shift in the system's dynamics from a single, dominant timescale to a more complex structure of timescales, facilitating a deeper understanding of the underlying physics. Our research uses three distinct methods - exact solution, dynamic mean-field theory, and simulations - to study the system's behavior in different regimes. This paper explores the implications of this phenomenon, examines its effects on cross-lingual model transfers, and proposes a framework to mitigate its influence. Our research shows that neural task representations can effectively compensate for the lack of detailed task specifications, and we provide a model-independent framework for cross-lingual transfers that can be adapted to various tasks with minimal adjustments. Our experiments involve transfers between English and 30 other languages, and we evaluate our approach on five different tasks: coref, prop, sst, tag, and nlp-ask. Our results reveal that with neural task representations, model transfers can achieve up to 70% of the performance achieved with direct training on target languages, and we achieve significant improvements over a baseline that relies solely on word embeddings for model transfers, particularly in tasks that require more intricate output responses. Our work addresses the challenge of implementing NLP tasks on datasets in languages in which adequate training data is not available, and we believe that neural task representations offer an effective solution to this problem. Heavy flooding and high winds cause widespread outages, particularly in coastal regions where storm surges exacerbate the situation. Our approach combines meteorological data with advanced flood modeling and power outage assessments to evaluate the effect of storm surges on electrical systems. We applied this method to a hypothetical storm surge event in a fictional coastal city, then applied it to real-life storm data from Hurricane Sandy to predict the extent of power disruptions in the affected area. Our unique methodology accounted for the unique impact of storm surges on electrical systems, ensuring accurate predictions of power outage numbers in line with actual outage reports. This innovative framework has numerous applications, including predictive modeling for utilities and emergency planners, ultimately helping them prepare for the most severe power outage scenarios. We use residual learning to capture the difference in these images to create our style. This style is applied equally to all images to produce the final output. Demos demonstrate the effectiveness of this method. It's also shown to work in the opposite direction, taking a bright image and reducing its dynamic range. The approach is based on the idea that image features are shift invariant, specifically regarding tone mapping. An analysis of our method's robustness to the order of bright and dim images is also provided. Although our method is framed within the context of forward and reverse tone mapping, it can be generalized to other image translation tasks. An implementation of our approach is available online. We discovered that this amount can be as low as Ω(n) for geometric hypergraphs, where n represents the number of vertices of the hypergraph. To achieve this result, we first prove that any geometric hypergraph containing at least 2n edges has a subhypergraph with at most 2n edges that includes all the vertices of the original hypergraph. We then demonstrate that this subhypergraph is also geometric by showing the edges of the subhypergraph can be formed by taking subsets of a set of convex polygons that overlap in certain combinations. We also established a lower bound for the geometricity degree by showing that any geometric hypergraph must have at least 4n edges in order for its edges to form a saturated geometric hypergraph. We arrived at this conclusion after finding that any 2n edges of a geometric hypergraph cannot all be contained within one convex polygon without any of the edges intersecting. We also established upper and lower bounds for the geometricity degree based on other geometricity parameters. Additionally, we found that for geometric hypergraphs with certain properties, such as those formed from triangles, the amount of edges needed can be as high as Ω(n^2) and up to O(n^2) edges. We also studied the amount of edges that need to be eliminated from a geometric hypergraph to constitute a saturated geometric hypergraph that consists of triangles, and found this amount can be as low as Ω(n) and up to O(n) edges. We also established results for geometric hypergraphs with at most k edges per vertex, and found the amount of edges needed can be as low as Ω(n/k) and up to O(n/k) edges. The atomic mass ratio of lithium to vanadium is studied through an examination of its energy levels, where the real part of the $^6$Li-$^51$V interaction is determined by calculating its $\alpha$-cluster components via the Kohn variational method. By utilizing these components in a resonance scattering approach, predicted energy levels of $^7$Li and $^7$V states are obtained, aligning with experimental data. Furthermore, a potential energy surface of $^6$Li+$^51$V is derived, where lithium is considered a zero-point vibrational entity, leading to a discussion on the lixation phenomenon and its connection to quasifission in high-energy collisions. The lixation phenomenon is proposed to result from the zero-point vibrational excitation of the $^6$Li alpha cluster, significantly increasing its interaction with other nucleons and leading to a deeper penetration of the cluster into the $^51$V nucleus. In high-energy collisions, this results in a rapid formation of a tight and high-quasiparticle $^6$Li-$^51$V compound system, which undergoes a smooth transition into a binary quasifission product, ultimately yielding a broader distribution of mass along with increased neutron evaporation. Based on this understanding, it is suggested that the mass ratio should near halve at an $E_{\rm c.m.}$ value around 120 MeV, ultimately dropping below 0.5 above this energy threshold. Lastly, an exploration into the component structure of the $^6$Li-$^51$V interaction via the multichannel Landau-Migdal approach is discussed, which would potentially allow for a more in-depth analysis of the lixation phenomenon, making it a phenomenon that is not just bound to resonance, but also undergoes significant changes throughout the entire energy spectrum of the bounded system. If this is the case, then it would be essential to reevaluate the role of $K$ isomerism in the entire lixation phenomenon. Moreover, it is suggested that the resonantly bounded $^6$Li-$^51$V system might possess certain properties that are typically attributed to diatomic molecules. Therefore, it is proposed that this resonantly bounded system should be named a resonantly bounded dimer (RBD). A recent advancement in robotic research allows robots to efficiently navigate through challenging environments by moving along walls and maintaining a steady grip on surfaces. This paper presents an innovative wall-following algorithm inspired by the behavior of eels as they move through the ocean. This method doesn't need any additional sensors; it uses only a normal camera, allowing robots to accurately keep to walls in complex situations. We also introduced an enhanced grip strategy that increases the robot's ability to adhere to walls, along with a simulation environment where the efficacy of this algorithm is tested and compared with other methods. The research shows that this algorithm is highly adaptable and can effectively navigate a variety of situations. For example, when the robot is moving too fast in relation to its grip, it can adjust its grip to catch up, and the robot can also recover if it loses its grip and falls away from the wall. The algorithm performs well in scenarios where the wall surface is uneven or partially occluded, and it also shows a high level of resilience when the sensor's field of view is limited. The research indicates that this algorithm has numerous applications in a variety of settings. The algorithm will be made publicly available along with our simulation environment, allowing for further testing and validation. This paper outlines a novel approach for identifying the most effective treatments in cases of colon cancer-induced immune reactions. Building on the diversity-theoretic framework introduced in 2018, we extend its application to the colion cancer model. To achieve this, we model the dynamics of both the immune system and colon cancer under a customized treatment, translating these dynamics into a Fokker-Planck equation. Subsequently, we identify the optimal treatment that maximizes cancer elimination while minimizing costs. Due to the complexity of the FP equation, we solve it numerically via Monte Carlo simulations, resulting in a comprehensive set of optimal treatment strategies. Furthermore, our approach allows us to analyze the performance of various treatment combinations. Notably, our research can be generalized to other disease models, enabling the discovery of customized treatments in a range of applications. We illustrate the utility of our approach by identifying the optimal treatment for an specific colon cancer-induced immune reaction, resulting in a measurable quantitative value that can be utilized in subsequent research on optimal treatment identification. We strongly believe that our approach will pave the way for groundbreaking discoveries in the field of treatment optimization. The proposed algorithm offers a versatile solution that is applicable to various D2D scheduling strategies, and has been validated by showing an improvement in sum data transfer rate and lower complex computation over other traditional methods. Furthermore, the results reveal a rapid decrease in computational complexity allowing for fast and efficient computation. The outcome is a substantial improvement in data transfer rate with minimal increased computational complexity. The findings suggest that deep learning can enable real-time scheduling in high-speed and large-scale wireless networks, enabling efficient data transfer and message exchange. The outcome offers a promising direction for future research in using deep learning for scheduling in D2D wireless networks, and the results can be further utilized in various D2D application scenarios. Calculations in the framework of post-Newtonian theory provide precise predictions for the high-speed motions of binary compact objects, offering a valuable alternative to numerical simulations at least through the point of gravitational wave detection. In this work, we use these theory-based predictions to examine how the remaining eccentricity of an inspiraling binary compact object system evolves during the late stages of its orbit, specifically when its orbital distance is greater than five times the distance at which the gravitational wave signal is initially detected. Our analysis focuses on the following factors: how remaining eccentricity varies according to the nature of the compact objects (black holes and neutron stars), and how it is affected by the gravitational waves emitted during the late inspiral phase. By comparing our theory-based predictions to the predictions generated through 34 new numerical simulations, we find that they closely match at least up to an orbital distance of equal to the distance at which the gravitational wave signal is initially detected. In the case of equal-mass black hole systems, the following factors influence the rate at which remaining eccentricity declines: gravity wave radiation, accretion, and viscosity. In the late stages of its orbit, an inspiraling binary compact object that consists of two black holes experiences a sharp decrease in remaining eccentricity. This decrease is primarily attributed to the emission of gravitational waves, although the effect is most pronounced when the orbital speed is below approximately one-thousandth of the speed of light, at which point the influence of radiation on the orbit becomes negligible. In contrast, an inspiraling black hole-neutron star binary exhibits a more complex behavior in its late stages, at which point it is influenced by a number of factors, including but not limited to gravity wave radiation, accretion, and viscosity, as well as variations in the structure of the neutron star. In the case of neutron star binaries, the effect of viscoelasticity is particularly pronounced, at which point it is primarily responsible for a sharp decrease in remaining eccentricity when the orbital speed is below approximately one-thousandth of the speed of light. In binary compact objects that consist of black holes and neutron stars, the effect of viscoelasticity is also significant, at which point it is primarily responsible for a sharp decrease in remaining eccentricity when the orbital speed is below approximately one-thousandth of the speed of light. The FELO, functioning as a laser, supplies the necessary seed for a free-electron laser (FEL) to reach its gain threshold, enabling the production of highly coherent X-ray pulses. The effectiveness of this approach was evaluated using the SARAYA 8.5 plasma accelerator, a state-of-the-art facility for generating high-brilliance FEL pulses, and comparisons were made with conventional FEL parameters. The concept of combining an FELO and an energy booster has also been explored, leading to the expectation of an X-ray pulse with an exceptionally high degree of coherence and an increased central energy relative to a conventional FEL driver. This research focuses on identifying unusual events within a temporal network, specifically to recognize incident occurrences within a safety monitoring system. Current methods for detecting anomalies in temporal networks fall into two categories: those considering temporal relationships and those considering network structure, but not both simultaneously. In contrast, this study aims to identify incidents by incorporating both aspects. First, we use deep learning to create safe condition models from normal incident data, then evaluate candidate trigger patterns triggered by incident occurrence and localized within a safety dynamic network. Due to the non-stationary properties of incident data, this study proposes the Dynamic Anomaly Subgraph problem. An efficient algorithm based on the Occlusion technique, called OCBN, as well as a convolutional neural network called DSN, are designed to solve this problem. By testing these methods on artificial data and significantly contributing to the recognition of incidents in real-world scenarios with our knowledge, this study showcases promising results and suggests valuable future research directions. Artificial data is employed to evaluate the performance of our methods due to the lack of extensive incident data, but this research does offer a valuable contribution to both anomaly detection and incident identification in a real-world setting. Additionally, this study has practical implications, as it has successfully detected incidents in real-world scenarios with our knowledge, indicating the potential of this research to improve safety monitoring systems. While deep learning methods may demand significant amounts of data, this study demonstrates that its approaches can produce results in real-world scenarios, even with limited data availability, by testing them on artificial data. In contrast, traditional methods may struggle to achieve the same level of performance, as they were tested using artificial data. Thus, this research not only validates the use of deep learning methods for detecting incidents but also showcases their efficacy, especially when tested on artificial data. Ultimately, this study Resolves dynamic anomaly detection, while offering new possibilities for safe monitoring systems. In conclusion, this research has successfully identified incidents in various real-world scenarios, as demonstrated with our knowledge, while also testing and evaluating the performance of its methods using artificial data. By doing so, this study has not only validated the use of deep learning methods for detecting incidents but also showcased their potential to improve safety monitoring systems. Therefore, this research has contributed to the development of new methods for detecting incidents. The growing presence of artificial intelligence systems has led to a corresponding need for their explanations. Since users may interact with these systems in various capacities, a one-size-fits-all approach to explaining their decisions or outcomes is impractical. We propose that requirements engineering can play a crucial role in helping developers create tailored explanation methods that cater to the diverse needs and expectations of users. By centering on the user perspective, we identify three primary concerns - transparency, accountability, and reliability - that serve as the building blocks for constructing explanation requirements. We utilize a practical approach, employing two real-world case studies, to demonstrate how existing problems related to explainability can be addressed by incorporating the user perspective in the explanation requirements engineering process. Through this, we contribute three-key lessons learned that can guide the application of requirements engineering in addressing the lagging explainability of state-of-the-art AI systems. Ultimately, this research outcome will enable AI developers to consult the user-centric explanation requirements and bridge the current gap between AI systems and their capacity to provide transparent and understandable decision-making logic or outcomes. With this in mind, this research has potential implications for improving user understanding in various areas, such as interactions with search engines, medical diagnostics, and predictive legal analyses. We conclude by highlighting potential future avenues for research, such as the investigation of user-centric explanation methods and the promotion of explainability across the entire AI lifecycle. We envision this research space to evolve further. Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically is crucial to understand their potential for cancer development and metamorphosis. Visualizing and analyzing these polyps requires expertise in histology and pathology. The process of pathologic analysis can be automated using deep learning, but first, a comprehensive dataset, including high-resolution images of colorectal lesions along with their corresponding diagnoses, is needed. This paper introduces UniToPatho, a comprehensive dataset consisting of over 20,000 H&E stained images, labeled and annotated by qualified pathologists. This dataset serves as a resource for developing and training machine learning models that can facilitate colorectal polyp classification and adenoma dysplasia evaluation. Our findings, based on the Bessel correction principle, indicate that the models trained on UniToPatho achieve superior performance compared to previous studies. The dataset is accessible at https://itb-histo-paths.github.io/UnitoPatho/index.html.

Deep learning-based solutions for Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) image processing have gained significant traction recently, yet deep model training is often hindered by a lack of large-scale, manually labeled datasets for SAR images. This problem is particularly evident in super-resolution tasks for SAR images. To overcome this challenge, this research proposes MrSARP, a novel generative architecture that integrates multiple levels of complexity for learning SAR image patterns. By leveraging a combination of reserved information and a hidden semi-supervised encoder, MrSARP addresses the issue of limited labeled data by reserving a portion of the input data for its encoder to learn from. This research evaluates the performance of MrSARP on a large dataset comprising over 300,000 training images and achieves impressive results on various metrics, surpassing state-of-the-art ARSNet and PFDNN models significantly. Notably, MrSARP's performance surpasses that of PFDNN, a model that employs Precedent-Focused Self-Attention with four times the parameters, in numerous tests. As a versatile model, MrSARP is expected to have far-reaching applications and implications in various fields that rely heavily on large datasets. This research demonstrates MrSARP's effectiveness on raw SAR data and adjacent fields, such as Coherent and Polarimetric SAR, and is likely to have a positive impact on resolving related challenges in these areas. MrSARP's open-source code and related data can be accessed via the link: https://github.com/cloakware/MrSARP. Additionally, the generated SAR images are available for download at: download.mrsarp.com. Experimental findings and additional information can be found on the project website: mrsarp.com. Lastly, a demo video showcasing the performance of MrSARP is available at: vid.mrsarp.com. This research aims to bridge the existing gap by providing a solution to the issue of limited labeled data for SAR images and presents a new standard for deep learning-based solutions in this domain. Open electrical systems can be modeled as having sources that drive current into networks consisting of resistive loops.  This modeling is part of a larger body of work known as random thermodynamics.  By treating the electrical current as a control parameter, it is possible to examine how systems respond to varying drives.  When this approach is applied to optimal driving techniques, it yields systems that exhibit maximum efficiency and optimal behavior. The efficient transfer of acoustic waves between adjacent materials is a crucial factor in numerous advanced technologies such as ultrasonic testing, biomedical imaging, and surface acoustic wave devices. Two factors significantly influence the transmission of acoustic waves: the direct coupling between the wavefront and the surface of the receiver, and the effect of the launched surface wave on the sender. Although the first factor can be optimized through refinement of the receiver surface, the second factor remains a persistent challenge. Researchers have recently made significant progress in understanding and overcoming this challenge, especially in relation to the transmission between piezoelectric materials. This article discusses the fundamental principles and the role of poling in the transmission of acoustic waves between adjacent piezoelectric materials, including examples that demonstrate near-complete transmission efficiency despite the thin air gap between them. Furthermore, the article highlights the mechanism by which the transmitted acoustic waves can become trapped in the receiver, a phenomenon that may be exploited in the development of innovative devices and sensors. Ultimately, this research is expected to contribute to the creation of highly efficient, innovative ultrasonic devices. My argument departs from the conventional view that Galileo was a proponent of
the mathematical method because I believe he was actually indifferent to it.
Galileo's own scientific approach is ill-defined if we reduce it solely to being
mathematical, as his main goal was to accumulate philosophical evidence to
support his core theses about the physical world. Through a detailed analysis of
his main scientific works, I demonstrate that Galileo relied on diverse logical
strategies, including both mathematical and non-mathematical methods, in his
endeavor to gather data that would convince other philosophers. The main non-
mathematical tool he used was analogical reasoning, which he considered
legitimate within the framework of natural philosophy. Ignoring the distinction
between mathematics and philosophy would distort the historical context of the
Scientific Revolution and lead to an inaccurate understanding of Galileo's own
role in it. Galileo's true contribution was to promote the non-empiristic aspect
of natural philosophy, not through his own evidence gathering procedures but
rather through his non-mathematical recommendations for how to conduct further
investigations. These recommendations, which I call "explanatory probes," were
intended not only to stimulate other inquisitors but also to demonstrate
that, as a philosopher, Galileo was in a better position to guide the entire
community. As such, the character of the Scientific Revolution was shaped by
Galileo's indifference to the mathematical method just as much as by his promotion
of the mathematical method, and this has significant implications for contemporary
discussions about the relationship between science and philosophy. In particular,
I believe that that relationship is more complex and nuanced than is commonly
acknowledged, and that Galileo's example teaches us that even the most
successful inquisitors may not always make the best investigators. Therefore,
even in the present day, scientists should not automatically become philosophers
at all, as their contributions to our understanding of the natural world may
be more significant if they were to focus on what I call "explanatory probes" rather
than engaging in reflections on first principles. Ultimately, I believe that
Galileo's indifference to the mathematical method offers us a fresh perspective
on the Scientific Revolution and its significance for modern-day debates. The
character of the Scientific Revolution was shaped not only by Galileo's promotion
of the mathematical method but also by his indifference to it, as well as by the
debates between two main philosophical camps

The analysis of magnetic island behavior during reconnection events has been advanced through the use of a novel computational model. This model integrates magnetohydrodynamics with the option for embedded Particle-In-Cell simulations on an adaptive grid. By dynamically allocating computational resources to areas of the simulation domain where the magnetic field complexity and energy production converge, this model achieves significant performance enhancements. In the course of reconnection studies, our method proves to be an effective and efficient solution that resolves the two primary limitations - a fixed spatial resolution and a fixed time step - inherent in traditional magnetohydrodynamics. As a result, our model yields highly precise and detailed insights into the full spectrum of reconnection phenomena, including the distinct characteristics of Sweet-Parker and null-point reconnections, the behavior of magnetic islands, and the emergence of energetic particles. Additionally, our model facilitates a significant increase in the domain size that can be simulated while maintaining a detailed resolution, thus paving the way for an in-depth examination of the role of magnetic islands in reconnection. Specifically, our model predicts a timeline for magnetic island merging that is influenced by an island's size, the reconnection rate, and local turbulence levels. Furthermore, our study confirms that magnetic island merging is a two-stage process, comprising an initial coalescence and a secondary turbulent phase. In conclusion, our model demonstrates that magnetic island behavior is primarily governed by an interaction between an island's inherent instability and the surrounding turbulent environment, rather than solely by inherent instability. We introduce Scribe, a novel system that makes program transformation accessible to users, encompassing a wide range of scenarios such as program rewriting, simplification, and element-level generalization. By leveraging Scribe, users can create customized training data for neural programers, enabling these models to acquire the skills of experienced programmers. Additionally, Scribe facilitates the application of programmatic reasoning techniques to the training of neural programs, thereby granting them the benefits of structural analysis. We illustrate the effectiveness of Scribe through its integration with the NPAPT framework, demonstrating its potential to enhance the capabilities of neural programs. Furthermore, Scribe is designed as an open-source extension to Python, making it easily integratable into various deep learning frameworks and accommodating a variety of training techniques. To showcase its potential, we present three concrete examples of Scribe-based program transformers, each serving a distinct purpose: (i) an automatic code reviewer; (ii) a neural-based code refactoring tool; and (iii) a program generalizer. These examples serve as a starting point, and we envision Scribe supporting a multitude of further use cases. We experimentally verified the feasibility and efficacy of Scribe, findings that can be summarized as follows: (a) Scribe-based training significantly enhances the performance of neural programs; (b) the efficacy of Scribe surpasses that of alternative methods relying on human intervention; and (c) the effects of Scribe persist even in scenarios with limited program transformation. To stimulate future research, we open-source Scribe and make it available to the public under the terms of the permissive BSD-3 license.
